#6422. Why do flamingos dance while they eat? This scientist found out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Erin Garcia de Jesús, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

On a family trip to Atlanta, Víctor Ortega Jiménez spent time taking pictures and videos of flamingos as they fed in their pond. It wasn’t to admire their long legs or flamboyant pink color. Instead, he noticed the “beautiful” ripples spreading across the water as the birds ate under the surface. But he didn’t know why the waves were happening.

It took “more than four years to answer that question,” says Ortega Jiménez, of the University of California, Berkeley. “But I think the answer was fascinating.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Ortega Jiménez’s focus is biomechanics, or the study of how mechanics applies to animal movement and structure. His goal is to understand how animal behaviors might lead to human-made engineering feats.

He discovered that, by retracting their heads, flamingos produce vortexlike traps with water to scoop up algae. They stomp around — or dance, if you will — amplifying the vortex. The series of motions brings the food to their crooked beaks. The beaks then filter in food, releasing silt and mud.

The impressive process can weed out particles the size of a single cell. This kind of self-cleaning filter for extremely small particles can be applied to remove microplastics and so-called forever chemicals called PFAS from water, Ortega Jiménez says.

“Nature is always full of secrets,” he says. “And I think that’s the riddle that keeps me going, trying to understand nature. That’s my way to see science: by observation and trying to be inspired and trying to solve a problem.”

#6421. The 6 Best Electric Snowblowers Are Plenty Powerful—and Quieter Alternatives to Gas Models

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Two more reasons to go green: Battery-powered outdoor equipment is also easier to operate and store.

If you’re looking for the quickest, least labor-intensive way to dig out after a big snowstorm this winter, a snowblower is it. While it’s only fall, it’s not too early to think about getting a snow blower if you found yourself wanting one during last year’s winter storms but struggled to find a retailer that wasn’t already out of stock. Getting ahead of the game is a good idea.

Electric models are more capable than ever, and in some cases meet or exceed their gas-powered brethren in some respects. Cordless, battery-electric blowers can clear a path up to roughly 2 feet wide through as much as 20 inches of snow. They start with the push of a button, require less maintenance than gas machines, and run relatively quietly. They’re also easier to store than their gas-powered counterparts.

Ahead, we review both two-stage snow blowers and single-stage snow throwers and recommend models from Toro, Ego, Milwaukee, and more.

Our selections for this list are based on our years of testing snow blowers of all varieties. Most of these examples we’ve tested in the last few years, and others are updated versions of models we’ve tested. We are also planning for a substantial update to this guide in the coming weeks with new models.

Tony Carrick, the original author of this article, is a regular PopMech contributor and writes about everything from landscaping to home improvement. He grew up in rural Pennsylvania, where he became well-acquainted with blizzards and the backbreaking labor of digging out after them. His recommendations are based on his personal experience testing snow blowers at home, along with plenty of research to inform the picks. He compared specs for a variety of corded and cordless models, while also plowing through recommendations and feedback from dozens of customer reviews.

Electric snow blowers may not be able to match the power of their gas-powered counterparts, but this self-propelled two-stage model from Ryobi comes close. It sports four rechargeable 40-volt 6-Ah batteries, which Ryobi claims can power the snow blower for up to 45 minutes, and move the same amount of snow as a 252-cc gas-powered two-stage snow blower. It has the power to scoop up a path that’s 24 inches wide and 21 inches deep, then chuck it up to 55 feet away.

We’re also impressed with the cockpit, which allows you to control the speed of the drive wheels and the auger, change the direction of the chute, and toggle the LED headlights without missing a beat. The handlebar even heats up so your hands don’t get numb as you're working.

Our only concern is with the charger. While we like the fact that this Ryobi supports rapid charging, the charger only has two slots, which means you’ll have to go through two rounds of recharging before you’re back to full power.

We like Ego’s battery-powered outdoor equipment because it’s among the best when it comes to power and run time—and this two-stage snow blower is no exception. With its two 56-volt, 7.5-Ah batteries and 24-inch-wide intake, the Power+ SNT2405 can clear an 8-inch layer of snow from an 18-car driveway on a single charge.

We also like the cockpit on this self-propelled machine. You can change speeds while in forward or reverse, adjust the auger speed, and change the chute direction all without having to leave the controls. It also comes equipped with four bright LED headlights, useful in the event your snow clearing efforts take you past sundown.

We also like the fact that Ego uses mostly steel construction with this machine, so you can expect it to hold up for many a winter.

Ego claims its 21-inch Power+ snow blower can throw snow up to 40 feet with a 180-degree, adjustable chute, which is pretty far for a cordless machine. In the wet sawdust test, we were able to throw 24 feet with the heavier, denser material—longer distances are certainly achievable with lighter, drier snow. It took the Power+ 4 minutes 16 seconds to clear the sawdust down to pavement in our area test.

Like most single-stage blowers, the Power+ is not self-propelled, so we needed to push it into the snow. In our dense, heavy sawdust, that took some effort to make forward progress. It’s not a bad thing, though, as it makes it easier to prevent the machine from digging in too deep and bogging down. In very wet or ice-packed snow, we expect you’ll have to put in a similar effort.

The Power+ has a variable-speed auger, so we were able to adjust speed for the conditions and conserve battery when less power was needed. There isn’t too much to worry about in the battery department, since it comes with two 5-Ah batteries, enough to clear 8 inches of snow on a 12-car driveway—that’s six cars long by two cars wide.

The Power+ comes with a dual-port charger, so the two batteries can be charged simultaneously to get you ready for the next round faster. Ego rounds things out with front-mounted LEDs for low-light and dark conditions, plus an easy-folding handle for stowing the unit when not in use.

If you don’t relish the idea of pushing heavy machinery through heavy snow, Snow Joe makes a lightweight single-stage snow blower that’s fairly easy to push around. At less than 38 pounds with batteries installed, the Snow Joe 24V-X2-SB18 is easy to roll out of storage, push down the driveway, and maneuver through turns.

The scraper bar clears snow right down to the pavement, and it can launch snow up to 20 feet away. On top of that, it’s very cheap—one of the most affordable cordless snow blowers we’ve found.

Unsurprisingly, that light weight and low price come with some compromises. The 18-inch-wide chute cuts a narrow path, so you’ll need to take a few extra passes to get the job done right compared to a wider machine. Meanwhile, its two 24-volt batteries offer a modest 40-minute run time.

Combine those two things, and the 24V-X2-SB18 is best reserved for smaller jobs like clearing decks, walkways, and compact driveways. If that’s what you need, though, it makes snow removal cheap and easy.

The 60-volt 26-inch Power Max e26 is one of the models we tested in November 2025, and it’s among the burliest two-stage cordless snow blowers we’ve used. It is built virtually the same as a gas model, except with an electric motor and two batteries. That includes the frame, drive system, auger, and auger housing.

Since it’s built the same, we can confirm it performs the same—so it could easily replace a similar gas model. No caveats here; the Power Max e26 isn’t a compromise in any significant way that we could determine. It comes with two batteries and a (claimed) runtime up to 70 minutes—enough to clear a driveway 30 car spaces long.

Operating the Power Max e26 was a pleasant experience, if you can call snow blowing pleasant. It has effective heated hand grips, and an axle with a differential that allows you to turn quickly, on a dime—no having to muscle it around.

The e26 easily handled our testing with wet sawdust, throwing it far enough to cross an average driveway—even when making a full 26-inch-wide pass. If you’ve questioned whether a cordless snow blower could ever be as good as a gas machine, the e26 answers that affirmatively.

Milwaukee’s M18 single-stage snow blower is the second machine we tested in November 2025, and it also impressed us. It's noticeably heavier than many other similar cordless models, which seems to be due to its metal frame. At 90 pounds, it isn’t heavy, at least in comparison to two-stage machines, but the weight is an advantage, helping prevent the blower from bouncing around or riding up when encountering denser, crusty snow.

We tested this snow blower with wet sawdust, which always presents a little bit of a challenge with single-stage snow blowers, as they have to lift the snow and eject it in one operation. Milwaukee’s M18 blower did this well enough in testing—and if it can throw wet sawdust, it will really throw the snow.

To facilitate ejecting snow, the M18’s chute is wider than that of most other models. This eliminates potential bottlenecks and ultimately clogs, where the snow passes from the blower body into the chute. Milwaukee's single auger is edged with a rubber paddle that both sweeps the pavement clean and pulls the machine forward. It does this well enough that, in some instances, we had to hold it back a little in testing.

The chute has a remote adjustment—you can crank a knob just below the handlebar to change the direction of the chute, allowing you to put snow where it needs to go. However, ejection elevation is manually adjusted at the top of the chute—but this isn't something you typically need to adjust as often.

Milwaukee claims the M18 blower can clear up to 11 parking places, or 500 feet of sidewalk on the two included 12.0-Ah batteries. But with two extra battery ports, you can double the runtime by adding another pair of batteries. We’ll be testing this more as we have snow available.

There are two types of snow blowers for homeowners, based on the number of “stages” in the mechanical process they use to collect and distribute snow.

Single-stage snow blowers have an auger that pulls the snow into a large intake at the front of the snow blower, and propels it out of a chute mounted to the top of the machine. Single-stage blowers, also frequently referred to as “snow throwers,” are small, lightweight and easy to maneuver, making them ideal for clearing light snowfall and smaller driveways and walks.

Dual-stage snow blowers, as the name suggests, have a two-stage process for collecting and expelling snow. Like single-stage models, they have an auger that pulls snow into the intake. The dual-stage snow blower follows up by pushing the snow into an impeller that ejects it out through the chute.

The one-two punch of auger and impeller allows a two-stage snow blower to remove more snow quicker, and throw it a longer distance. That makes them perfect for large driveways. That said, they are larger and heavier than single-stage machines, so they may not be able to maneuver around narrow walking paths as easily.

The width and depth of a snow blower’s intake determine how much snow it can move with each pass, and thus, how long it takes you to get the job done. Most single-stage electric snow blowers have a clearing width of around 20 inches and a clearing depth of around 8 inches. That’s good for carving out walks and medium-sized areas. Some heavy-duty two-stage electric snow blowers can remove a 24-inch-wide and 20-inch-deep swath of snow, which will make quick work of a large driveway.

Throwing distance refers to how far a snow blower can launch snow out of the chute. This gives you a sense of how to plan when and how you’ll dispose of the snow in your path. The average single-stage snow blower typically has a short throwing distance—around 25 feet. Unsurprisingly, a two-stage snow blower can send its snow as far as 50 feet.

Snow blowers typically have a throttle that allows you to change their mechanical speed, which will adjust how far it throws your snow. There are also controls that allow you to rotate the chute to change the direction of the flow of snow. If you can map out your snow-blowing route, check and make sure your snow blower throws the snow far enough to keep it out of your way until it melts.

Most electric snow blowers receive power from multiple large rechargeable batteries, which allow them to produce nearly as much power as a gas snow blower. No battery supplies uninterrupted power for as long as a tank of gas, though: On average, you should expect a battery-powered snow blower to run for about 30 to 45 minutes on a single charge. You can extend that time if you have multiple batteries, but the low run time still caps how much ground they can cover.

Though we largely consider them to be obsolete, some manufacturers also still produce corded electric snow blowers, which plug into a standard electrical outlet. They’re often cheaper than battery-powered models and run as long as you need them to. However, having a power cord substantially reduces their range: You will likely need to purchase an extension cord to extend its reach slightly beyond the length of the area you need to clear. No matter how much slack you have, though, the cable makes the whole process a little more awkward.

“Cordless snow blowers are easier, better, and safer to use,” says Popular Mechanics Test Editor Brad Ford. “Corded is old, out-of-date tech in most cases.”

They’re also limited to smaller, 15-amp motors that run on the power an outlet can provide. That usually translates to narrower clearing widths, shallower clearing depths, and shorter throw distances. Unless you have a very tight budget, we highly recommend going with a battery-powered electric snow blower rather than a corded one.

The most important thing you can do to keep your electric snow blower running season after season is to simply make sure that you store your charger and batteries indoors when you aren’t charging or using them. Lithium cells aren't able to hold the same amount of charge when the temperature drops below freezing. By storing and charging those batteries indoors, you’ll get the most run time out of them.

If you use a corded snow blower, you shouldn’t plug it into any old extension cord. These machines draw a lot of power, and not every cord can handle it. Using the wrong one can create a fire hazard or damage your snow blower. Make sure to check your snow blower’s specs before buying an extension cord to pair with it, so you can be sure it can handle its amperage.

Most corded electric snow blowers have a 12-amp rating, in which case you’ll want a 12-gauge extension cord that can provide at least 12 amps of power. You’ll also want to make sure it’s long enough for you to reach the far end of whatever walkway or road you plan to clear, preferably with some slack to spare for maneuverability. We recommend starting with 100 feet and scaling up based on your property.

Regardless, it would be wise to buy an extension cord to match the specs you need for your snow blower, rather than using one that you happen to have lying around.

With advancements in battery technology, there are now powerful two-stage cordless snow blowers capable of clearing deeper, heavier snow.

That said, the most powerful electric snow blowers still don’t match the snow-moving capabilities of the largest gas-powered snow blowers on the market. The most powerful electric snow blowers work best at maximum depths of about a foot, while some gas-powered models can clear snow up to 2 feet deep.

People who had no recollection of a lucid dream over the past three years developed the skill after one month of performing a novel training regimen twice a week, neuroscientists report.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming — in which the dreamer is aware that they are dreaming and can sometimes influence the dream's trajectory — is a skill that can be honed, a new study finds. And the researchers found that doing this is surprisingly easy, after training participants to do exactly that using virtual reality (VR) twice a week for just one month.

The study's results could have practical benefits, said Daniel Morris, a cognitive neuroscientist at Northwestern University who studies dreams and was not involved with the work. "Lucid dreaming can benefit people with nightmares by allowing them to transform their nightmares into positive dreams and feel greater agency in their dreams," Morris told Live Science in an email.

Before this study, published Sept. 28 in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, neuroscientists tried to induce lucid dreaming with various methods. These included meditation exercises and so-called reality checks, in which participants ask themselves while awake whether unusual phenomena they encounter — such as people wearing odd Halloween costumes — are real or if they're dreaming. The idea is that they will ask themselves the same question in their sleep during bizarre dreams.

However, "for most people, our day-to-day lives may not feel 'dream-like,'" Morris said, explaining why reality checks have had mixed results and don't reliably trigger lucid dreaming.

Since dream-like scenarios are rare in waking life, the neuroscientists behind the new study used VR simulations of bizarre situations to complement reality-check exercises.

The team, based at the University of Trento in Italy, recruited university students and asked them to meditate and then perform the VR training. The meditation was intended to increase students' awareness of what they were thinking about in a given moment. Each time they encountered bizarre happenings in the VR environment, such as objects or people violating laws of physics or rapid switches from one scene to another, they performed reality checks.

After the training, participants went home and were asked to keep a dream diary that they wrote in every morning. They also filled out daily questionnaires, citing the number of dreams they recalled and how many they remembered being lucid.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The participants experienced lucid dreams four times more often than participants did in a second group that did reality checks without performing any meditation or VR training. The study also included another comparison group, in which participants carried out reality checks during realistic rather than dream-like VR simulations; these participants were over eight times less likely to report lucid dreams. This latter comparison ensured that the results were not caused solely by the use of VR, the researchers said.

When participants encountered something strange, like branches covering a door, they actively asked themselves whether it was real.

It was particularly surprising to find that such little training with the dream-like VR simulations was needed to develop lucid dreaming as a skill, said study co-author Nicola De Pisapia, a neuroscientist at the University of Trento. His team ran the experiment for only a month because any longer would have been too demanding for the participants, De Pisapia noted.

Study co-author Andrea Signorelli, a doctoral student in De Pisapia's lab, thinks the VR intervention is at the heart of why the approach worked. People often don't realize that they're dreaming because the dreams "fool" your senses and feel realistic in the moment, he explained.

"Virtual reality is the technology to fool you on stereoscopic vision and auditory information," he said. The term "stereoscopic" refers to techniques that create 3D illusions from 2D images by mimicking how human eyes see.

"It's basically the most immersive technology that we have at the moment," making it a good intervention for reality check exercises, Signorelli said.

The team also compared the number of lucid dreams participants reported against their total number of recalled dreams, which revealed an interesting pattern. On average, participants in each group recalled more dreams after starting the experiment than they did beforehand. However, the dream-simulating VR group recalled the fewest dreams overall after entering the experiment, even though they had the highest number of lucid dreams.

Signorelli speculated that perhaps it takes a lot of energy to have lucid dreams, which could divert resources away from recalling other dreams. Morris argued that, alternatively, participants in the lucid-dream VR group "may have been less motivated to report non-lucid dreams than the control groups." So there may have been some bias in the reporting.

The study had some limitations, such as its small sample size of 38 participants. Plus, neither of the two control groups were asked to meditate, so it is impossible to say whether the meditations or the dreamlike VR sessions had more influence over lucid dreaming in the test group.

The team is now doing a follow-up study in which the meditation part has been removed, Signorelli said, to reveal whether the VR dream scenarios are the critical factor, as suspected.

Signorelli said that he would like to see lucid-dream training tailored for each individual. For example, the VR simulations could be personalized to simulate a recurrent nightmare that a given person experiences, training them to recognize triggers specific to that dream, he said.

"Other future research could explore the potential therapeutic benefits of this intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety, or PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder]," Morris suggested.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Signorelli, A., Tormen, F., Dal Bianco, B., & De Pisapia, N. (2026). Virtual reality as a metacognitive training tool for lucid dreaming. Frontiers in Psychology, 17(1924370). https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1924370

#6419. America’s Next Catastrophic Industrial Disaster May Already Be Underway

As fiercer storms collide with an aging industrial system, a unique kind of catastrophe is becoming more commonplace—and no one, it seems, is fully prepared to stop it.

On August 24, 2020, as Tropical Storm Laura churned up fury and foam in the Gulf of Mexico, employees at BioLab Inc. were racing to fill the trailers backed into the loading docks of the chlorine plant, located just outside of Lake Charles, Louisiana, with pallets of woven sacks. Each sack was stuffed with 2,750 pounds of granulated trichloroisocyanuric acid—trichlor for short—a chemical used to kill algae and bacteria in swimming pools. Trichlor dissolved slowly when submerged in water, the employees had learned in their annual safety training, but became hot enough to explode when exposed to small amounts of it—say, a slow leak or shallow flood, the kind of damage that might happen in a coastal region during a Category 4 storm.

By the next day Laura was officially a hurricane, and about 825,000 pounds of trichlor had left the warehouse, bound for a BioLab facility in Conyers, Georgia. Employees waited for the last two trucks that would carry the remaining one million pounds of the hazardous chemical to higher ground. But those trucks never arrived.

The plant’s 111-person staff had been whittled down to a hurricane crew, nine workers assigned to monitor the facility on-site during a storm. They arrived around 5 p.m. and began slinging sandbags and securing loose items. As the majority of Calcasieu Parish residents sat in long lines of traffic pointing away from the coast, the crew heaved the remaining 500 tons of trichlor on top of triple-stacked pallets—the idea was to keep the trichlor dry if floodwater did infiltrate the building. Plus, they’d be around if anything went wrong during the storm.

But as the sun rose the following morning, the solemn TV meteorologists all said the same thing: The impacts of Hurricane Laura, which became the strongest hurricane to strike Southwest Louisiana since the U.S. started keeping official records in 1851, would be “unsurvivable.” By 9:30 a.m., BioLab management had directed the hurricane crew to lock up the facility and evacuate with the rest of their neighbors.

So no one was in the warehouse during the early morning hours of Thursday, August 27, when Laura’s vicious, 150-mile-per-hour winds plucked portions of the roof off the building. No one was there to hear the drops of rain pelting those woven sacks of pool chemicals, to hear the pellets inside begin to crackle and hiss. No one saw those first few licks of flame, the first gust of black, poisonous smoke that would soon darken the sky.

“It smelled like if you took a swimming pool of human hair and lit it on fire,” remembers John O’Donnell, who arrived in Lake Charles later that morning to check on his house after the storm had passed. “I’ll never be able to forget what that smell smelled like.”

O’Donnell’s own roof had been damaged, but now his more pressing concern was the curdling, cast-iron cloud of chlorine gas that hovered over the town. Once used as a weapon of terror during WWI, chlorine can cause an array of symptoms including vomiting, blisters, shortness of breath, and burning pain in the lungs, throat, nose, and eyes.

As O’Donnell’s eyes began to burn, a photojournalist covering the hurricane wandered into his driveway. “What is that?” the photojournalist asked, looking skyward.

“That’s why your phone is about to go off,” said 33-year-old O’Donnell, a disaster recovery strategist who grew up in Southwest Louisiana, a storm-battered region dotted with petrochemical plants and emergency sirens. Just then, the shelter-in-place alert O’Donnell predicted blared from their phones. But shelter where? Six months into the COVID-19 pandemic, lockdown mandates had eased, but congregating indoors was still a bad idea. Anyway, it was 80-something degrees, and there wasn’t a building for miles that had electricity or water.

O’Donnell got back in his car and headed “as far away . . . as possible,” he says, a challenge given the debris and downed trees that lay strewn across the roads. “That was a really scary moment for everybody.”

It was a terrifying scene—but not an isolated one. For decades, experts have warned about the looming threat of so-called Natech disasters—technological failures triggered by natural hazards. The 1972 flood that ruptured a West Virginia coal slurry impoundment, destroying 550 homes and killing 125 people. The 1994 Southern California earthquake that shattered an oil pipeline, sending nearly 200,000 gallons of crude oil into a nearby river. The 9.0 earthquake off the coast of Japan in 2011 that produced a rare, double-wave tsunami, causing a meltdown at Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant in what is now considered one of the world’s most destructive nuclear catastrophes and the most expensive disaster in modern history.

As climate change drives more extreme weather, the conditions that produce these cascading disasters are becoming more common. “There are few events that are only natural disasters now,” says Liesel Ritchie, PhD, a sociologist at Virginia Tech who studies their social impacts. “And the more technology advances, the more likely these tightly coupled systems are to fail.” Yet even as the risks grow, readiness has not kept pace. Experts like Ritchie say the country remains woefully unprepared. The focus is still on natural disasters, she says, “because Natech events seem to be so rare.”

But they may not be as rare as we think. And across the country, millions of people live and work near industrial facilities like the one in Lake Charles, often unaware how vulnerable they are.

In 1994, Pamela Sands Showalter, then a University of Toledo geographer, and the late Mary Fran Myers, a disaster researcher at the University of Colorado, wrote in the journal Risk Analysis that “the number of incidents where natural and technological disasters interact is rising while preparations, which recognize the complications inherent in such combined events, remain cursory.”

As evidence, these preeminent disaster scholars pointed to the results of a survey they had conducted of emergency management agencies in 20 states that revealed an emerging trend in the number of chemical, oil, and radiological releases caused by natural disasters during the preceding 10 years. The results also showed that few legislative bodies had even considered the risk, let alone addressed it.

“Natech” disasters, as Showalter and Myers first called them, were “a growing, but as yet unstudied problem.”

Three-plus decades later, not much has changed. The risk of Natech disasters continues to grow, while efforts to prevent or prepare for them have largely stalled.

Between 1990 and 2017, Natech events essentially doubled in the U.S. In 2017, Hurricane Harvey caused 46 chemical leaks and nearly 100 hazardous substance spills. In 2021, Winter Storm Uri created prolonged power and water outages in Texas that contributed to more than 246 deaths. And in 2023, the megafires that devastated the island of Maui were the deadly consequence of high winds and sparking power lines.

Meanwhile, there is still no single federal law or agency dedicated to mitigating the risk of Natech disasters. Instead, preparedness is implemented through a patchwork of institutions—FEMA, OSHA, and the EPA, to name a few—and regulations regarding things like workplace safety and hazardous substances.

Further, because the U.S. emergency management system is designed as a bottom-up structure, where local governments are first responders—and because each region of the country deals with its own unique climatic and industrial risks—Natech prevention and response are often passed down by default to the state, county, and municipal governments.

The problem with this protocol, according to Ritchie, is that “expertise is not as strong as it is at the federal level.” Neither is funding (few towns have the training, let alone the equipment, to deal with a toxic chemical release). Additionally, planning for emergencies tends to happen in silos, so that an agency tasked with clearing roads after a storm has little to no interaction with the folks who might respond to an oil spill. Industry managers and government officials, meanwhile, don’t often engage in sustained and transparent dialogue. The disconnect between institutions often hampers a coordinated response during a disaster, prolonging the event and worsening the danger.

The natural and technical components of the disaster, on the other hand, work in tandem to intensify their impact. And these are not simply concurrent disasters, says O’Donnell, who has since taken a role as community resilience officer at the Baton Rouge Area Foundation. “They’re compounding disasters.”

After Hurricane Laura, for example, a power outage caused by the storm prevented the electric water pumps in BioLab’s fire protection system from functioning, allowing the fire to spread. As emergency crews rushed to shut down the interstate and put out the blaze, that was time they were not assisting the 8,000 families whose homes were lost or destroyed during the Category 4 hurricane. A closed interstate further delayed utility companies from restoring electricity and water to the tens of thousands without it, now sweltering in the September heat. The chemical fire raged for a full 24 hours, preventing people who still had a home from returning to get started on recovery.

Delayed recovery, whether it’s the additional hours for mold to fester inside homes or the expense of extra nights in a hotel, is often especially burdensome for those who live where the risk for Natech disasters is the highest: heavily industrialized, economically disadvantaged cities like Lake Charles, where almost a quarter of the population lives in poverty. Residents in these places already suffer from higher-than-average rates of health issues, thanks to prolonged exposure to pollution, and possess fewer resources to get back on their feet in the aftermath of disasters.

Perhaps most insidiously, Natech events can fracture communities and damage trust in human institutions. While a natural disaster tends to inspire cooperation and widespread mutual support, “man-made” disasters create “a far more severe and long-lasting pattern of social, economic, cultural, and psychological impacts,” according to the late UC Santa Barbara environmental sociologist William Freudenburg, PhD. In the aftermath of a technological disaster, fear, uncertainty, blame, and division abound. What’s often missing is collective action.

In the months after the fire, area residents did not come together to demand accountability or remuneration, even though the ensuing investigation found that the company was aware its facility had not been built to withstand severe hurricane damage or rainwater infiltration, despite the known risks involved.

For better or worse, Lake Charles is “tied to this chemical industry,” says James Hiatt, a former refinery worker who founded For Better Bayou, a local environmental justice nonprofit. As many as 45 percent of the non-farm jobs in Calcasieu and Cameron Parishes are connected in some way to the area’s approximately 30 chemical plants or petroleum refineries, which together account for more than half of the local tax base. This dependence on the industry means residents can be reluctant to speak out against offending companies or even press for regulation that might prevent the next disaster.

“I wish I could tell you it woke people up,” O’Donnell says. Local environmental groups “made the usual noise,” but in November 2022, BioLab cut the ribbon on its brand-new trichlor production facility in Lake Charles, rebuilt where the old one had burned down.

Meanwhile, less than two years later, another BioLab facility would go up in flames.

On the afternoon of Sunday, September 29, 2024, Iffat Walker was driving east on Interstate 20 to her home in Conyers, Georgia, a city of about 20,000 people just outside of Atlanta. Traffic was unusually backed up, and she was inching along the highway. That’s when she noticed the thick black cloud looming over the horizon.

“You couldn’t tell what it was,” she says, “I thought maybe a car fire.” But as she crept closer to the smoke, a strong chemical smell wafted through her car. She quickly rolled the windows up, but her skin began to tingle. By the time she arrived home about 20 minutes later, angry welts had bloomed on her arms.

“I was alarmed because I was sitting in it for such a long time,” says Walker, a nonprofit director. “I’m panicking at this point.”

It wasn’t until she turned on the news that Walker learned a facility called BioLab, which produced and stored millions of pounds of trichlor, had caught fire that morning, releasing a plume of highly toxic chlorine gas over the Atlanta metropolitan area.

It was not the disaster Georgians had expected that week. Just four days earlier, Governor Brian Kemp had declared a state of emergency ahead of Hurricane Helene. Although Helene ended up dumping more than 10 inches of rain on Conyers in just two days, it seemed the area had avoided severe catastrophe; that would turn out not to be true.

In fact, according to an investigation by the U.S. Chemical Safety Board (CSB) released in May 2025, BioLab employees on fire-watch duty inside the facility during the storm had reported multiple roof leaks. And, according to the CSB report, while no rain fell the day before the fire, and the employee who called 911 the morning of the blaze claimed that water from a burst sprinkler had made contact with the pallets of trichlor, the same employee later stated, “I think that it could’ve been water off the ceiling.” (What caused the fire has never been determined; BioLab declined to be interviewed.)

By Sunday evening, the warehouse was destroyed, and the fire was largely extinguished. But the danger was far from over.

The next day, Madelyne Reese woke up at her home about five miles outside of Conyers, where she sleeps with the windows open, and smelled something funny. She assumed it was just the lingering odor of the bleach she had used to clean that weekend, but when she opened the back door to let her dog out, she says, “I got smacked in the face with it.”

It had been 24 hours since the fire at the BioLab facility had started, but Reese had received no indication of the airborne contaminant—no sirens, no text messages. While neighborhoods in the immediate vicinity had been evacuated Sunday morning, residents in the surrounding areas received a patchwork of messages; some were told to evacuate, others to shelter in place. Some, like Reese, didn’t receive an alert until Monday afternoon. On Tuesday, the shelter-in-place order that had been issued and lifted on Monday was implemented again, as the toxic plume shifted with the wind.

By then, conditions had turned “brutal,” says Reese, a human resources director. “The smog hit and you could not see a foot and a half in front of you.” On that hot, early autumn day, Reese turned off the air conditioning and ran masking tape down the seams of her windows. “I was just trapped in here. I’ve never experienced anything like it.” Four days later, Reese’s horse, a black Tennessee Walker she’d rescued from a kill pen, suddenly developed a cough and had trouble breathing.

In the aftermath of the fire, the roughly 15,000 students in the Rockdale County Public School District attended classes online, while businesses in the two-mile contamination zone remained shuttered. Monitoring stations showed chlorine levels up to 20 times the Environmental Protection Agency’s exposure guidelines. (A 2026 study by scientists at the Georgia Institute of Technology would show that the air also contained dangerously high levels of bromine and isocyanic acid, toxic chemicals that can cause lung problems as well as irritation of the eyes, nose, throat, and skin.) People in surrounding areas complained of headaches, rashes, and dizziness and watched their flowerbeds wither.

Yet information remained scarce. What caused the incident? What chemicals were in the air? Should residents wear masks? “Complete silence,” says Reese. “Our government wasn’t giving us any answers.” So Reese started a Facebook group called Stand Against BioLab in Rockdale County. “We all needed to talk, we all needed to figure it out,” she says. The group quickly swelled to over 1,500 members.

They learned that this BioLab facility had actually caught fire three times in the last two decades (earning it the nickname “Firelab” with emergency management personnel), and that the company, one of Rockdale County’s largest employers, had received generous tax breaks since it opened in 1973.

Other community groups coalesced and disseminated petitions and planned protests. Farmers came together to test for pollutants on their land. Walker’s nonprofit, Community Action NOW!, partnered with the Morehouse School of Medicine to launch a three-year study to track long-term health impacts resulting from the fire.

And collectively, these groups began to call for legal action—and for the facility to be shut down.

Their activism worked. Less than a month after the fire, Rockdale County officials filed a federal lawsuit seeking compensation for impacted residents and called for the company to leave Conyers.

While the county’s lawsuit was partially dismissed, including some demands for damages, that litigation is still active, as is a class action suit. And in May 2025, BioLab announced it had completed remediation of the site and would no longer produce trichlor in Conyers (though it would continue to store the chemical there).

“I’d like to think it was . . . how vocal we were as a community,” says Reese, who admits the experience has left her jaded. “But there are a million BioLabs out there that are not being held to true standards.”

Days after BioLab’s announcement, the CSB released its report, which revealed that on the morning of the fire, the facility had contained double the amount of trichlor the company had previously disclosed—including half a million pounds of the chemical that had been shipped from Lake Charles in 2024 as Hurricane Francine bore down on the Gulf Coast.

Following the investigation, OSHA proposed $61,473 in penalties against BioLab, whose parent company, KIK Custom Products, has reported estimated annual revenues of more than $2 billion. (The penalty was paid in full, according to a Department of Labor spokesperson, and the case is now closed.)

On March 11, 2011, a magnitude 9.0 undersea earthquake struck off Japan’s northeastern coast, triggering a massive tsunami that inundated the Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Plant, which sat on a 30-foot bluff overlooking the Pacific Ocean. While the reactors shut down safely, seawater flooded the plant’s backup generators. After days without cooling, three of the plant’s four reactor cores overheated and began to melt down, releasing lethal amounts of radiation into the atmosphere and ocean in the worst nuclear disaster since Chernobyl, the 1986 explosion at a Soviet power plant that displaced more than 200,000 people and caused long-term environmental contamination. Parts of the Daiichi area remain so radioactively hot that the robots sent in to assess the damage in 2017 were instantly fried.

A Japanese parliamentary panel later called the disaster “clearly man-made,” blaming systemic failures across every institution involved—the government, regulatory authorities, and the company that owned the plant.

They “betrayed the nation’s right to be safe from nuclear accidents,” the panel’s report said.

In the years since, Japan has taken an aggressive, wide-ranging approach to preventing similar disasters, including the creation of an independent watchdog agency to enforce regulations that explicitly require plants to consider extreme natural hazards and compounding disasters. Existing plants were required to install higher seawalls and more resilient backup power sources and must now continuously assess seismic and tsunami risks.

The country’s new policies aren’t built around the assumption that these disasters are possible, but rather that they are inevitable.

That is decidedly not the case in the U.S., where many of the agencies responsible for preventing, mitigating, or responding to Natech disasters are now being downsized or defunded. For example, the Trump Administration has canceled or delayed billions of dollars in FEMA grants meant to harden infrastructure against hurricanes, fires, and floods. Meanwhile, the EPA has shed a quarter of its workforce, including many staff who focused on environmental justice for disadvantaged communities dealing with the long-term impact of pollution, places like Lake Charles. The White House has even tried to eliminate the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, an independent body that investigates the causes of chemical releases and proposes ways accidents could be avoided. (Congress ultimately saved the agency.)

And then there are cuts to climate research that could inform future planning and policy pertaining to Natech disasters. In 2025, the Administration ordered NOAA to stop tracking extreme weather events that cause over $1 billion in damage and canceled National Science Foundation grants for more than 100 research projects on climate change.

This disinvestment is having an “adverse impact on . . . communities that need this information,” Virginia Tech’s Ritchie says. But she believes there are still things communities can do to protect themselves. Ritchie points out that major industrial projects (like a mine, a dam, or a large factory) involving federal permits or funding require review under the 1969 National Environmental Policy Act, a process that mandates an environmental impact evaluation. These assessments include an opportunity for public comment on potential socio-economic benefits and risks associated with a project, as well as what the community stands to lose in the event of a disaster or hazard. It doesn’t guarantee this input will be addressed, she says, but it can lead to negotiations between communities, developers, and governments over things like mitigation measures and compensation—not just financial restitution but programs that address quality of life, such as a new community center or coverage for mental health services.

On an individual level, being prepared can make all the difference, according to Madelyne Reese, who was unaware there was even a chemical plant near her home. “Understand who is operating in your city and your county,” she says. Invest in the appropriate PPE and develop an evacuation plan. “Don’t wait until it’s in your backyard.”

Four months after it reopened, the BioLab plant in Lake Charles once again experienced a chlorine leak. Then, in July 2024, another thick plume of smoke arose over the warehouse. Both incidents caused a temporary closure of I-10 and a shelter-in-place order. While environmental activists have called for the facility to be shut down, those voices remain in the minority.

Still, if you ask James Hiatt, who still remembers that August 2020 day when the wreckage of his city lay scattered beneath a roiling cloud of chlorine smoke, the subject of BioLab’s threat to the community “is never black and white; there’s a lot of gray.”

BioLab employs more than 100 residents and supports the county’s tax base, providing revenue for public schools and sheriffs’ departments. It donates money and volunteer hours to local nonprofits and community events, including school programs and field trips. And, argues Jim Rock, the executive director of the Lake Area Industrial Alliance—a coalition of refineries, liquid natural gas operators, and chemical manufacturers—the company has its own incentives for prioritizing safety. “They don’t want something bad to happen to them or their industrial neighbors,” he says, pointing to the improvements BioLab made when it opened the new facility in 2022—like elevated work floors and structures that can withstand 150mph winds. “I’m more confident in the integrity of facilities now . . . than I was 10 or 20 years ago,” he says.

Rock, who worked for decades in chemical plants, insists the industry is safe. “We’re constantly being audited by both state and federal inspectors to ensure that we’re doing everything we’re supposed to be doing,” he says. “Those rules don’t get lax over time. [The facilities are] historically safe places . . . because they have to be. You got to take extra precautions because you got extra hazards.”

As for the people who live near these operations, researchers have found that residents in disaster-prone areas often have little choice but to look on the bright side. “A chronic disaster is one that gathers force slowly and insidiously, creeping around one’s defenses rather than smashing through them,” wrote the late Yale University sociologist Kai Erikson in A New Species of Trouble, a seminal book that examines the unique and disruptive effects of human-caused disasters. “People are unable to mobilize their normal defenses against the threat, sometimes because they have elected consciously or subconsciously to ignore it, sometimes because they have been misinformed about it, and sometimes because they cannot do anything to avoid it in any case.”

Hiatt says that his neighbors’ ability to stay positive in the face of grave danger is both a shortcoming and a strength.

“We are resilient,” says Hiatt. But he doesn’t mince words when it comes to the path ahead. “If we don’t stop what we’ve been doing, take a different road, this place will not be here in 100 years.”

And when Hiatt says “we,” he doesn’t just mean the residents of Southwest Louisiana.

According to a 2025 UCLA study, more than 5,500 hazardous sites across the country are projected to be at risk of coastal flooding by the end of the century, including facilities that handle sewage, toxic waste, and oil and gas. In the Midwest, the Chicago area is experiencing a surge in tornadoes, a looming threat to the region’s high concentration of toxic waste sites and coal ash ponds. Residents of Appalachia, where abandoned coal mines dot the landscape, see more frequent and intense flooding events than ever.

The few Americans lucky enough to live far from industrial facilities still rely on them for their everyday lives. For example, BioLab is one of the country’s largest producers of the chlorine used in pools and spas. Other Southwest Louisiana plants, meanwhile, churn out the building blocks for essential products like plastics, fertilizers, clothing, medical supplies, and electronics. The state’s 15 oil refineries account for about one-sixth of the U.S.’s refining capacity; its natural gas heats homes all over the country.

“We’re all part of a system that’s causing . . . harm,” says Hiatt. “We don’t have to align politically to see we’re interconnected and inter- dependent.”

Natech disasters are an existential threat. If we want to prevent them, he says, we have to begin by recognizing and acknowledging who’s at risk: all of us.

#6418. Birds that are supposed to be completely safe from extinction are actually losing their genetic diversity very quickly

Sixty-two common songbirds lost nearly half their genetic diversity in 50 years, and the most abundant species lost the most.

A songbird you can find on almost any hillside seems like it would be part of an abundant bird species with nothing to worry about in terms of population decline. In the Gaoligong Mountains of southwestern China, the bigger a songbird’s population, the faster it has been losing genetic diversity.

Across all 62 species the researchers compared, genetic diversity fell by an average of 43% to 49% in about 50 years. Every one of those species is listed as Least Concern, the lowest level of extinction risk.

Ri Liu, Feng Dong and their colleagues at the Kunming Institute of Zoology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, sequenced DNA from birds collected in the 1960s and 1970s. Then they compared it with DNA from birds sampled in the same mountains since 2000.

Only songbirds were sampled, and only in this one range. Birds have lost more genetic diversity than any other major animal group worldwide, so the team expects other animals here to be losing some too.

Genetic diversity is the sum of the small differences in DNA across a population. A species with a lot of it has more ways to adapt when conditions change.

The team measured that diversity two ways. Across a whole population, variation fell by an average of 48.8%, with species ranging from 18.1% to 77.2%.

Within a single bird, variation between the two copies of its genome fell by 42.9%, ranging from 21.8% to 80%. Not one of the 62 species held steady.

By either measure, that’s a far steeper fall than earlier work had suggested. A 2019 analysis of 91 species, which used short repeating stretches of DNA rather than whole genomes, estimated a loss of about 6% over roughly a century. The Gaoligong birds lost more than that every decade.

The losses do match the steepest theoretical forecast. A 2021 projection, built on the 73% drop in monitored vertebrate populations since 1970, predicted that genetic diversity could fall by more than half in 50 years.

The team then asked which traits went with the biggest losses. Several did. The unexpected one was the size of a species’ population worldwide.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dong said the direction of that result surprised the team. “We expected large populations to buffer against genetic erosion,” he said.

“Instead, we found the opposite: the more abundant a species was, the more genetic diversity it lost over the past five decades.”

The reason, in Dong’s account, is that a large population only stays genetically rich because birds keep moving and breeding across one continuous stretch of habitat.

Cut that habitat into pieces and a big population becomes many small, isolated ones, each losing variation on its own. “So the very species we assumed were safest turn out to be experiencing the heaviest genetic erosion,” Dong said.

Population size was a minor factor, though. It accounted for less than a tenth of the variation between species in how much they lost. And the population figures are global estimates, which may not match how many of each bird actually live in these mountains.

When people clear a forest, two things happen to the birds. Some habitat disappears outright, so fewer birds fit in what’s left, and what remains breaks into patches, so birds in one patch stop meeting birds in the next.

If the problem were outright loss, species that produce few young should suffer most. If it were isolation, strong fliers should suffer least, because they can still cross the gaps.

Strong fliers lost the least. The team scored each species’ ability to travel from its wing shape, and the better travelers lost less diversity per generation.

Clutch size, adult survival, and breeding elevation made no measurable difference. The only stronger predictor was the size of a species’ recent population decline.

Forest patches across the Gaoligong range have multiplied more than tenfold in recent decades, and the average patch is now under a tenth of its old size.

The worst breakup is at low to middle elevations, and that matters because rivers and steep terrain already isolate the range. The lowlands are the routes birds use to move between neighboring mountains.

Conservation planning “should treat connectivity – not just population size or protected area coverage – as a core conservation target,” Dong told Earth.com. In practice, he said, that means keeping and rebuilding low-elevation corridors between otherwise isolated populations.

The old birds came from a museum. The Kunming Natural History Museum of Zoology holds specimens collected across the Gaoligong Mountains in the 1960s and 1970s, and the team extracted DNA from them.

The modern DNA came from tissue samples taken between the 2000s and 2020s and stored in a tissue bank for wild species in Kunming.

Each species was represented by four or five birds per era. That’s a small number, and the team cites earlier work showing it is enough to capture how much variation a population holds.

The median collection year was 1973 for the old birds and 2022 for the new ones. For these small birds, 49 years is about 20 generations.

And those museum specimens were collected before forest fragmentation here intensified, so they show what the birds’ genomes looked like beforehand.

On the IUCN Red List, all 62 species are in the lowest-risk category, Least Concern, and Yunnan province’s own red list rates them about the same. The range itself already has formal protection.

The Gaoligong Mountains lie where the eastern Himalayas meet the mountains of Indo-Burma and southwest China, and they are part of a World Heritage site. They hold nearly a tenth of the world’s songbird species on about 0.02% of Earth’s land.

The losses are also larger than the world’s biodiversity agreement treats as tolerable. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022, set a 10% loss of genetic diversity as the limit for a species to keep its ability to evolve. The Gaoligong songbirds are already well past it.

Dong said conservation groups should stop treating “Least Concern” as a synonym for “genetically safe,” and that genetic monitoring should extend to common species rather than stopping at the rare ones.

The study ruled out mutation rate and elevation as explanations for the losses. It can’t say whether past hunting, climate change, or invasive species added to the damage alongside fragmentation.

The oldest birds in the comparison date from the 1960s, and the authors wrote that their figures may still understate the true historical loss.

The bigger open question is whether other animals and plants in the same mountains are losing diversity the way these songbirds are. The team expects they are, to a lesser degree, and hasn’t measured it.

Dong said genomic monitoring should start where the gap between a species’ official status and its actual genetic health is likely to be widest.

That means biodiversity hotspots with rapid recent fragmentation, and common, widespread species that go unmonitored because they aren’t listed as threatened. Low-elevation corridors in mountain hotspots, where connectivity loss is most severe, would be among the priority regions, he said.

Genetic indicators have been proposed for the global biodiversity framework, but they aren’t yet part of routine monitoring. The baseline for that monitoring, Dong said, already exists in museum collections like the one in Kunming.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6417. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

It seems like a simple question, but it needs serious taxonomic sleuthing. Are sharks or trees the oldest?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You may have heard that sharks are older than trees. And yes, sharks are truly ancient, with an evolutionary lineage dating back hundreds of millions of years.

But are they really older than trees? Experts told Live Science that the answer depends on what we classify as a shark.

"It's all in the fine print," John Maisey, the curator-in-charge emeritus of fossil fish at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, told Live Science. "The takeaway is that the shark lineage within the fishes generally does go back further than trees. But it really depends on how you define what we mean by shark."

The modern sharks we see today first emerged around 195 million years ago, during the Jurassic period. Fossils of ancient sharks from this time can be traced to living lineages, namely Hexanchiformes, an order of sharks identified by their six or seven gills and single dorsal fin.

This means that modern sharks, at least, are not older than trees. Experts generally agree that trees first evolved in the Middle Devonian epoch, around 380 million to 390 million years ago. "I think it's not very controversial, when we had the first trees," Cindy Looy, a paleobotanist at the University of California, Berkeley, told Live Science.

For instance, the first true tree in the evolutionary record is considered to be Archaeopteris, an extinct genus discovered in a 385 million-year-old fossil forest near Cairo, New York. Looking at these fossils, Archaeopteris has many characteristics of trees we have today, including a tall, woody trunk; leaves; and a deep root system. Other early trees ‪—‬ such as Eospermatopteris found in ancient forests near Gilboa, New York, and Calamophyton in southwest England ‪—‬ also appeared in the fossil record 390 million and 393 million years ago, respectively.

But when we look at the extinct relatives of modern sharks, "that's where it gets a bit wobbly," Maisey said. There are fossils from the sister groups of modern sharks that can be traced back through the Permian period and into the Devonian period (around 359 million to 420 million years ago). The most abundant group are hybodonts, an extinct group of spiny fish that have a unique calcification pattern in their cartilage that is similar to that of modern sharks.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

A microscopic image of skin cells from the dogfish shark.

"It’s called tessellated calcified cartilage, and that's a very important hallmark of most of the shark-like fishes and their ancestors," said Maisey, who has studied a spiny fish fossil called Doliodus problematicus from the early Devonian. If this definition is used, these sharks first appeared around 400 million years ago, before trees emerged.

Sharks' rough skin can be traced even further back, with the dermal denticles — the tooth-like scales that roughen a shark's skin — first appearing in the fossil record around 450 million years ago.

These transition fossils, where fish were evolving into sharks and gaining shark-like traits, introduce a gray area in the definition of sharks. "When you get back into the ancient past, when you're not dealing with things that we have living examples to compare with anymore, then it becomes a bit more tricky [to figure out what they are]," Maisey said.

Fossils also present a very limited picture. Many contain only fragments of an animal, like a fallen tooth, so scientists are still piecing together the clues of exactly how and when sharks arose. That means every fish fossil discovery often leads to more questions about what other transition fossils could be out there, Maisey said.

There is also much to be discovered about trees, Looy added. Terrestrial fossils, especially ones that clearly show parts of a tree, are quite rare. Finding a fossil forest requires a lot of luck, she said, although there is little indication that trees were present before the Middle Devonian.

"That's why I think the fossil record is so intriguing," Maisey said. "Because it may not give us all the answers, but it certainly raises questions."

#6415. A Mineral Fingerprint Taken From Stonehenge Just Deepened the Mystery of Its Ancient Origins

Ice couldn’t have carried the six-tonne slab hundreds of miles. Ancient people had to—and we don't know why.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Before anyone could set Stonehenge’s Altar Stone in place, someone had to get it to southern England. According to geological research, the six-tonne sandstone slab came from northeast Scotland—a journey of hundreds of miles with a cargo that couldn’t be replaced if it were lost.

“My view is that the evidence strongly favours transport by Neolithic people, most plausibly involving a maritime journey,” Chris Kirkland, a professor of geology at Curtin University in Australia, tells Popular Mechanics. Kirkland helped trace the stone to Scotland in a 2024 study that overturned the long-held belief that it came from Wales. At the time, we looked at how a six-tonne slab might have traveled that far, possibly by sea. Since then, two studies—one of them Kirkland’s—have tested whether glaciers could have spared people some of the hauling. Kirkland’s reading is that they probably didn’t, which leaves archaeologists with a harder question than how the stone was moved. “Transporting a six-tonne stone across Britain would have demanded considerable organisation, cooperation and communication between distant communities,” he says. Were people coming together just to move this stone, or could they already count on help from communities far from home?

The Altar Stone is made of sand eroded from older rocks, and the mineral grains in that sand record where it came from. Researchers date some of the grains by measuring how much of their uranium has decayed into lead, then look for sandstone elsewhere with the same pattern of ages. “The mineral fingerprint points to northeast Scotland, specifically the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin,” Kirkland says—roughly 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Stonehenge in a straight line, and farther by any real route. Later work narrowed the closest match to Caithness, around Sarclet, though the exact outcrop the slab was cut from hasn’t yet been found.

The ice would still leave people with a job

Two studies published this year tested whether glaciers could have done part of the work. In Communications Earth & Environment, Kirkland and Anthony Clarke examined mineral grains in modern stream sediments around Stonehenge and found no trace of the distant material that glacial delivery would have left behind. A separate study in the Journal of Quaternary Science modeled ice flow from Scotland and found that ice could at most have carried the stone toward Dogger Bank, now beneath the North Sea—not to Salisbury Plain.

Kirkland cautions that a possible glacial path “is not evidence that the stone actually followed it.” Around the Caithness rocks that best match the Altar Stone, glaciers mostly carried material north and east, away from southern Britain. And even if ice had delivered the slab to Dogger Bank, it would have had to arrive in one piece, and people would then have had to retrieve it before rising seas submerged the area—with hundreds of kilometers still to go. Too much would have to go right, Kirkland says. He can’t rule out some help from ice, but he thinks people brought the stone from Scotland themselves.

The cargo needed people who could work together

Kirkland favors a sea route because of what an overland one would involve: hauling six tonnes of stone along rivers and bogs over nearly the entire length of Britain. A sea route would bypass many of those barriers, though such a voyage carried risks of its own, and a combination—using boats for part of the trip, hauling overland for the rest—is possible. No archaeological evidence yet identifies the route or the vessels.

Whatever the route, the harder problem is the people. Did a single group stay with the Altar Stone all the way to Stonehenge, or did it pass from one community to the next, each knowing where it was headed and why it mattered? If the journey stretched over generations, then its destination and its purpose had to be handed down along with the stone, Kirkland says. Archaeologists already have evidence of long-distance connections across Neolithic Britain; the Altar Stone would show what those connections could accomplish. Pinpointing the outcrop it came from would give them a starting point for reconstructing how.

Some of the Altar Stone’s grains were already billions of years old when they settled into the sandstone, Kirkland says. That history is written in the rock. The far more recent story of the people who moved it is harder to recover. If they brought it from Scotland, they took on an enormous amount of work for something they could have left where it was. Finding out how they did it would be an achievement. Finding out why they thought it worth doing would tell us even more.

#6414. Scientists discover hidden genetic clues that may help explain autism

Scientists have discovered overlooked DNA sequences that may help explain autism, revealing genetic changes missed by conventional testing.

Scientists have linked hundreds of genetic changes to autism, yet genetic testing can identify a cause in only about 15 percent of cases.

A new study suggests that some of the missing answers may be hiding in overlooked stretches of DNA.

Benjamin Blencowe of the University of Toronto‘s Donnelly Centre co-led the work with Quaid Morris of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Blencowe also works at King’s College London and the Francis Crick Institute.

The results are computer predictions checked against thousands of family genomes, and there’s no clinical test yet.

A gene isn’t read straight through. Cells copy it into a working message, then cut out some pieces and keep others, so one gene can make slightly different proteins in different tissues.

Some of these retained pieces, called microexons, are only three to 27 DNA letters long. Despite their tiny size, they can influence how proteins function in the brain.

Neurons use microexons much more than other cells do, and the same ones show up across vertebrates. Blencowe’s lab had already found that the brains of autistic people often use them incorrectly.

Mice with only one working copy of the main switch for them show autism-like behavior.

What nobody had was a full list. Most earlier searches used whole brain tissue, which can miss a fragment that only certain kinds of neurons use.

Guillermo Parada, a postdoctoral fellow in Blencowe’s London group and co-lead author, built a tool that scans RNA data, the working copies of genes, for microexon-shaped pieces.

He ran it over more than 100 terabytes of public data. He also included data from single cell nuclei, so a piece that only one kind of neuron uses could still show up.

The scan covered 4,790 human tissue samples and 47,380 single nuclei from the cortex.

It turned up 1,514 human microexons that no catalog had listed, and 292 of them are used differently in nerve cells than elsewhere. A matching search in mice found another 1,115.

Many of the new pieces, more often than known ones, insert a stop signal that makes the cell destroy the message instead of altering a protein. That gives neurons a way to turn a gene down.

The next question was what tells a neuron to keep a microexon included when editing the message for making a protein.

Parada and co-lead author Hannes Bretschneider worked with Morris to train a machine learning model on about 1,800 known neuronal microexons and 91,920 look-alike stretches that cells don’t use.

It reads 300 letters on each side of a fragment and scores how likely a neuron is to use it.

The team then changed every letter in those windows on the computer and recorded how the score changed.

The positions that mattered most matched the DNA that evolution has kept the same across vertebrates.

“What surprised me was that the sequences the model identified as important closely matched those conserved throughout vertebrate evolution,” Parada said.

The model also flagged a short pattern just upstream of some fragments as a signal to leave the piece out. In mouse cells, lowering the protein that binds there, QKI, made those microexons show up more often.

With their model in place, the researchers could investigate how genetic changes found in autistic people might disrupt the way neurons use microexons.

Working with Stephen Scherer and Brett Trost of The Hospital for Sick Children, they applied it to whole genomes from three large collections.

Two of them together held 2,666 pairs of siblings in which one is autistic and the other isn’t.

Rare changes, those seen in under 1 percent of reference genomes, had larger predicted effects than common ones. The same subset of microexons turned up as affected in all three collections.

“Using our model, we were able to show that rare genetic variants generally have the largest predicted effects on the splicing of neuronal microexons,” Blencowe said.

The results showed that autistic siblings carried more predicted genetic disruptions than their non-autistic siblings.

The three collections together held 25,132 people from 7,391 families, and in that group 72 of the genetic variants were tied to an autism diagnosis.

They turned up in 2.5 percent of the autistic participants and in none of their unaffected siblings.

Although these variants appeared in only a small percentage of autistic participants, they offered potential explanations for cases in which previous genetic testing had found no cause.

Of the people carrying those variants, 82 percent had no previously identified genetic cause.

The affected genes cluster at synapses, the junctions where neurons pass signals, and several were already on autism gene lists.

Nearly all of this is prediction. The team tested a few of the flagged variants in lab-grown human neurons, and those did change how the microexon was used.

A flagged variant isn’t a diagnosis, either. More than a third of everyone in the study, autistic or not, carries at least one change predicted to affect a microexon. The ones tied to autism were the rare few with large predicted effects.

The model learned its rules from known microexons, and only 59 of the new human pieces followed them, so others may obey a code it doesn’t yet have.

And only 12 percent of the new brain-specific human pieces have a clear match in mice, which limits what mouse experiments can check.

How a disrupted microexon changes the proteins a neuron builds is the open question.

“In terms of future work, it will be important to understand how disrupted microexons affect interactions between proteins that are important for nervous system development and function,” Blencowe said.

The team has published its prediction for every variant it scored, so other groups can run new genomes against it.

That includes genomes from people with schizophrenia or epilepsy, where microexons may also be disrupted.

The findings suggest that some of autism’s missing genetic explanations may lie not within genes themselves, but in overlooked DNA sequences that help determine how those genes are used.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.
