#6413. The 6 Best Laptops You Can Buy

From wallet-friendly buys to big-money AI and content-creation powerhouses, we ranked today’s best portable computers.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Whether you're in the mood for a movie night, want to keep your social media game strong, plan an online grocery run, or settle in for a marathon gaming session, a good laptop is a trusty sidekick. Choosing one, however, is not a quick or simple decision. You’ll need to find the right machine to supercharge your productivity or fuel your passion for gaming. Just beware: Picking the wrong machine could get in the way of your passions instead of enhancing them.

Luckily, the laptop market offers options for every need and budget, and we've handpicked the best for you. Still, before you whip out that credit card, you first need to choose sides in the age-old Mac vs. Windows debate. Apple's MacBooks shine with top-tier build quality and a rock-solid platform. They're a dream come true for those who don't rely on Windows-specific software.

However, some folks think that Apple's ecosystem feels a bit like the Hotel California—you can check out anytime you like, but you can never leave. Separately, despite Apple's best efforts, the Mac ecosystem still has some software limitations, especially for avid PC gamers.

Now, let's talk style. Do you want a traditional laptop or one that can transform into a superhero? If you desire a laptop that moonlights as a tablet, a 2-in-1 device is your new BFF. These nifty gadgets come with a keyboard that vanishes when you don't need it, making them perfect for streaming, unleashing your inner artist on the touchscreen, and more. But here's the catch: touchscreens can sometimes make you miss the crystal-clear clarity of a traditional screen, especially when you're knee-deep in an epic writing session.

We pored over the specs and reviews of dozens of the latest laptops to assemble this list of the best notebooks you can buy today. We looked for laptops we would be happy to use ourselves, while also finding models that fit a range of budgets and preferences. Our tech staff personally own and use several of these machines at home, including the MacBook Pro, the Microsoft Surface lineup, and MacBook Neo, and can vouch for long-term quality and durability.

Apple’s current MacBook Pro is a bit of a lame duck, with a new and improved version coming out very soon with upgraded M6 silicon, but the current M5 model is still my favorite laptop, pound for pound. The M5 MacBook Pro offers an unbeatable mix of timelessly elegant design, top-tier craftsmanship, outstanding performance, and long battery life in a compact package.

On the performance front, the entry-level MacBook Pro handled everything we threw at it—from toggling between multiple apps to running blockbuster games like Cyberpunk 2077. Best of all, unlike PC rivals with similar hardware capabilities, the notebook can deliver a full day of mixed use on a single charge.

The M5 MacBook Pro is only available with a 14.2-inch display. Much more powerful variants with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips are available in two screen sizes—14.2- and 16.2-inch. With more CPU and GPU cores and significantly higher memory bandwidth, the M5 Pro and Max can handle heavy workflows—from AI-related tasks to high-resolution video editing projects—anytime, anywhere.

True to its “Pro” moniker, even the base MacBook Pro is powerful, made for users who need more than basic compute power for creative projects like image or video editing, audio production, or local AI workflows. If you’re using your Mac for email, Google Docs, and web browsing, you may be better off with a MacBook Air or even my budget pick, the MacBook Neo.

MApple genuinely shook up the entire computing world when it launched the Macbook Neo, a budget-tier Mac built around an iPhone processor that starts at less than $700. Up to this point, the cheapest new Mac was traditionally the Macbook Air, which cost just over a $1,000, which forced Mac users to spend a pretty penny to gain access to their preferred operating system, even if they didn’t need the power it offered.

You’d think that a “budget” Mac would somehow feel less than to justify the higher spend for an Air, but the truth is that the Neo is realistically more than enough machine for folks who just need the basic. Compared to similarly priced Windows machines, the Neo offers stellar all-around performance and great battery life, making it kind of a no-brainer for a lot of folks. It’s a bit thicker than an Air, but makes up for it on the style front with a small array of iMac-esque colorways.

Make no mistake, this is not a powerhouse, though: the Neo runs on the A18 Pro chip, which is not the newest mobile processor, and only features 8GB of RAM in the base configuration, which is enough for browsing and email, but will likely slow down and struggle with anything complex. While it drives the price up a bit, I would urge most folks to go with the slightly pricier 512GB version, which also adds a TouchID fingerprint sensor. Even with the base model, though, the Neo is cooler, and a better buy than just about any other machine under $1,000 you’ll find on this side of a Black Friday sale.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop is a formidable PC alternative to our top Apple pick, pairing beautiful design and craftsmanship with top-tier Qualcomm silicon that delivers stellar performance at a similar price. Weighing either just under or slightly over three pounds, depending on the screen size, this metal-clad notebook is impressively light and slim, given its hardware specs and performance.

Hardware-wise, the Microsoft Surface Laptop impresses with a sharp PixelSense touchscreen, the latest Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus or X2 Elite chip, plenty of memory, and a comprehensive set of futureproof wired and wireless connectivity features. In my experience, both the entry-level and top-spec versions delivered excellent all-around performance and long battery life.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop comes in three screen sizes—13-, 13.8-, and 15-inch — unlike the MacBook Air or Pro and any PC laptop rival. The 13-inch version with a six-core Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 chip is the most affordable. Upping your budget for a 13.8- or 15-inch model, alongside a more powerful chip, will get you a sharper and brighter display panel with a higher refresh rate and Dolby Vision HDR support.

The recently launched Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with the brand-new Nvidia RTX Spark chip is the PC laptop to get if you are a PC power user with a big upgrade budget. The notebook’s first-of-its-kind silicon makes it great for demanding workflows—from AI-related tasks to AAA gameplay.

The Asus ROG Strix G16 is an upgrade-worthy gaming laptop for players looking to balance serious gaming specs with portability. With gaming laptops, there’s often a fine line between making an underpowered machine that lacks the specs to keep up with even a budget-tier desktop, and a huge “desktop replacement” that’s too heavy to carry on a daily basis. The Strix G16 walks that line well, delivering strong performance while keeping things relatively light.

Gaming laptops generally run heavier than performance machines, so while six pounds may sound like a lot, it's not that bad when you factor in the power at your disposal. The configuration we tested, with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU, an Intel Core Ultra 9 processor, and 32 GB of RAM, will handle new games on high or ultra settings with ease. They'll also look great on a 2.5K G-Sync display that maxes out at 240Hz, ensuring smooth, lifelike gameplay.

Depending on your budget, you can scale this laptop's hardware up or down to meet your needs. If you can live with slightly less performance, there's a more budget-friendly sub-$1,500 version with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 GPU. On the other end, this monstrously powerful config costs nearly $4,000, but your games will look absolutely incredible.

Chromebooks are historically known for being a cheap, basic notebook option, which have been widely adopted for young students who need a school-only machine. But with tech prices going the way they’ve been going and Google releasing a new, more powerful class of AI-focused Googlebooks starting at $899, that price advantage has largely evaporated. Given that, we’re only inclined to recommend high-performance Chromebooks, rather than the cheapest models.

For $750, Lenovo’s Chromebook Plus 14 is a high-end Chromebook, but still feels fairly budget-friendly compared to the wider world of laptops. It features a MediaTek chip and 16 GB of RAM, which gives you pretty snappy responsiveness for basic email and web browsing, and across ChromeOS-friendly Android apps.

The best part, I think, is its display: A sharp, 14-inch OLED touchscreen that makes streams look great. For work and school, it also has a surprisingly good high-resolution webcam and Dolby Atmos-capable speakers. And it can run up to 17 hours on a single charge, which should easily get it through a workday of mixed use.

If you want a lightweight machine that looks and feels ready for hard work using Google’s vast suite of productivity apps and Gemini, this is a very reasonable option that can save you a few hundred bucks.

The Microsoft Surface Pro has been a stellar laptop-caliber tablet experience for a long time, and this year is no different. This Windows-powered slate is sleek, capable, and supremely versatile. Yes, you’ll need to buy a keyboard case to complete its transformation to full-blown laptop, but I think it’s absolutely worth it to do so.

Getting the laptop option mentioned above requires spending more on a Surface Pro keyboard and Slim Pen 2 bundle, but the investment is well worth it. The essential accessories, along with the Pro’s adjustable viewing stand, are instrumental in giving it such commendable versatility.

Equipped with Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Series silicon, the Microsoft Surface Pro balances abundant power, stellar multitasking, and long battery life. We prefer the higher-end version, which features a stunning OLED screen. Lower-priced iterations use an IPS panel, down to a 12-inch display panel in the starter model.

You'll want a laptop that cuts through every task you throw at it while also lasting as long as you do. The selections below are packed with the latest processing and graphics technology to rise to the occasion.

If you travel frequently or commute with your computer, look for thin, light designs like the MacBook Air—the 13-inch model weighs in at just 2.7 pounds and the 15-inch at 3.3 pounds.

Gamers or content creators will want higher-end processors and graphics cards as well as bright, detailed screens. Students, and those who will spend most of their time logging into classes and watching the occasional movie or surfing the web, might want to consider a convertible laptop that also functions as a tablet.

More to Consider: MacBook Air vs. MacBook Pro • Best Laptop Docking Stations • Best Wireless Mouse • Best Gaming Keyboards

With the latest laptops, battery life keeps improving. The reason newer laptops last longer on the same size battery is because modern processors are getting more energy efficient. Today’s laptops will run between 8 and 20 hours on a single charge. Look for a battery that lasts at least 10 hours.

There are more than a dozen types of ports, including HDMI for video out and USB-C, which can be for almost anything with the right adaptor, such as charging, but most users will only need a USB-C port. That’s because it’s possible to connect almost any type of peripheral to USB-C by itself or using an adaptor.

If you don’t want to pack an adapter, consider a laptop with HDMI ports that can output video and audio from your laptop to a TV, monitor, or projector. They can support high-definition resolutions up to 4K and surround sound formats. Another handy option is ethernet ports that can connect your laptop to a wired network for faster and more reliable internet access.

The fastest processors on the market now offer blistering speeds and are great for gaming or video editing. But quicker speeds can sometimes make for a pricier laptop that has less battery life.

In laptop chips, Intel’s most popular lineup is its Core series, while Apple’s is its proprietary M-series processors (starting with the base M1). The middle ground in the Core and Ryzen lineups offers the best mix of performance and value. The most expensive laptops offer Intel Core i9 H-Series processors while mid-range models tend to have Core i5 processors that offer a good balance between price and performance.

Screen quality is also crucial to a satisfying experience. Buy the best screen you can afford; your eyes will thank you later. Higher-resolution screens allow for greater image detail, though fonts on high-resolution displays can be small and difficult to read.

The most suitable screen size for most people ranges from 13- to 15-inches—the sweet spot between portability and enough real estate to get things done. The most common resolutions on laptops and 2-in-1 PCs currently hover just above 1920 x 1080 (also known as 1080p or Full HD). This keeps panel prices relatively low and fonts still large enough to view comfortably.

Pick a keyboard with a broad enough design and widely spaced keys if you’ll be doing a lot of typing. Also consider key travel (how far a key needs to be depressed until the keystroke is recognized), which can vary widely between models. Larger laptops tend to have better keyboards since the dimensions don't have be downsized for smaller frames.

The more money you spend on your laptop, the longer you can expect it to last. In general, Macs have a reputation for lasting longer than Windows laptops. I have an eight-year-old MacBook Air that’s still going strong.

One factor to consider is that operating system updates that are released regularly tend to take up hard drive space, so if you buy a model with a larger drive, your laptop may last longer. To make the most of your laptop’s lifespan, keep the laptop clean, cool, updated, and backed up.

The weak spots of inexpensive laptops tend to be the keyboard, trackpad, and display. Manufacturers may skimp on these items hoping that potential buyers will focus more on processor speed. For starters, even if your funds are limited, look for a screen with at least Full HD (1920-by-1080) resolution.

It pays to be fussy when it comes to a laptop keyboard as that’s the component you’ll be interacting with the most. Buying a laptop with keyboard backlighting can help you see the keys better and avoid typing mistakes.

Some keyboards have adjustable brightness and color options for backlighting. Another important feature is a laptop keyboard with a full-size layout instead of a compact or tenkeyless layout without a numeric keypad.

#6412. Why people with ADHD struggle to stop watching short videos

In a survey of 302 adults, people with ADHD more often lost track of time while using short-video apps, and felt regret and guilt afterward.

A short-video feed never ends. Swipe past one clip on TikTok, Instagram Reels or YouTube Shorts and the next one is already playing, chosen to match what you’ve watched before.

In a survey of 302 adults, people with ADHD said those picks matched what they’d opened the app for just as well as they did for people without ADHD.

What set them apart was everything else: more trouble stopping, more lost time, and more regret once the app was closed.

The problem, the researchers wrote, isn’t bad recommendations. It’s a feed with no built-in place to stop.

The work comes from Elisabeth Lex and colleagues at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz) in Austria.

The research was released as a preprint ahead of ASSETS 2026, a computing accessibility conference held in Portugal in late October.

Earlier studies have tied heavy social media use and short-video habits to attention problems, but few have put numbers on how these feeds affect people who have ADHD.

The team recruited 302 adults through Prolific, a website that pays people to take part in research.

Of those 150 participants, 65 reported a formal ADHD diagnosis, while 85 identified themselves as having ADHD. This allowed the researchers to compare responses between the two groups

Splitting the ADHD group this way let the team check whether a formal diagnosis changed the answers. Participants ranged from young adults to people in their 70s.

YouTube Shorts was the most popular app, ahead of Instagram Reels and TikTok.

Each person rated 15 statements about their own viewing on a scale of 1 to 7, such as “Once I start watching short-content videos, I find it difficult to stop.”

The whole questionnaire took a typical participant under five minutes.

Participants with ADHD agreed more strongly that they often watched longer than they meant to and found it hard to stop once they’d started.

Asked how hard it was to pull away from the feed, the typical person with ADHD answered 5 on the 7-point scale. The typical person without it answered 3.

People with ADHD were also more likely to say they lost track of time while watching. Researchers call that time blindness – losing the sense of how many minutes have gone by.

Lex’s team named the pattern the engagement trap.

“By the ‘engagement trap,’ we mean a situation in which (video) recommendations are, on the one hand, perceived as highly relevant, but, on the other hand, people find it very difficult to tear themselves away from the screen and consciously control their own behavior,” Lex said.

The differences continued after people closed the app. Participants with ADHD more often said they regretted the time they’d spent, felt it hadn’t been valuable, and had put off things they meant to do.

They also reported lower mood after a long session than before it, and more guilt.

The biggest gap of all was frustration with their own difficulty disengaging. Even so, the differences were modest – small to medium by standard statistical yardsticks.

The team found no statistically reliable difference between people whose ADHD had been diagnosed by a doctor and people who identified it themselves.

“Our findings show that recommender systems optimized for engagement place a disproportionate emotional and behavioral burden on people with ADHD,” Lex explained.

Earlier research from a team led by Thomas Mildner found that people with ADHD were better than others at spotting manipulative design on social media.

Lex’s team wrote that a short-video feed works differently. There’s no deceptive visual element to spot, only a stream with no end.

With nothing to tell a viewer when to quit, stopping depends on self-control and a sense of how much time has passed. Those are the same abilities ADHD tends to strain, the authors wrote.

This may contribute to hyperfocus, a state of intense concentration that can make it difficult to disengage without an outside cue.

The survey also described seven possible app features, none of them built yet. They ranged from a gentle usage reminder to a mode that turns off the feed entirely.

None of them would require people to step away from the apps altogether.

People in every group liked the ideas, giving a typical rating of 5 on the 7-point scale. A fixed number of videos per session and an enforced break after a set time scored highest.

“To redress this imbalance, we must move away from optimization focused purely on engagement towards human-centered design practices that explicitly support users’ sense of time and their intentional control,” Lex said.

Everyone reported on their own habits from memory, and no one’s screen time was measured.

People with ADHD may also experience more guilt about scrolling, potentially influencing how negatively they describe their viewing habits.

The researchers did not independently verify ADHD diagnoses or ask about medication use, which may have influenced participants’ ability to stop watching.

The authors want future studies to compare how long people think they watched with how long they really did, using recorded watch time.

Whether a fixed video limit or a forced break actually cuts viewing time will take working versions of those features to find out.

The full study has not been published in a journal yet and is available as a preprint on arXiv.

#6411. A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud emerges every day during spring and summer on Mars, a long wispy ribbon downwind of the Arsia Mons volcano. This image of the cloud was captured by a camera aboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express mission.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.

While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

D.E. Siskind et al. Understanding the effects of polar mesospheric clouds on the environment of the upper mesosphere and lower thermosphere. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres. 2018. doi: 10.1029/2018JD028830

Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats." In it, he explores deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it amounts to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.

Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."

Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?

James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?

And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?

OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?

JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.

The Pink Orchid Mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) is an insect that uses camouflage as a form of protection in the wild.

OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?

JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.

I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?

There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.

OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?

JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.

OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?

JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.

OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?

JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.

Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.

OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.

JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.

OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?

JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.

OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?

JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.

Male cuttlefish can change their body pattern to trick competing suitors.

OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?

JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.

As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?

A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.

OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?

JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.

It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.

We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.

OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?

JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.

You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.

OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?

JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6409. Late-night snacking may be putting your liver at risk

A study of nearly 200,000 people links late-night eating to higher risks of fatty liver disease and cirrhosis, even after accounting for diet and weight.

When people think about the health effects of late-night snacking, they usually focus on calories. But new research suggests that when you eat may matter just as much.

Now, a 16-year study involving nearly 200,000 nurses and other health professionals has linked late-night eating to an increased risk of fatty liver disease.

People who said they ate after dinner or after bedtime went on to develop fatty liver disease and cirrhosis more often than people who didn’t.

That gap stayed after weight, diet quality and alcohol were taken into account. The authors can’t say the late eating caused the damage.

What they can say is that meal timing was linked to liver disease on its own, apart from how much or how well people ate.

Robert Wilechansky, a liver specialist at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU), led the analysis with colleagues at OHSU and Massachusetts General Hospital.

Andrew McHill, a sleep and circadian physiologist at OHSU who studies the body clock, was a co-author of the study.

In an interview with Earth.com, McHill said the point of the study is broader than any one snack.

“It is not only what or how much you eat, but also the timing of when you eat that matters for your health,” he noted.

The data came from three long-running American health surveys.

These were the Nurses’ Health Study, its younger sister study, and the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study.

Together they contributed 199,155 people with no liver disease at the start. Most were women and the median age was 59. At the start, 22 percent had obesity and 5 percent had diabetes.

Every two to four years, participants reported what they ate and when.

Anyone who said they usually ate after dinner or after bedtime counted as a late-night eater. About 29 percent of the participants were in this category.

The surveys also asked whether people skipped breakfast and how many times a day they ate.

Participants also reported whether a doctor had diagnosed them with liver disease during follow-up surveys.

Over a median of 16 years, 4,492 people developed fatty liver disease, in which fat builds up in liver cells. Another 315 developed cirrhosis, the scarring that follows years of damage.

Late-night eaters developed fatty liver disease at a rate 36 percent higher than everyone else, and cirrhosis at a rate 28 percent higher.

Those figures already account for age, body mass index, daily calories, diabetes, cholesterol, smoking, exercise, alcohol and a standard score of diet quality.

Skipping breakfast and eating fewer or more meals a day looked risky at first. Those links disappeared once the same factors were counted, and only the late eating survived.

When the team also accounted for night-shift work, the cirrhosis link grew stronger rather than weaker, to 49 percent higher.

Setting aside anyone diagnosed in the first four years barely moved the numbers either, which argues against disease that was already under way.

McHill told Earth.com the team had expected a link, but not one that size.

“I think we were somewhat surprised by the strength of the relationship,” he said, especially after accounting for body weight, poor diet and drinking.

The liver has its own internal clock. Earlier research has shown that the timing of meals influences how the liver processes nutrients.

“We know the liver is very much in tune with the body’s circadian rhythms,” Wilechansky said.

Eating most of the day’s calories in the evening has been linked to obesity and poorer metabolic health.

A 2026 study found that in people with fatty liver disease, the liver was more resistant to insulin at night than in people with obesity alone.

McHill said eating when the body clock is promoting sleep makes the body less efficient at processing food.

He added that animal studies have shown the liver to be one of the organs most sensitive to a mismatch between eating and sleeping.

Asked by Earth.com what a habitual late snacker should take from this, McHill drew a line between a treat and a habit.

A dessert now and then is unlikely to hurt the liver, he said. A nightly habit, kept up over years, may carry health risks that a person doesn’t notice.

The people in these surveys were mostly white, well-educated health workers. They had lower rates of obesity and diabetes than the country as a whole, and lower rates of liver disease too.

The researchers had no liver scans or blood tests to confirm the diagnoses or assess how severe the disease had become.

Eating times were asked about in only a few survey rounds, so some late eaters were probably counted as early ones.

The authors said that kind of error tends to shrink a real link rather than invent one.

Wilechansky said only a small fraction of people with fatty liver disease go on to serious forms such as cirrhosis.

Whether moving dinner earlier would change anyone’s liver is the question the surveys can’t answer.

That is the next study. McHill said his team is recruiting people for a trial that will record meal times with photographic food diaries and track the liver with hospital imaging.

The trial could help answer a question that years of observational research cannot: Can changing when we eat actually protect the liver?

The full study was published in the journal Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology.

#6408. Chickasaw Nation archaeology shows what happened to the iron de Soto’s army left behind

Researchers think Chickasaw craftspeople reshaped iron left by de Soto’s fleeing army in 1541 into their own tools and ornaments.

At Native American sites in the 1500s Southeast, archaeologists usually find only a little European metal, rarely reworked and often buried with the dead.

In northeastern Mississippi, researchers think the Chickasaw ended up with far more of it than usual after Hernando de Soto’s Spanish army fled in 1541. Many of the pieces show signs that local craftspeople reshaped them into tools and ornaments.

Charles Cobb, a historical archaeologist at the Florida Museum of Natural History, led the study. His co-authors came from the South Carolina Institute of Archaeology and Anthropology, the University of Mississippi, and the Chickasaw Nation itself.

Cobb and his co-authors say the reworked shapes seem to follow Indigenous conventions rather than European ones. The tie to de Soto has a limit, though.

Radiocarbon dating can’t confirm mid-1500s layers at the site, so the dating relies on the types of objects found and Spanish accounts of the expedition.

De Soto set out in 1539 with more than 600 people and never built a permanent settlement. By December 1540, his army had reached a Chickasaw town that Spanish accounts call Chikasha. The leader of the surrounding region let him keep his troops there for the winter.

It went badly. Cobb’s team writes that the Spaniards fell into their usual pattern of violence and constant demands for supplies.

Just before the army was due to leave in spring, de Soto demanded hundreds of porters to carry its gear. The Chickasaw answered with a surprise attack and set the town on fire.

Spanish accounts the team cites say at least a dozen Europeans died and scores of horses and pigs burned. De Soto’s forces got away after a short, violent fight.

Brad Lieb is a co-author and directs Chickasaw archaeology for the Chickasaw Nation’s Heritage Preservation Division. He said the finds show how the Chickasaw adapted to the invasion and earned a name as a people who couldn’t be conquered.

The Chickasaw Nation launched the project in 2015 to find ancestral sites in its traditional territory in northern Mississippi and to give Chickasaw college students fieldwork experience.

At a cluster of sites called Stark Farms, the team brought metal detectors, and iron tools, reworked axes, and rolled copper beads showed up almost immediately.

Across five seasons, 2015 to 2019, crews swept the core of the sites in lanes about 5 feet (1.5 meters) wide and marked every metal object from before modern times.

The total reached at least 83 pieces of iron, copper alloy, and lead, likely dating to the 1500s. Others are a mouth harp and a gilded-cross medallion, probably from a bridle.

Stark Farms looks like other towns of its time, with farmers who relied on maize and a way of life that seems related to the Mississippian culture.

But the team recovered an unusually large amount of European metal there, more than at other 1500s sites, except in towns Europeans built themselves. Detectors found almost none at other nearby sites.

With no graves found, Cobb’s team believes the metal came mainly from everyday settings, not from burials of high-status people. Stark Farms “must have been more of an open season,” Cobb said.

Cutting and scraping tools were the most common reworked pieces. Celts, which are ground axe heads with no hole for a handle, came next.

On two axes, people bent the metal until the eye where a handle fits broke off. Other celts came from horseshoe pieces and fragments that look like rapier blades.

Two iron celts go further. One nearly copies a traditional stone axe head, with smooth, even grinding across its whole surface. The authors write that both required a large piece of iron and significant labor.

The copper-alloy pieces, mostly brass in an early chemical analysis, became pendants, beads, and small cones that people probably attached to clothing.

Two cones still held cordage. The makers didn’t rely on a forge. They bent and folded pieces instead of cutting them and spent a lot of effort grinding the edges smooth.

The expedition also carried a large amount of chain, some of it for shackling Native Americans as captives and porters. A few modest chain links turned up at Stark Farms.

Some finds look like battlefield leftovers. They include lead shot sized for an early musket and a cast-iron ball of about 4.3 ounces (122.5 grams) that may have come from a small cannon. Such items don’t normally turn up as trade goods, the authors write.

Mapping where metal like this landed also helped a team in Pennsylvania place a 1758 skirmish on one stretch of ground.

The authors say such events may not have been rare. Months earlier, de Soto’s men lost even more equipment in a pitched battle at the town of Mabila in western Alabama.

In the Southwest, Francisco Vázquez de Coronado’s expedition fought the Tiguex War from 1540 to 1542 and left military artifacts at Pueblo sites.

Coronado’s men also abandoned a bronze cannon. In late 1541, settlers from that expedition fled the town of San Geronimo III in southern Arizona without it. Archaeologist Deni Seymour, who found the cannon, said the Spanish didn’t return to that area for 150 years.

Mississippi tells the same story. Cobb’s team sees no sign of a significant European presence there for about 150 years after de Soto left.

Most of the metal came from plowed soil, so the team lacks a tight record of what lay around each piece. They say they wish they had that record for every object.

They also don’t think Stark Farms is Chikasha itself, where the Spanish camped. So far, they’ve found no sign of widespread burning, no horse or pig bones, and no European pottery.

Their working idea is that the metal reached people in a spread-out settlement some distance from the camp. Those residents traded with the Spaniards over the winter and gathered what the army left at the battle site. The study doesn’t say which pieces arrived which way.

A site with burned buildings, horse bones, pig bones, and Spanish pottery would be a stronger candidate for Chikasha itself. Until one turns up, the route the metal took from de Soto’s camp to Chickasaw homes stays a hypothesis.

The full study was published in the journal American Antiquity.

Volunteer with the Mississippi Department of Archives and History if you want hands-on work. Its volunteers help preserve and share the state’s historic resources.

Look for International Archaeology Day events through the Archaeological Institute of America. The group and its local societies celebrate it every year on the third Saturday in October and list events on a public calendar.

Watch the Chickasaw Nation’s video on the Battle of Chicasa for the Chickasaw telling of the fight against de Soto.

Walk the Chickasaw Village Site on the Natchez Trace Parkway in Tupelo, Mississippi. The National Park Service site has signs on Chickasaw history and a trail through a surviving piece of prairie.

Join a state archaeological society through the Society for American Archaeology. The society calls this the best first step toward fieldwork and says volunteers are always needed at state archaeology day and month events.

#6406. What makes some foxes friendly? Scientists find clues in their brains

Scientists discovered differences in aggression-linked brain cells in tame and aggressive foxes, offering new clues to how domestication changes the brain.

For decades, scientists in Siberia have bred foxes that feel comfortable around people.

By choosing the friendliest animals to have pups, generation after generation, they produced foxes with very different temperaments from their aggressive relatives.

Now, a small study offers a clue to what changed in their brains. The friendly foxes had fewer of one kind of nerve cell in a specific brain region than foxes bred to be aggressive.

These cells interest scientists because switching on the same kind of cell in mice makes them attack other mice. The fox study involved just nine brains, so it offers a starting point for understanding the change.

Molecular biologist Eirene Markenscoff-Papadimitriou, an assistant professor in Cornell University‘s Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, led the work with colleagues in the US and Russia.

“We wanted to understand, what are the neurological underpinnings of these changes in behaviors that occurred very rapidly with this selection,” Markenscoff-Papadimitriou said.

The experiment began on silver fox farms in Siberia in the late 1950s. Silver foxes belong to the same species as red foxes but have a different coat color.

Geneticist Dmitry Belyaev and his colleagues noticed that some farmed foxes seemed more comfortable around their caretakers. They chose these animals to breed with one another.

After just six generations, the researchers were producing pups that actively sought out interactions with people.

The friendlier foxes also developed features common in domesticated animals, including floppy ears and shorter snouts.

The scientists also bred a separate group for aggressive behavior. These two groups now let researchers examine what happens when breeding pushes the same species toward opposite temperaments.

The team looked at the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the brain. They focused on a part called the ventromedial hypothalamus, which helps control energy use, mothering and other social behavior.

In mice, this area also helps drive aggression. Earlier studies had drawn attention to nerve cells there that contain a protein called estrogen receptor alpha.

The protein allows cells to respond to the hormone estrogen. In mouse experiments, researchers used light to switch on cells containing this protein.

“If you activate them, the mouse will immediately attack another mouse,” Markenscoff-Papadimitriou said. Her team wanted to find out whether friendly and aggressive foxes had different numbers of these cells.

Scientists who run the Russian fox colony sent the team nine brains: three from tame foxes, three from aggressive foxes and three from wild foxes.

The researchers preserved the brains and cut them into very thin slices. They then added glowing labels that attach to particular genetic messages inside cells, helping them identify different types of nerve cells.

“The tame fox hypothalamus had fewer of these estrogen receptor-expressing neurons, which are known to be part of the aggression circuit,” Markenscoff-Papadimitriou said.

Compared with aggressive foxes, tame foxes had fewer of these cells in the lower, outer part of the ventromedial hypothalamus.

The difference appeared only in a particular subtype that mouse studies have linked to aggressive states.

The finding does not mean tame foxes have fewer nerve cells throughout their brains. The difference involved one specific type of cell in one small area.

With only three brains from each group, the researchers need more evidence to understand how widely the pattern holds.

They also did not test what these cells do in a living fox, so the evidence connecting them to attacks still comes from mice.

The central question remains unanswered: does having fewer of these cells help make a fox friendly? The change could also be a side effect of something else that breeding altered.

Markenscoff-Papadimitriou said the findings could help explain how selective breeding changes brain structure over relatively short periods.

Her team’s next goal is to understand why domestication changes this brain region, which researchers still know little about in foxes. Genes may offer some answers.

Study co-author Anna Kukekova, who studies fox genetics at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, may investigate how mutations in different parts of the genome affect the development of these cells.

For now, the findings suggest that breeding foxes for friendliness may have changed more than their behavior.

It may also have reshaped a small part of the brain involved in aggression, offering a new clue to how domestication works.

The study is published in the journal Current Biology.

In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.

Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.

James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.

It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Meerkats are tricked by fork-tailed drongos mimicking the alarm calls, so the birds can swoop in and steal their food.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.

Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. #6404. Common pregnancy supplement linked to less fussiness in babies

A new study suggests that vitamin C supplements during pregnancy may be linked to less fussiness and fewer negative emotions in babies at six months.

Women who took more vitamin C in supplements during pregnancy tended to have less fussy babies at six months, a study in Oregon found.

The finding offers a clue to a question researchers have been trying to answer: how might a mother’s distress during pregnancy relate to her baby’s early emotions?

The team followed 302 pregnant women around Portland. Those who reported more depression, anxiety, and stress tended to have babies who showed more negative emotions, and they also took less vitamin C in supplements.

Differences in supplement use accounted for a small part of that relationship.

Vitamin C from food showed no similar pattern, and the study cannot establish whether supplements actually influenced the babies’ behavior.

Elizabeth Wood, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Oregon Health and Science University, led the work.

She and senior author Elinor Sullivan, a professor of psychiatry and behavioral neuroscience, work with the university’s Center for Mental Health Innovation.

Our bodies can’t make vitamin C. During pregnancy, a baby therefore relies entirely on its mother’s supply.

The fetus usually gets priority, so a newborn can have more vitamin C in its umbilical cord blood than its mother has in her blood. But research in guinea pigs found that this advantage disappeared when the mother herself ran short.

In those animals, a shortage during pregnancy also left the young with a smaller hippocampus, the part of the brain involved in memory. The brain normally holds high concentrations of vitamin C.

Pregnancy raises the body’s need for the vitamin. The recommended daily amount for adult women rises from 75 milligrams before pregnancy to 85 milligrams during it.

The women gave birth between 2019 and 2021, and most of the information came from weeks 37 to 39 of pregnancy.

Each woman filled out five questionnaires about depression, anxiety, and stress, which the team combined into one measure of distress.

To find out what the women ate, dietitians asked them to recall all the food and drink they’d had in the previous 24 hours. They repeated the exercise on three unscheduled days over two weeks.

The women also listed their supplements, including the name, brand, dose, and how often they took each one. Photographs of the bottle labels helped the researchers check those details.

About six months after birth, caregivers filled out a questionnaire about their babies. One question asked how often a baby cried when frustrated.

The researchers wanted to measure “negative affect,” a term for how readily someone feels and shows emotions such as sadness and irritability.

High levels in infancy can be an early sign of greater risk for mental health problems later, though a fussy baby won’t necessarily develop one.

The pattern involving supplements was clear enough to show up in the analysis: more vitamin C from supplements went along with less negative affect in babies.

Women with more distress took less of it, and their babies tended to show more negative emotions.

Vitamin C from meals had no reliable connection to the babies’ emotions. Nor did the amount women got from food relate to the amount they took in supplements.

Together, the findings suggested that supplement intake accounted for a small part of the link between distress during pregnancy and a baby’s emotions.

The team allowed for differences in the mothers’ ages, diet quality, and whether they’d given birth before. They also took into account the mothers’ distress six months after delivery.

Because the body absorbs a smaller proportion of vitamin C at higher doses, the researchers capped the amount counted from supplements at 500 milligrams per day.

The results held up when they used another calculation to account for poor absorption.

Total vitamin C from food and supplements still went along with fewer negative emotions in babies. However, that combined amount no longer explained the connection with the mothers’ distress.

The study didn’t establish why more distressed women took less vitamin C in supplements.

The authors suggested that women with less distress may find it easier to keep up a daily habit, perhaps because they’re in better overall health or find health information easier to understand.

Household income wasn’t linked to supplement intake in this group. Knowledge, motivation, and a doctor’s advice might have more to do with the habit, the authors wrote.

“The most encouraging takeaway here is that nutrition is relatively modifiable, especially when people have adequate resources and support,” Sullivan said.

“Vitamin C supplements are inexpensive, easy to access and something patients can start incorporating immediately and consistently into their daily lives.”

The team didn’t test the women’s blood for vitamin C, which might have given a better idea of what reached their babies. Supplement amounts came from labels, and US supplements face limited regulation.

Nearly all the women took prenatal vitamins, which contain several nutrients at once. Even after the researchers adjusted for this, other nutrients or generally healthier habits could still explain some of the findings.

About 73% of the women were White and non-Hispanic, so the results may not apply equally to other groups. The data are openly available through the National Institute of Mental Health Data Archive.

About 25% of pregnant women in the US get less vitamin C from food than the estimated average requirement of 70 milligrams a day, the authors noted.

A 2019 analysis in JAMA Network Open found that counting supplements brought that share down to 11.5%, a drop of more than half.

Only 48 women in the Oregon study fell below the 70-milligram mark. Within that small group, supplements didn’t measurably weaken the connection between distress and babies’ emotions.

The authors thought there were probably too few women in this group to draw a firm conclusion.

Taking a supplement may be easier than changing a whole diet or easing distress during pregnancy, the researchers wrote.

They proposed randomized trials, which assign some women to take vitamin C and others to a comparison group, to find out whether it helps.

The authors pointed to vitamin C’s low toxicity as a reason to explore the idea.

The daily upper intake limit for pregnant adults is 2,000 milligrams from all sources, a safety limit rather than a recommended supplement dose.

The team also plans to follow the children as they grow and look for later clinical diagnoses. “Nutrition is a crucial component for a healthy pregnancy, and as we’re learning more and more, also for a healthy early childhood,” Wood said.

For now, the findings raise an intriguing possibility: a mother’s vitamin C intake during pregnancy may be connected to her baby’s early emotional development, but whether supplements make a difference remains unknown.

The study is published in the journal Developmental Psychology.

#6403. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

#6402. Japan Just Powered Up a Quantum Computer Built From Single Atoms—and It May Not Need a Giant Freezer to Run

Just how big could the quantum leap really be?

One of Japan’s leading scientists in quantum computing says that his lab has switched on the power to “Japan’s first full-stack, neutral atom quantum computer,” according to a recent press release.

This announcement is not linked with peer reviewed research, but the lab leader, photo-molecular physicist Kenji Ohmori, has decades of research, publication, and leadership in the field. The computer, named Shunkai, is part of a nationwide Japanese consortium of universities and corporate interests that seeks to realize “a fault-tolerant universal quantum computer that will revolutionize economy, industry, and security by 2050.”

There are many flavors of experimental quantum computers on our busy planet today. That’s because, to date, there’s definitely never been a “fault-tolerant universal quantum computer” by a very long stretch. When traditional digital computers were developed, they had guardrails because of the way our electrical and logic industries had developed before them. Quantum computing is a deeply different paradigm where the next step is more ambiguous: all the options have drawbacks and limitations that are more confusing and pervasive than what we have now. It’s like VHS versus Betamax, but on steroids.

Neutral atom quantum computing is one of the suggested paradigms for a robust and usable quantum computer. These setups use special atoms whose electrons circle in a further orbit from the nucleus than expected, after being stimulated to sort of “puff up” so the electrons piggyback to an outer ring. This means a single atom can function as a qubit, or quantum bit—the smallest unit of information equivalent to a bit in a traditional computer—compared with two atoms in most other quantum computers.

Japan’s Institute for Molecular Science said in their statement that these single-atom qubits, which can function without being cooled to near absolute zero, can even work at room temperature “without the need for a refrigerator.” That’s interesting, because “room temperature” in quantum computing means above freezing, and you do need a refrigerator to reach the lower part of that temperature range. You just don’t need a deep freezer powered by liquid nitrogen. Time will tell precisely how “room temperature” Shunkai actually is.

The term “full stack” refers to the levels or layers of abstraction in a computer system. When you open your laptop or use your smartphone, you interact with it and experience computing results in realtime, without any additional technology or devices. That’s because the computer presents you with seamless results, but underneath, your input passes through multiple layers as it’s turned into computable code and run through software and eventually hardware. Many quantum computer prototypes work as just the processor, but Shunkai’s team says their machine will work as a complete computing experience and even be available for outside users to work on.

In the statement, Shunkai is described as “operational,” but that doesn’t seem to include work or results—just a completed assembly that can be turned on. The team’s goals are still listed in the future tense, and Ohmori’s consortium goals also include a cold atom quantum computer, meaning one that’s supercooled. The consortium’s other goals include “a society in which human beings can be free from limitations of body, brain, space, and time by 2050.” It’s just not clear how achievable any of these goals are yet.
