#6401. Sunflowers reveal a surprising secret about how plants sense light

New research reveals why sunflowers sometimes grow toward weaker light instead of brighter sources, challenging assumptions about plant behavior.

Plants grow toward light, so it seems natural that they would always bend toward whatever shines brightest.

Young sunflowers don’t always follow that rule. When two equally strong lamps shone on them from opposite sides, the seedlings grew toward a third, weaker lamp instead.

The researchers concluded that plants don’t simply grow wherever the most light is.

Different sides of a sunflower stem respond to the light they receive. Those signals combine to guide growth, allowing two equally strong lights from opposite directions to effectively cancel each other out.

Yasmine Meroz, a professor at Tel Aviv University, carried out the study with Ahron Kempinski, Amir Porat, and Mathieu Rivière. All four are part of the university’s Center for Physics and Chemistry of Living Systems.

“What is fascinating is that plants can integrate complex information about their environment without a brain or central processing system,” Meroz said.

“The computation emerges from the way light is sensed and processed locally across the stem.”

The team worked only with sunflower seedlings about a week old, grown and tested indoors under blue lamps. How full-grown plants handle light coming from many directions outdoors hasn’t been tested.

In many animals, sense organs such as skin collect signals and a brain sorts them out. A plant has no brain to do that job.

Instead, the light-sensing proteins that steer its bending are found mainly in the outermost layer of cells on the stem. Each patch of the stem’s surface responds to the light that lands on it.

Some light also passes straight through. Using a 3D-printed sleeve to hold seedling stems in front of a light meter, the team ran 31 measurements.

On average, about 10% of the light hitting a stem got through, giving the sensors on the far side a weak signal pointing the opposite way. A stem bends by growing faster on one side than the other.

The team’s model adds up the light signals from every side to work out which way the stem will grow.

Young sunflowers famously track the sun as it moves across the sky.

The sunflowers in this study were much younger, grown at 77°F (25°C) and picked when they stood 0.4 to 1.2 inches (1 to 3 cm) tall.

The team painted two fluorescent dots near each seedling’s tip under dim green light, so the plants wouldn’t start reacting to light too early.

Strips of blue LEDs then lit five seedlings at a time while the plants were photographed from the side for at least 21 hours.

The angle between the two dots showed how far each tip had bent. After about 16 hours, the seedlings settled at a steady angle.

With one lamp, brighter light made the seedlings bend further. But across a tenfold range of brightness, the bend didn’t keep pace.

The team’s measurements fit a pattern in which a light twice as bright produces a signal well short of twice as strong.

Senses in many species work this way, responding to how much a signal changes compared with where it started.

The researchers compare this response to human hearing, where a 10-decibel increase is typically perceived as roughly twice as loud.

Compression of this kind lets a plant respond across a wide range of light, from shade under other leaves to direct sunlight, the researchers wrote.

Next, the team placed seedlings between two lamps facing each other at different strengths.

The seedlings bent toward the brighter lamp, and a bigger gap in brightness meant a bigger bend, though again not in a straight-line way.

The team’s model, using the compression measured with one lamp, predicted where those seedlings would settle. It matched the measurements well, with one small miss the team put down to slightly uneven lighting.

By the model’s logic, two lamps of equal strength on opposite sides should cancel each other out.

The two-lamp runs already suggested as much, because nearly matched lamps barely moved the seedlings off vertical.

So the team added a third lamp at a right angle to the first two. The two strong lamps were set almost exactly equal, and the third was less than half as bright as either one.

The team filmed 34 seedlings from above for 21 hours, and a computer program trained to recognize leaves tracked where each plant grew.

On average, the seedlings grew almost straight toward the weak lamp, less than 1 degree off, though individual plants varied widely around that average.

The researchers wrote that this result isn’t intuitive for a plant that needs light to make food. In their view, the finding shows that plants don’t grow to collect as much light as possible.

The same math predicts something stranger. With two lamps at a right angle, one brighter than the other, the most light comes from a direction between them, closer to the brighter lamp.

But in the team’s model, the plant compresses each lamp’s signal before adding them up, which changes how strong the two signals are compared with each other.

So the direction the plant favors ends up a little off from the direction of the most light.

The researchers call this a kind of optical illusion, though it doesn’t mean the plant sees anything.

In their calculations, the gap is at most about 6 degrees, and it disappears when the two lamps are equally bright or when only one is on.

“Our work shows how the physical organization of a sensory system can determine how an organism perceives and responds to its environment,” Meroz said.

The team couldn’t measure the illusion in its living seedlings.

Growing sunflower stems trace circling motions, and in the final three hours of the three-lamp test, a seedling’s growth direction typically varied by about 17 degrees.

A 6-degree shift is too small to see against that much motion. The team’s analysis found that the circling wouldn’t average the distortion away.

Meroz’s lab in the university’s School of Plant Sciences and Food Security has studied the same circling in crowded sunflowers before. Here, that motion limited what the experiment could detect.

The model also missed one detail of the movement. Real seedlings bent past their final angle and then eased back, and the simulated ones didn’t.

The team suggested that uneven growth along the stem, or the stem sagging under its own weight, could explain why.

Bacteria and some other single cells also sense their surroundings across their whole surface, with no brain in charge.

“This principle may extend far beyond plants, to cells, bacteria, and other living systems that rely on distributed sensing,” Meroz said.

For now, the optical illusion remains a mathematical prediction. Confirming it will require measurements precise enough to distinguish the subtle effect from the seedlings’ natural circling movements.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6399. A college student searching rocky glaciers in Yellowstone finally discovered one of the rarest insects in the world

A University of Wyoming student discovered three rare ice crawlers in Yellowstone, marking the first known sightings of these cold-loving insects in Wyoming.

In summer 2026, a college student named Will Anderson found three rare bugs called ice crawlers on rocky glaciers in Yellowstone National Park.

As a student at the University of Wyoming, Anderson had spent the whole previous year looking for them without any luck. Ice crawlers are some of the rarest insects on Earth.

Ice crawlers belong to Grylloblattodea, one of the rarest orders of insects in the world. Only 35 species have been described, and many are known only from single localities.

Anderson is a biology major from Casper and a junior in the Wyoming Research Scholars Program. He works with Audrey Lindsteadt, a third-year Ph.D. student in the university’s Program in Ecology and Evolution.

“I am interested in this insect because there is so much not known about them, with their life history, habitat, and distribution all not being fully understood,” Anderson said.

“I also am passionate about and interested in their alpine habitats, which are understudied,” he added.

Starting in late July 2025, the pair surveyed 14 rock glaciers in the Red Mountains next to Heart Lake, in southwestern Yellowstone. They found no ice crawlers, even though Anderson also checked snowfields and set overnight traps.

Most snowfields had already melted by then. The area also had fewer glaciers than ideal, and most of them were small or inactive.

“Despite the close proximity to their known distribution and the plentiful suitable habitat, Gryllos have never been found in Wyoming,” Lindsteadt explained. “Therefore, Will hypothesized the rock glaciers and nearby snowfields that we are studying could have Gryllos.”

On a cold, snowy six-day backpacking trip in late June and early July 2026, Anderson found two ice crawlers near Antler Peak in northwest Yellowstone. Both turned up under rocks he flipped on a large rock glacier.

In mid-July, a mother grizzly and her two-year-old cub bluff-charged the pair and blocked their planned route.

They scrambled up Grey Peak instead and slid down to its two rock glaciers, where Anderson caught a third one. In August, he searched several alpine glaciers in Grand Teton National Park but came up empty.

Over the summer of 2026, he and Lindsteadt walked about 170 miles (274 kilometers).

“The specimens I collected in Wyoming are so far identified to the species Grylloblatta campodeiformis, which is the most widespread North American species, having populations in Montana, British Columbia, and Alberta,” Anderson noted.

He briefly kept two of the insects alive. He could not tell whether they were feeding on the dead insects and plant matter he gave them.

Ice crawlers are wingless insects that stay active in cold conditions, according to North Carolina State University entomologists. Most species are active below freezing and usually die above 50°F (10°C).

They develop through incomplete metamorphosis, from egg to nymph to adult, and their growth is slow. Some may need up to seven years to complete a single generation.

The University of Wyoming describes them as extremophiles that live at temperatures as low as 21°F (-6°C) in humid alpine settings.

By day, they hide under cool rocks near snow and ice. At night, they scavenge, eating mostly other invertebrates, including insects blown onto the snow, along with some plant material.

Little is known of their diet when they live more permanently under the snow, or in the soil through summer and winter.

The order lives in northeastern Asia, Siberia, the western U.S. and Canada. In North America, small, isolated populations occupy mountains and caves in several western states, British Columbia and Alberta.

Rock glaciers resemble alpine glaciers, but a layer of debris covers their ice, insulating and protecting it.

Lindsteadt suspects that ice crawlers prefer rock glaciers to non-glacial talus fields or snowfields because rock glaciers are colder, more humid and more permanent.

“Obviously, with just three species detections, we cannot confidently identify their habitat preferences,” Lindsteadt said. “But they at least point us in a promising direction.”

Yellowstone holds 58 known rock glaciers, and none had been visited or studied before this project. Next summer, the team plans to survey 17 rock glaciers in eastern Yellowstone and revisit others.

Ice crawlers are generally restricted to high-elevation glaciers or low-elevation caves with permanent ice, according to Purdue University entomologists.

The same entomologists warn that many of these habitats are at risk as glaciers and ice fields recede with climate change.

In Anderson’s view, the insects probably play a small part in these ecosystems because of their rarity, but they still belong to the food chains and nutrient cycles of their extreme habitats.

“More importantly, we can use ice crawlers to better understand how these ecosystems work and be more effective managers of them,” he argued.

He is also working on a paper he hopes to publish in a leading alpine or entomology journal.

Anderson will present the findings at the Entomological Society of America’s 74th annual meeting in Columbus, Ohio, on November 8 to 11.

The information was obtained from the University of Wyoming.

#6397. Ozempic and similar drugs have a surprising benefit that goes beyond weight loss

New research suggests that Ozempic and Wegovy may reduce long-term sick leave, benefiting employers and taxpayers without increasing workers' earnings.

Ozempic is best known for lowering blood sugar and body weight. But does better health also mean more time at work and higher earnings? A study from Denmark found that the answer isn’t so simple.

Adults there who started Ozempic spent less time on long-term sick leave in the years that followed. But they were no more likely to hold a job than similar adults who hadn’t started the drug yet, and their income didn’t rise.

The money saved went to employers and local governments, which pay for sick leave in Denmark, instead of to the patients themselves.

Meltem Daysal of the University of Copenhagen and four colleagues, including economists at the ROCKWOOL Foundation and Duke University, carried out the analysis.

Their paper is an early release that the authors may still revise, and it compares patients in national health and tax records instead of assigning anyone to take the drug.

Ozempic, a brand of the drug semaglutide, became available in Denmark in August 2018.

During the study years, it was approved there for adults whose type 2 diabetes wasn’t under control with diet, exercise and earlier medicines.

The team started with 9,794 Danes who began taking Ozempic in its first 17 months on sale.

Comparing them with people who never took it would mislead, because patients who start a new diabetes drug tend to differ from those who don’t.

So the researchers paired each early starter with someone who began Ozempic four years later. Each pair was matched on age, sex, diabetes and obesity, and then on income, education, marriage and how often they saw a family doctor.

The matching produced 7,011 pairs. Until the later starters began their own treatment, they showed what might have happened to the early starters without the drug.

Everyone was between 30 and 59 at the end of 2017. That way, all of them would still be under 65, and more likely to be working, when the study ended.

In the United States, many patients stop these drugs early. One study of American patients with private insurance found that only 40% to 60% were still taking them after a year.

The Danish patients stuck with it. Four years after their first prescription, 75% of the early starters were still filling prescriptions for semaglutide, and most of those who quit did so in the first year.

Ozempic is subsidized in Denmark, where a month’s supply cost 1,117 Danish kroner, about $212, in 2019. A patient’s yearly out-of-pocket spending on subsidized prescriptions was capped at 4,300 kroner, about $681.

Earlier research has often blamed side effects when patients quit. The authors suggested that what patients pay may also play a big part in whether they stay on the drug for years.

In this study, sick leave counted as long-term once a spell ran past 30 days. Before starting Ozempic, the patients spent about 5.5% of their months on long-term sick leave.

Over the four years after the first prescription, that share fell by about 1 percentage point compared with the later starters, a drop of 17.3%. Put simply, long sick leave became about a sixth less common among the people taking the drug.

In the first two years, the early starters spent about 0.8 percentage points less of their time on long sick leave than the later starters. In years three and four, the gap reached about 1.1 points.

Payments from local governments, which cover sick leave after the first 30 days, fell by 19.4% over the same period.

The authors interpreted the decline as evidence of a treatment effect, noting that sick leave had followed similar patterns in both groups before the early starters began treatment.

The decline appeared in nearly every group the team checked when it split patients by sex, age and education. Women had the largest drop, while the estimates for men and for people under 50 were less certain.

The records can’t show exactly why sick leave fell, but the team found some clues in them.

After starting Ozempic, patients were less likely to visit an emergency department and less likely to fill prescriptions for heart and blood vessel medicines.

Earlier randomized trials, including one from 2016, found that semaglutide lowers the risk of serious heart problems such as heart attacks and strokes in high-risk patients. Events like those often keep a person away from work for weeks.

The authors called that a plausible explanation for the drop in sick leave, not a proven one. Their records include no weight or blood sugar measurements, so the team couldn’t track how each patient’s health changed.

Over the same four years, the team found no change in whether patients had jobs, whether they were in the workforce at all, or how much they earned.

The estimates were precise enough to rule out a rise in employment of more than 0.4 percentage points and a rise in income of more than 0.7%.

The authors traced this to the way Denmark pays for illness.

Employers cover the first 30 days of a worker’s sick leave, and the local government takes over after that. For workers who earn below a cap, those payments can replace all of their usual pay.

So when a worker missed fewer weeks, their income stayed about the same. The savings went to employers and taxpayers.

The team estimated those savings at about 4,163 kroner a year for each employed patient, or 1.3% of a year’s earnings. If shorter sick spells fell by the same share, the total would reach 4,766 kroner, about $722, or 1.5% of earnings.

For Denmark’s budget, this means the drug costs the public less than its pharmacy price suggests. Even so, the authors wrote, the savings remain far smaller than what GLP-1 treatments cost in 2026.

Sick pay in the United States is less generous than in Denmark. There, the authors suggested, similar health gains might show up instead as higher earnings, more hours, or fewer people losing their jobs.

A 2026 study of American women who started GLP-1 drugs to lose weight found large increases in employment among those who hadn’t been working.

The Danish authors wrote that the two studies differ in both their setting and their patients.

The team also checked Wegovy, the semaglutide brand approved in Denmark for weight management.

Among 67,736 new Wegovy users, long-term sick leave fell by about 1 percentage point within the first year, and jobs and income again didn’t rise.

Less than a year of records is too short to judge the long run, and the authors treated the Wegovy job and income results with caution.

Whether the gains last for people who take these drugs mainly to lose weight is still an open question.

Answering it will take longer records of weight-loss patients, ideally from countries where a sick day costs workers more than it does in Denmark.

The study appeared as an IZA Discussion Paper.

#6395. Rising temperatures may have a dangerous effect on mental health

New research reveals how extreme heat may increase suicide risk by disrupting sleep and emotional regulation, highlighting a hidden mental health threat.

Extreme heat can do more than exhaust the body. It may also disrupt sleep, weaken emotional control, and increase vulnerability to serious psychological distress.

A new study has identified temperatures at which extreme heat is associated with increased psychological distress, revealing how disrupted sleep and emotional regulation may contribute to suicide risk.

The research was led by scientists from Georgetown University and the World Bank. It draws on a nationally representative panel study of nearly 7,500 adults in Bangladesh.

The researchers found that extreme heat was associated with an increased risk of suicide-related thoughts, with disrupted sleep playing a surprisingly important role.

“Rising global temperatures threaten human mental health on a massive scale,” said lead author Syed Shabab Wahid, an assistant professor of global health at Georgetown.

“In climate-vulnerable nations such as Bangladesh, this heat stress can translate into severe psychological strain and elevated suicide risk.”

The study tracked two interconnected pathways between heat and suicidal cognition: disrupted sleep and emotional dysregulation.

The association between temperature and suicide-related thoughts became statistically significant at 28°C and was strongest at 35°C.

Temperatures this high are common in Bangladesh during the summer months.

At that upper threshold, nearly 30 percent of the total association between heat and suicide risk ran through poor sleep quality alone. Emotional dysregulation accounted for a smaller but still significant 1.8 percent.

Together, poor sleep and difficulties regulating emotions statistically accounted for roughly a third of the observed relationship between heat and suicide-related thoughts.

The study design is worth understanding, because it shaped what the researchers could and couldn’t conclude.

Participants were interviewed twice – once in winter (January–February 2024) and once at the height of summer (May–June 2024).

Suicide risk was measured using the Brief Suicide Cognitions Scale, a validated tool that captures the sense of unbearability, unlovability, and unsolvability that precedes suicidal behavior.

Heat exposure was operationalized as the number of days with maximum temperatures at or above 35°C in the two weeks prior to each interview.

The panel structure meant the same individuals answered both rounds, which allowed the team to compare the same person’s mental state across seasons.

Summer scores were meaningfully worse: average suicide cognition scores rose from 10.99 in winter to 12.96 in summer.

Sleep quality declined. Emotional regulation worsened. Both effects were consistent across age groups, though older adults and women showed the steepest deterioration.

“Imagine a smartphone with a drained battery, overheating processor, and critical apps crashing all at once. Sustained ambient heat acts on the human brain and body in the same way,” Wahid explained.

“The body cannot cool down at night, leading to broken rest and depleting mental reserves. When the emotional processor overheats without restorative recovery, coping mechanisms collapse under stress.”

The study found that risk was notably higher during summer among less educated and poorer populations.

These differences may reflect unequal access to cooling, greater exposure to outdoor heat, and housing conditions that make it harder to escape high temperatures.

Individuals with disabilities showed consistently elevated risk across seasons. Unemployed people reported higher suicide cognition scores than those in most other employment categories.

Urban residents were more susceptible than rural ones. This may reflect the urban heat island effect. Concrete and asphalt absorb and radiate heat in ways that push nighttime temperatures higher.

There’s a global dimension to these findings that goes beyond Bangladesh.

Previous meta-analyses have found that a 1°C increase in monthly mean temperature is associated with a 1.5 to 1.7 percent increase in suicidal outcomes.

Bangladesh sits in a region the IPCC projects will experience some of the worst heatwaves of the coming decades. But the mechanisms the study identified are not unique to South Asia.

“Rather than treating climate-related mental health crises as unpreventable events, public health systems can now focus on intermediate, modifiable targets,” Wahid said. Sleep is one of them.

“Health agencies can monitor heat waves alongside sleep quality disruption indicators to mobilize preventative interventions. Interventions centered on sleep preservation, household cooling access, and community-based emotional regulation training should serve as effective suicide prevention tools during heatwaves.”

The paper points toward green roofing, passive architecture, and low-cost cooling technologies as structural interventions with documented effects on indoor temperatures in Bangladesh.

A pilot study found that buildings with vegetation-covered green roofing maintained temperatures 3.5°C lower than bare rooftops.

Such reductions could help make indoor environments more comfortable during extreme heat, potentially protecting sleep and reducing heat-related stress.

The study has some important limitations.

First, it relies on ambient outdoor temperature rather than indoor measurements. That’s a known proxy problem in Bangladesh, where air conditioning is rare and indoor heat tracks outdoor heat closely.

Humidity data wasn’t available, meaning the full thermal stress experienced by respondents – particularly relevant in a country where wet-bulb temperatures can reach dangerous levels – is likely underestimated.

What the study offers is new evidence that poor sleep and difficulties regulating emotions may help explain the relationship between extreme heat and suicide-related thoughts.

These findings point toward practical ways to reduce the psychological toll of rising temperatures.

Protecting sleep, improving access to cooling, and supporting mental health could become increasingly important as extreme heat becomes more common.

The study is published in the journal Environmental Research.

#6394. China restored its mangrove forests, and something remarkable happened

A 22-year study reveals how China's mangrove restoration efforts transformed coastal habitats and coincided with a dramatic rise in recorded bird diversity.

For decades, China’s coastal mangrove forests were cleared to make room for shrimp farms, ports, and development. By the 1990s, roughly two-thirds of these once-extensive forests had disappeared.

Then China launched an ambitious restoration effort, transforming large stretches of its coastline and creating new opportunities for wildlife to recover.

A study led by Ningbo University tracked what happened next. The researchers used 22 years of satellite imagery across five coastal provinces plus Hong Kong and Macao.

The team analyzed 13,308 Landsat images through Google Earth Engine, and bird survey records were pulled from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility.

The images revealed that the mangrove area grew 166 percent between 1998 and 2020, from around 10,600 hectares to more than 28,000.

Recorded bird species nearly tripled, from 148 to 397. The number of IUCN-threatened species found in these habitats almost doubled.

The sharpest growth came between 2003 and 2008 – 4,558 hectares in five years, the fastest expansion in the study period.

That expansion followed China’s 2000 Wetland Protection Action Plan, which helped direct attention and resources toward coastal habitat recovery. Later environmental protections reinforced those efforts.

Guangdong, Hong Kong, Macao, and Guangxi accounted for more than 88 percent of the national increase. Hainan added 1,678 hectares, while Zhejiang and Fujian – too far north to sustain them reliably – saw modest gains.

The latter occasionally even lost what had been planted, because cold snaps kill seedlings and typhoons don’t negotiate.

In 2008, Typhoon Nuri wiped out 80 percent of newly planted mangrove seedlings in Guangdong in a single pass. This is what restoration in dynamic coastal environments actually looks like up close.

The logic seems simple: plant trees and birds arrive. But the actual mechanism – which the Ningbo team reconstructed using partial least squares path modeling – is much weirder.

Mangrove area had the strongest direct effect on species richness. But the strongest direct driver of overall bird diversity wasn’t the forest itself – it was phytoplankton.

Expanding mangrove forests can influence water chemistry and nutrient flows in adjacent coastal waters.

The researchers found that mangrove expansion was associated with changes in coastal conditions that supported phytoplankton, an important foundation of marine food webs.

These changes may have benefited fish, shrimp, and the birds that feed on them.

Climate, meanwhile, had only indirect effects. It made conditions more suitable for mangrove growth as temperatures rose and rainfall increased.

Average vegetation cover across mangrove stands rose from 31 to 38 percent over the study period.

This suggests the forests were not only expanding but also becoming denser, providing more of the sheltered habitat that birds need for breeding and roosting.

But the researchers also identified an important uncertainty: how much of the apparent increase in bird diversity reflects ecological recovery, and how much comes from improved monitoring?

China’s birdwatching community has exploded over the past two decades, riding rising incomes and platforms like eBird.

Species that were always present but never recorded are now being logged. The jump from 148 to 397 species almost certainly mixes true ecological recovery with improved detection, and there’s no clean statistical way to separate them.

While this acknowledgment doesn’t invalidate the findings – the forest recovery is unambiguous in the satellite data – it should temper any instinct to take the bird numbers at face value.

There’s a second caveat worth noting: mangrove expansion sometimes converts intertidal mudflats, and mudflats are irreplaceable foraging habitat for migratory shorebirds.

Net gain in trees can mean net loss for specific species. Conservation math is rarely as clean as headline percentages suggest.

China’s experience demonstrates that sustained restoration efforts can help reverse decades of mangrove loss.

But it also shows that ecological recovery is complicated, shaped by storms, changing habitats, and the needs of different species.

Restoring coastal ecosystems requires more than planting trees. It requires understanding the entire web of life they support.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation.

#6393. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

#6392. AI is revealing a hidden world of animal behavior

Artificial intelligence is revealing subtle patterns in animal behavior that scientists have long overlooked, opening new possibilities for research.

For decades, scientists studying mice in laboratory mazes have largely tracked their movements as single dots on video screens.

That dot shows how far the animal went and how fast, but it can’t tell a mouse frozen in fear from one that has fallen asleep or stopped to groom.

Artificial intelligence now lets researchers track the whole body instead, from the curve of the spine to the position of each limb.

A new review of the field finds that this shift has changed what behavior research can measure.

But one of the major obstacles left is something no camera can fix: scientists still don’t share clear definitions for many of the behaviors they study.

The review comes from Ke Chen, Yaning Han, and colleagues. They work at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, two Chinese universities, and a Guangzhou biotech company.

The team’s research summarizes published research rather than reporting new experiments. Most examples involve laboratory mice and rats.

In classic behavior experiments, researchers place an animal in a simple, controlled space and record a handful of numbers.

A Y-shaped maze can test memory by measuring how often a mouse chooses the correct path to food.

In an open-field test, a mouse explores an empty arena. Researchers count how often it ventures into the exposed middle and treat that as a sign of anxiety.

Other setups, such as the Barnes maze, work on the same principle.

Tests like these are easy to standardize. But researchers using them see little of what an animal does on its own. Carrying a mouse from its home cage into an unfamiliar apparatus may also change how it behaves.

The authors described a bigger problem in the gap between these tests and brain research.

Today’s probes can record from thousands of brain cells at once, yet those recordings are often compared against a single number, such as speed or time spent in one zone.

The newer approach uses video, and AI software learns to mark chosen points on the animal’s body in every frame, turning a running mouse into a moving stick figure. Researchers call this pose estimation.

One of the most widely used programs, an open-source tool called DeepLabCut, needs only a modest number of hand-labeled images to get started.

By one estimate cited in a 2021 review, carefully labeling every frame of a one-hour video takes 22 person-hours.

Some labs also add infrared cameras or ultrasonic microphones that pick up calls too high for human ears.

A second layer of software sorts the tracked movements into behaviors. Some programs learn from clips people have already labeled, while others group similar movements without labels.

The label-free approach has turned up movements lasting less than a second that human observers had missed. Still, a pattern a computer can separate isn’t automatically a meaningful behavior, the authors wrote.

Some of the tools the review describes came from teams that included its own authors.

Chen and Kang Huang work for Guangdong BayOne Biotech, which holds patents related to a behavior-analysis technology called BehaviorAtlas. The other three authors reported no financial stake in the company.

Tracking one animal at a time is the simpler job. Once several mice share a space, the software also has to keep track of which mouse is which, and lab mice make that hard.

Many lab mice come from inbred strains or the same litter, so they look nearly identical. Curling up changes a mouse’s outline, and gnawing can leave patches of missing fur.

In the review’s comparison of tracking tools, a program called SLEAP achieved roughly 90% of its maximum tracking accuracy using only about 200 labeled video frames.

Even so, it mixed up the identities of mice about 23 times in every 100,000 video frames, compared with fewer than once for fruit flies.

A single swap matters more than it sounds. If it goes uncorrected, every later measurement for those animals can end up credited to the wrong mouse.

Implanted radio tags tell individuals apart reliably, and farms use the same kind of tag to monitor how much feed and water livestock take in. But implanting a tag is invasive, and the discomfort may change how the animal behaves.

The authors asked how long and how sharply a mouse has to swerve before its path counts as a left or right turn, rather than walking forward.

Without an agreed answer, researchers may rely on their own judgment.

Broader labels are harder. Anxiety-like behavior can mean less time on the open arms of a raised, cross-shaped maze, or a mouse that hugs the walls of an open arena.

Both carry the same name, but the authors wrote that the two tests may capture different things.

Social behavior adds another layer. With two mice, it’s unclear at what distance one counts as approaching the other.

When a third mouse enters the picture, two animals might gang up on one, or one might intervene in a conflict between the others.

In mouse models of Parkinson’s disease, a few points on one forelimb may be enough to spot a tremor.

Researchers running a more detailed study might need to separate normal grasping, shaky grasping and tremor at rest.

Because labs tailor their setups this way, their data often can’t be combined or compared. A shared data format called Neurodata Without Borders is an important first step, the authors wrote, but labs have taken it up unevenly.

The review’s more speculative ideas start with what the authors call “behavioral nucleotides.” In DNA, chemical units called nucleotides line up in sequences that carry genetic information.

The authors suggested describing each sampled moment of movement as a list of numbers and treating it as one candidate unit of behavior.

Strung together by rules they call behavioral syntax, those units would build into larger patterns tied to functions such as foraging or avoiding danger.

If that works, researchers could borrow tools built for analyzing DNA, such as lining up two sequences to compare them.

Researchers might also make short-range forecasts, stated as probabilities, of what an animal will do next.

The idea will only be useful if the units can be defined the same way every time, and chopping smooth movement into steps may lose some gradual changes.

The team also proposed “bilingual robotic animals,” robots that send precise, repeatable signals to live animals. Changing one signal at a time could slowly build a rough dictionary of animal body language.

But a robot can look, move and smell different from a real rat, so an animal may react to its strangeness rather than to the signal.

It’s still an open question whether any of this will help human patients.

Better tracking may make preclinical research, the lab work that comes before testing in people, more precise and easier to repeat.

That promise is limited by species differences, the authors wrote, and by the loose fit between lab tests and human psychiatric conditions.

Computer-generated animals could ease some of the need for live experiments. Virtual mice built from anatomical 3D models can produce training video with the labels already attached.

The National Institutes of Health has also emphasized research methods that reduce animal use.

In one study, software trained on synthetic video estimated poses about as well as software trained on hand-labeled footage.

Other studies measured different things, which makes their numbers hard to compare.

The authors recommended creating shared collections of real-world test videos so researchers can compare how well AI tools perform, whether they were trained on real footage, computer-generated videos or both.

The full study was published in the journal The Innovation Reviews.

#6390. Hubble discovers something strange is missing from nearby galaxies

Hubble reveals a mystery in nearby dwarf galaxies, where powerful stellar explosions appear to have swept away much of their oxygen.

The universe is filled with mysteries, and sometimes the most surprising discoveries involve something that should be there but isn’t.

NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope has uncovered one such puzzle in nearby dwarf galaxies.

These small collections of stars appear to be missing enormous amounts of oxygen that should have accumulated over billions of years.

A new study of 37 dwarf galaxies suggests that powerful explosions and stellar winds have been sweeping oxygen out of these galaxies far more efficiently than scientists previously thought.

The findings offer a new perspective on how galaxies evolve and how the chemical ingredients of the universe spread through space.

The spectacular Hubble image above shows NGC 4449, an irregular dwarf galaxy located approximately 12 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Canes Venatici.

Unlike the graceful spiral structure of the Milky Way, NGC 4449 has a chaotic appearance.

Bright blue stars are scattered across its irregular shape, while glowing pink clouds mark regions of active star formation.

These colorful features reveal a galaxy filled with energetic young stars and enormous clouds of gas and dust.

But beneath this dazzling appearance lies a surprising chemical mystery.

NGC 4449 was among the 37 galaxies examined in the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project.

Researchers discovered that dwarf galaxies retain only a small fraction of the oxygen their stars are expected to produce.

Oxygen is one of the most abundant elements in the universe. Much of it forms inside massive stars through nuclear reactions.

When these stars reach the end of their lives, many explode as supernovae, releasing oxygen and other elements into their surroundings.

Over time, these materials help enrich the gas from which future generations of stars and planets form.

Scientists expected to find more of this oxygen remaining inside dwarf galaxies. Instead, the new observations suggest that much of it has escaped.

“Oxygen is produced by stars, which are inside of galaxies,” explained Grace Telford, an assistant professor of physics and astronomy at the University of Utah.

Because dwarf galaxies have relatively weak gravitational fields, they struggle to hold onto gas propelled outward by powerful stellar winds and supernova explosions.

The study suggests that these winds are even more effective at removing oxygen than existing computer models predict.

The research team used archival observations from Hubble to examine individual stars and reconstruct the galaxies’ histories of star formation.

They combined these observations with data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope and ground-based radio telescopes.

By examining oxygen associated with stars, gas, and dust, the researchers could estimate how much oxygen the galaxies had produced and how much remained.

The missing material may be drifting through the diffuse gas surrounding the galaxies or may have escaped farther into intergalactic space.

Exactly where most of it ended up remains uncertain.

The findings are important because oxygen serves as a useful marker for other heavy elements created by stars.

Understanding where these elements travel helps astronomers explain how galaxies develop and enrich their surroundings.

The discovery raises new questions about how small galaxies influence the wider universe.

If dwarf galaxies regularly expel large amounts of oxygen and other elements, they may help distribute materials throughout the universe.

These materials could eventually form new stars and planetary systems.

Kristen Wingfield McQuinn is the GLOW project’s principal investigator and an associate professor at Rutgers University.

“It also helps us learn where and how much galaxies are enriching the space between galaxies, called the intergalactic medium,” said McQuinn.

Researchers hope to investigate even smaller galaxies using NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, followed by detailed observations from Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope.

For now, NGC 4449 offers a striking reminder that galaxies are not isolated collections of stars.

They constantly exchange matter with the space around them, shaping the chemical history of the universe.

The study was published in The Astrophysical Journal.

Archaeologists have unearthed a human-shaped funeral offering that may represent an ancient Japanese priestess.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a ghostly human-shaped artifact at a fifth-century burial mound in Japan. The clay figurine's appearance suggests it represents a female shaman who once guarded a tomb.

The artifact was unearthed at the archaeological site of Nishikaminomiya, northwest of Tokyo, according to a translated statement from Japan's Gunma prefectural government. At the site, archaeologists found nearly a dozen burial mounds known as "kofun" dated to the fifth and sixth centuries.

This time period in Japanese history, which lasted from about A.D. 300 to 710, is called the Kofun period. Many tombs in this period had cylindrical clay sculptures called "haniwa" that were used as offerings to the dead and were often thought to contain the souls of the deceased.

The newly unearthed haniwa is about 16 inches (40 centimeters) tall; but only the head and torso remain, so it would have originally been a lot larger. The figurine was discovered in a moat around an enormous burial mound that measured about 145 feet (45 meters) in diameter. It's likely that the haniwa was originally placed near a boat-shaped sarcophagus archaeologists discovered in the mound and that it slipped down the hill over time to land in the moat, according to the statement.

An aerial view of the tomb where archaeologists found the shrine maiden statuette.

Experts think the haniwa represents a female shaman known as a "miko," or "shrine maiden." These priestesses bridge the gap between the human and spiritual realms in the Shinto religion. During the Kofun period, miko would have performed important funeral rituals and offered spiritual guidance.

The haniwa figurine has a traditional Japanese topknot hairstyle called a "shimada," which indicates that the haniwa represents a miko, according to the statement. Both of the figurine's wrists have bracelets made from clay and red pigment. The haniwa's fingers have been carefully molded, and the figurine has a prominent nose. In addition, she wears a red sash painted on her torso and holds a rod-shaped ritual implement in her left hand.

"These details suggest that considerable care was taken in making the figure, even in features that would not be visible from a distance," representatives of the Gunma prefectural government said in the statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Archaeologists discovered the haniwa this year during excavations of the main burial mound at Nishikaminomiya, but they have been working at the site since 2020.

The haniwa is currently on display at the Gunma Prefectural Archaeological Research Center's Excavation Information Museum in the city of Shibukawa.

#6387. Carbon removal could reverse economic damage, but some countries would benefit more than others

Removing carbon dioxide could help economies recover from warming, but models suggest richer countries would benefit the most.

Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere could help reverse some economic damage caused by global warming.

But a new modeling study suggests that richer countries would gain the most, while many places would still face losses left over from warming.

Many climate assessments already count on carbon removal to help meet the Paris Agreement targets. This study asks what a cooler climate might mean for economies around the world.

Wenting Hu of the Institute of Atmospheric Physics, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, led the work with Wenguan Wang of Zhejiang University.

Their team combined climate simulations with an AI model of the world economy.

The model estimated that removal would boost output in almost every region, but only Asia and Europe would recover at least as much as they lost during warming.

The researchers stress that their simplified scenarios do not directly predict any economy’s future.

Earlier research has linked economic growth in states and provinces to daily changes in temperature and rainfall, including extreme weather.

Some methods describe those links with straight lines or simple curves, which the authors say may miss much of the complexity.

Studies of carbon removal have also tended to focus on the cost of removing the gas. Less attention has gone to what economies might gain from a cooler climate.

To explore that question, the team built EconClimNet, a deep learning model. This type of AI learns patterns from large amounts of data.

The researchers gathered economic records from 1,554 states, provinces, and similar regions across 77 countries.

They matched those records with 111 local weather measures from 1979 to 2016, including the number of wet days each year.

The model also accounts for national borders. It connects regions within the same country more closely because their economies tend to rise and fall together.

The team trained it on data from 1979 to 2008, then tested it on unfamiliar data from 2014 to 2016.

For total economic output, it scored 0.77 on a scale where one means a perfect match, compared with 0.59 for the next-best AI method.

The researchers then used six climate models from CMIP6, an international project that compares models using shared experiments. Each simulation began with carbon dioxide at its 1850 level.

The gas increased by 1% a year until it reached four times that level, then followed the same path in reverse. Each phase lasted 140 years.

Temperature and rainfall changes peaked about 20 years after carbon dioxide did. Even when the gas returned to its starting level, the planet stayed warmer and wetter, with smaller temperature swings from day to day.

The researchers measured how closely four weather features returned to their earlier state: average temperature, daily temperature swings, the number of wet days, and the heaviest two-day rainfall.

A recovery score of 100% meant a full return.

Across most of the globe, all four scored above 80%. Daily temperature swings recovered best, while average temperature and wet days recovered less fully on nearly every continent.

Northern North America and central Eurasia showed poorer recovery in average temperature and remained warmer. In these simulations, removing carbon dioxide did not return the climate fully to its earlier state.

When the team fed these climates into EconClimNet, global economic output generally fell as carbon dioxide rose.

Output improved in almost every region once removal began, and rainfall measures ranked among the weather factors the model relied on most.

Oceania had the steepest losses during warming, with a median decline in output of about $1.53 million a year. It also had the largest gains during removal, about $1.41 million a year, but those gains did not cover its earlier losses.

Asia gained about $1.23 million a year during removal, more than the $1.13 million a year it lost during warming. Europe roughly broke even, with gains and losses of about $1.22 million a year.

Every other continent recovered less than it had lost. These figures describe trends in the model, rather than forecasts for real economies.

The team divided countries into richer and poorer halves using economic output per person. Both groups lost output as carbon dioxide rose.

Richer countries saw larger losses, with a median decline of about $1.57 million a year, and every sector shrank. In poorer countries, manufacturing grew slightly, but losses in farming and services outweighed that growth.

The authors suggested that manufacturing in poorer countries may cope better with extreme conditions.

When carbon dioxide fell, both groups improved, with richer countries gaining more: about $1.56 million a year at the median.

Services, including retail, banking, and tourism, gained the most during removal. The longest stretch of wet days in a row was the weather measure that mattered most to the model’s results for this sector.

Earlier studies have found that services respond strongly to rainfall. Services also make up more of richer countries’ economies, which the authors say likely helps explain their larger gains.

Farming changed little overall and lost output in richer countries during removal. Those countries cooled more sharply, which the authors suggested could bring more crop damage from frost and cold fronts.

The researchers called for removal plans to support vulnerable nations in the interests of climate justice.

They pointed to climate finance, including carbon markets and loans on easier terms, as ways to help places that would gain less.

The study followed a deliberately simple path: carbon dioxide rose and fell steadily, while everything else affecting climate stayed at 1850 levels.

Removing so much gas so quickly would create major technical and practical challenges with current technology.

The authors cautioned that their conclusions do not “represent a near-term implementation roadmap.”

They did not model any particular removal method, such as planting forests, capturing carbon dioxide directly from the air, or adding alkaline minerals to seawater.

Real projects would also need to account for their costs and energy demands.

EconClimNet assumes that past links between weather and economic output hold for nearly three centuries of simulated time.

The authors acknowledged that some apparent gains may partly reflect quirks of the model.

Its economic records cover only 77 countries, and the team left out regions without data. The model also gives limited insight into why it produces particular answers or what causes the changes it identifies.

The researchers plan to make its reasoning easier to inspect. They say further climate experiments will also help distinguish real economic gains from effects created by the model itself.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation.

#6386. Planetary wreckage around a dead star may hint at Earth’s future

Mysterious rings of planetary debris around a dead star suggest that rocky worlds may survive stellar death, offering clues to Earth's distant future.

When a star like the Sun nears the end of its life, it swells dramatically, potentially swallowing the planets closest to it.

Around one dead star, though, the wreckage didn’t settle into a single ring, the way it has around every other dead star with a known gas disc. It formed two rings with a clear gap between them.

The team suspects that two rocky bodies survived the star’s transformation and that each may be supplying gas to a separate ring.

Astronomers call small rocky bodies like these planetesimals.

Nicola Gentile Fusillo, an astronomer at the University of Trieste in Italy, led the study.

“We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals,” he said.

Neither body has been seen directly. The team inferred both of them from the way the gas around the star behaves.

Near the end of its life, a star like the Sun expands and sheds its outer layers, engulfing nearby planets. Rocky bodies that survive can break apart.

Their pieces end up circling the dead star in a flat disc of dust and gas, and some of that rubble falls onto the star.

What’s left of the star itself is a white dwarf, the dense, burnt-out core. By the team’s estimates, this one holds about half the Sun’s mass in a ball roughly one and a half times as wide as Earth.

This white dwarf, called WD J1328–1450, became one somewhere around 73 million years ago.

The dusty disc around it is one of the brightest ever found around a white dwarf. Only a small share of these discs also contain gas. This one does.

The team studied the star with the X-shooter instrument on the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope in Chile.

The instrument spreads a star’s light out by color. In a spinning disc of glowing gas, the gas moving toward Earth and the gas moving away split each bright line into two peaks.

All 21 gas discs known before this one show that pair of peaks. This star’s calcium and oxygen lines show four. The team matched them to two rings of gas, one inside the other.

The inner ring stretches from about 60,000 to 147,000 miles (97,000 to 237,000 km) from the star.

The outer ring starts about 234,000 miles (376,000 km) out, close to the Moon’s distance from Earth, and reaches roughly 835,000 miles (1.34 million km).

Together, the rings span a region nearly twice the Sun’s diameter.

The shape of the lines held steady between observations in 2021 and 2023, about two years apart.

Co-author Felipe Lagos-Vilches is an astronomer at the University of Warwick in the UK and at the Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile.

“The structure we see in this system is particularly intriguing because the two gaseous rings are remarkably stable and remain separated by a gap,” he said.

When gas drifts away from where it formed, it cools and turns back into solid grains. So the gas stays close to its source.

Around another white dwarf, SDSS J1228+1040, astronomers had already picked up a signal in the gas that repeats about every two hours.

Astronomers could explain it only with a dense solid body inside the disc, making gas as it interacts with the dust.

Gentile Fusillo’s team argues the same thing is happening here, twice. Gas made in two separate places would form two separate rings.

At such close distances, the white dwarf’s gravity places severe constraints on the size and strength of any surviving rocky body.

The inner body is probably the size of a typical asteroid, no more than about 107 miles (172 km) across. The outer one could be far bigger, as large as Pluto or even our Moon.

The gas contains calcium, oxygen, magnesium and iron, a mix that matches the rocky material in our own solar system. But magnesium glows only in the inner ring.

If the outer ring had the same balance of magnesium to calcium, the magnesium would have shown up clearly. It didn’t.

The missing magnesium is a clue, because different kinds of rock contain different amounts of it.

Earth’s mantle, the thick rocky layer under the crust, has about eight times as much magnesium as calcium. Earth’s crust has less than twice as much.

The chemical differences suggest the rings could contain material from two different rocky bodies.

Or they may have come from two layers of a single broken planet, with magnesium-rich mantle in one ring and magnesium-poor crust in the other.

“The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized,” Fusillo said.

In the far future, the Sun will become a white dwarf too, and that change may destroy Earth. The two rings also resemble the rings seen in discs around young stars, where planets are still forming.

“The system therefore offers a remarkable glimpse of what the future of planetary systems, including systems like our own, might look like,” Lagos-Vilches said.

The team can’t pin down the exact orbits of the two bodies.

Another setup could also produce four peaks. A single disc that bulges upward could shade the region where the gap appears to be, though no existing model of these discs supports that idea.

Two white dwarfs, each with its own disc, would need conditions the team calls extremely fine-tuned.

The star is also taking in rocky material more slowly than its bright disc would suggest. The team suspects the disc may be relatively young, with material falling onto the star for only 300,000 to 600,000 years.

Neither of the leading explanations for how gas forms in these discs can fully account for the mysterious gap between the rings.

For astronomers, that mystery opens a new window into what happens when planetary systems fall apart. Even after a star dies, the remains of its planets may have a complex story left to tell.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

#6385. Scientists uncover a troubling pattern beneath Earth’s frozen ground

A global study of 156 monitoring sites reveals widespread permafrost thaw, raising concerns about infrastructure, carbon emissions, and climate change.

Every summer for the past three decades, Anna Klene has driven north across Alaska’s Brooks Range, and pushed a metal rod into the ground.

She records the depth at which it hits frozen earth. Then she moves on to the next site, and the next. It’s not glamorous science.

“It’s not super sophisticated,” she said. “You push down on the probe, put your finger on the rod and you can measure how many centimeters into the ground it went.”

These simple, long-term measurements have now produced something significant: the first global assessment of long-term permafrost monitoring data.

The findings confirm what climate scientists have feared. Permafrost is thawing broadly, persistently, and in ways that matter far beyond the frozen ground itself.

The measurement Klene takes is called active layer thickness. It refers to the depth of the ground above permafrost that freezes and thaws each year.

In a stable system, that layer stays roughly constant from one decade to the next.

When it deepens over time, it can signal that the underlying permafrost is warming and becoming less stable.

Permafrost is not simply frozen dirt. It’s soil, rock, and sediment bound together by ice that has remained frozen for at least two consecutive years. In many places, that happened for thousands of years.

Permafrost underlies 15 percent of exposed land surface in the Northern Hemisphere and almost all of Antarctica’s ice-free areas.

And it holds something that makes its stability a matter of global consequence. Roughly 70 percent of the organic carbon stored in permafrost soils sits in just the top three meters.

As the ground thaws, microbes can break down previously frozen organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere.

The study draws on data from 156 monitoring sites gathered between 2000 and 2024. The average record length per site is 20 years.

The pattern is consistent and troubling. Active layer thickness increased significantly at 55 percent of Arctic sites and 38 percent of Antarctic sites.

In mountain permafrost regions over 90 percent of sites showed significant increases. Several sites saw the active layer double in thickness over the study period.

At two Norwegian mountain sites, Juvvasshøe and Snøheim, the active layer increased by 8.45 centimeters per year. At Swiss Alpine sites, increases of 9 to 36 centimeters per year were recorded.

In the Arctic lowlands, sites with thick organic layers, including peatlands and densely vegetated areas, showed smaller increases.

That happens because the insulating properties of organic matter buffer the soil against air temperature swings.

It is the bare, sandy, and bedrock sites that are changing fastest. Alaska’s North Slope recorded active layer increases at most sites between 0.3 and 0.6 centimeters per year.

Sites previously impacted by wildfires showed larger increases, because fire removes the insulating vegetation layer, exposing frozen ground directly to summer warmth.

“One of Earth’s most important indicators of climate change is permafrost as it directly reacts to rising temperatures,” said lead author Dmitry Streletskiy, a geography professor at George Washington University.

“The significance of this study lies in the fact that we’re not just looking at isolated hotspots anymore.”

The regression analysis behind the study found that summer warmth is the dominant driver of active layer change in Arctic lowland permafrost.

Total liquid precipitation has a smaller but significant additional effect: wet summers deepen the thaw more than dry ones. Cold seasons, by contrast, have minimal influence once site-specific characteristics are controlled for.

Mountain permafrost behaves differently and is harder to model. The sites are highly heterogeneous and the available climate data at high elevations isn’t fine-grained enough to fully explain everything.

Some mountain sites, particularly in the Swiss Alps, are changing at rates that dwarf anything seen in the Arctic lowlands.

The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in China deserves particular attention.

Active layer changes on the Third Pole – so called because it holds more ice than anywhere on Earth outside the polar regions – averaged 3.2 centimeters per year from 2000 to 2024.

That’s roughly four times the Arctic average for continuous permafrost.

The plateau is warming faster than almost anywhere else on the planet, and it sits beneath infrastructure that crosses some of the most challenging terrain in the world.

Permafrost degradation is not an abstract threat.

Roads, railways, airports, pipelines, and buildings across northern Alaska, Canada, Siberia, and the Tibetan Plateau are built on the assumption that the ground beneath them stays frozen.

When it doesn’t, foundations shift, roads buckle, and infrastructure built over decades requires expensive repair or abandonment.

Communities in northern Alaska have already been forced to consider relocation as coastlines destabilize and the ground under their homes subsides.

“It’s hard to see that the first frost and the first snow are shifting by a day or two a decade,” Klene said.

“It’s hard to see that kind of change and really appreciate that it will have a big impact over time. But with these long-term monitoring sites, we can see that this gradual change is happening, and it’s going to affect the whole system.”

That system includes the carbon cycle. Continued warming threatens to shrink the extent of permafrost worldwide, with consequences that could unfold for generations.

What that means in terms of carbon release remains one of the largest uncertainties in climate science.

The study is published in the journal Communications: Earth and Environment.

#6384. A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers

A new proof-of-concept test surveys RNA in urine to spot bladder cancer. RNA carries information that can reveal what cancer is present and how it is behaving.

Andrew Brookes/Connect Images/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.

Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”

Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.

The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.

Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

#6383. Astronomers found the first star that would look green to the human eye

Astronomers have identified the first known green star, a white dwarf tinted by sodium from planetary debris, alongside unusually colored stars.

A dead star called WD J1330+6435 is the first known star that would appear green to human eyes. Astronomers at the University of Warwick identified it while working out the true colors of nearby white dwarfs.

The star’s green tint comes from sodium in rocky material it has pulled in from its own planetary system. That sodium absorbs the orange part of the star’s light.

The same work flagged WD J1011+2845, just 48 light-years from Earth, as what may be the reddest star ever recorded.

White dwarfs are the dense remnants left behind when Sun-like stars reach the end of their lives. None is close enough for its color to be seen directly.

The researchers worked from each star’s spectrum, the pattern produced when starlight is split apart by wavelength, and ran those spectra through a model of human color vision.

The sample covered the 151 white dwarfs within 20 parsecs, or about 65 light-years, of Earth.

The results correct a common misconception in astronomy that white dwarfs are typically blue. Hotter, bluer white dwarfs are brighter, so surveys based on brightness alone over-represent them.

Dr. Mark Hollands, a Warwick Prize Fellow in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Group at the university, led the work.

“Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like ‘perfect radiators,’ so their colour is set almost entirely by temperature,” Hollands said.

“It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colours nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me,” he added.

WD J1330+6435 has a temperature of roughly 7,200°F (4,000°C). It has accreted rocky material from its planetary system, enriching its atmosphere with calcium, lithium and sodium.

The atmospheres of these stars can reach roughly the density of water, millions of times denser than the Sun’s visible surface, the university explained.

Because this star’s atmosphere is so dense, the sodium absorbs light across a broad range of yellow, orange and red wavelengths. What remains gives the star a chartreuse green appearance in the team’s models.

As far as the researchers are aware, no other star, living or dead, has ever been credibly reported as green. That makes WD J1330+6435 the first known genuinely green star in the Galaxy.

“Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star,” Hollands noted. “It feels like something out of science fiction.”

White dwarfs that pull in the remains of planets carry elements such as lithium, sodium and calcium in their atmospheres, where astronomers can read them in starlight.

In 2021, Hollands and his colleagues reported lithium in four cool, old white dwarfs with cooling ages of five to ten billion years. WD J1330+6435, catalogued then as SDSS J1330+6435, was one of the four.

That work placed the star about 87 parsecs, or roughly 280 light-years, from Earth.

The amounts of lithium and potassium compared with sodium and calcium “strongly suggest that all four white dwarfs have accreted fragments of planetary crusts,” the authors wrote in Nature Astronomy.

Another star in that set, WD J2317+1830, also showed extra infrared light, a sign that it was still drawing material from a surrounding disk of dust and rock.

In the new color study, white dwarfs enriched with fragments of shattered asteroids and comets tend toward yellow. Carbon-rich white dwarfs are typically pink or purple.

In WD J0902+2010, the convection zone has reached the core and lifted interior carbon to the surface. There, carbon forms C2 molecules that absorb blue, green and yellow light, so the star would look pink to the human eye.

WD J1011+2845 goes further. Carbon molecules distort its light so heavily that almost all of it is squeezed into wavelengths beyond 600 nanometers, producing a deep salmon-pink glow.

Cooler white dwarfs with mixed hydrogen and helium atmospheres often take on a cyan or pale blue tinge. That color comes from hydrogen molecules colliding with helium atoms in their ultra-dense atmospheres.

Sirius B, the nearest white dwarf to the Solar System, has a hot hydrogen atmosphere that gives it a bluish color in the models.

Of the 151 nearby white dwarfs, five showed unusual coloring: two yellow and three pink. That suggests roughly one in 30 white dwarfs in the Universe shines with an unusually colored light.

For the remaining 146 stars, the median color temperature was about 6,800 kelvin, roughly 11,800°F (6,530°C), which people perceive as white.

Professor Boris Gänsicke of the Department of Physics at Warwick co-authored the study.

“One in thirty might not sound like a huge fraction, but across the entire population of white dwarfs in the Universe, that is still a lot of oddly coloured stars out there,” Gänsicke said.

“Yet if we take the median across a representative population of white dwarfs, we found that the average white dwarf really is white,” he explained.

The study was published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.
