This Roman glass cup can change from jade green to ruby red, and it features a mythical king who tried to banish Dionysus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Roman-era Lycurgus Cup has a color-changing effect depending on the light source.

The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman-era glass goblet that changes color from jade green to ruby red depending on if a light is shining on its front or back. But experts are unsure where the cup was found, where it was made, or whether the glassblower who made it created the color-changing effect on purpose.

In 1958, the British Museum acquired the cup from the Rothschild banking family, which had owned the artifact since the mid-19th century. Known colloquially as the Lycurgus Cup for its depiction of the mythical king who angered the god Dionysus, the glass is about 6.3 inches (15.9 centimeters) tall and weighs around 1.6 pounds (700 grams).

The glass is a remarkably well-preserved example of a Roman "cage-cup," according to a 1959 study of the artifact by archaeologists D. B. Harden and Jocelyn Toynbee. Only a handful of cage-cups still exist, and experts believe the goblets were made by cutting and grinding decoration into thick glass. Because small bridges were left to ensure the decoration remained on the glass, the overall effect is like a cage. Harden and Toynbee estimated that the Lycurgus Cup was manufactured in the fourth century, likely in Italy, but they noted that the bronze frame that forms the stem and rim of the goblet is probably a 19th-century addition.

Depicted on the cup is the myth of the punishment of Lycurgus, king of the Thracian tribe called the Edoni (also called the Edonians). Lycurgus did not approve of the worship of Dionysus and banished the god into the sea with an ax. But one of Dionysus' priestesses, Ambrosia, decided to fight Lycurgus. Ambrosia changed herself into a vine and wound herself around Lycurgus, who was unable to escape. The other priestesses thronged around them and tormented Lycurgus. Given that Dionysus was a god of wine and merriment, the depiction of Lycurgus' punishment may have been particularly appropriate for this goblet. Additionally, the change in color from green to red may have been meant to mimic the ripening of grapes on the vine.

Color-changing cups, also called dichroic cups, were mentioned in ancient Roman historical records. For example, a second-century letter possibly penned by Emperor Hadrian to his brother-in-law mentions a gift of two dichroic cups to use during banquets. But very few fragments of this mysterious type of glass survive today, a 2007 study noted.

For decades, experts have been working out how ancient Romans produced dichroic cups, and some have even replicated the Lycurgus Cup's color-changing effect. A 1963 study confirmed that the key seems to be the addition of microscopic nanoparticles of gold and silver during glassblowing that produce the appearance of milky-green glass when lit from the front and nearly translucent red glass when lit from behind. The metal nanoparticles are smaller than grains of sand and interact with light, creating the perception of a color change.

A replica of dichroic glass made by Corning Glassworks in the 1960s went from green to amethyst in the light, the 2007 study reported, and in 2020, researchers included silver and gold nanoparticles in 3D printing to replicate the color-changing properties of the glass.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

More recently, experts at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. reproduced the dichroic glass by reverse-engineering the "recipe" from the original Lycurgus Cup. The team then commissioned a glass artist to create a Lycurgus-inspired design from the replica.

But because so few examples of dichroic glass exist, experts are still unsure whether Roman artisans created the color-changing effect on purpose or whether traces of gold, which would have been available in an ancient craft studio, slipped into the molten glass and made a rare and unusual material that mystified even the most skilled glassblowers.

For more stunning archaeological discoveries, check out our Astonishing Artifacts archives.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6366. The Sky Today on Sunday, November 1: The Moon in Cancer

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

October 31: Glimpse the ghostly Phantom Galaxy

Daylight saving time ends at 2 A.M. local daylight time this morning, when clocks fall back one hour to 1 A.M. local standard time.

Early this morning, the waning gibbous Moon is in Cancer, just west of the naked-eye Beehive Cluster (M44). The cluster might be hard to catch today without optical aid due to the nearby light of our satellite, but should show up nicely in binoculars or even your telescope’s finder scope. Its stars are spread so widely — across nearly 100’ of sky — that observing them through a telescope at higher magnification only shows the cluster’s central regions.

East of the Moon, Mars and Jupiter shine brightly in western Leo, to the upper right of the bright star Regulus. Brighter Jupiter should be particularly easy to spot, located halfway between the Red Planet and the blue-white star.

The Moon will reach Last Quarter phase this afternoon at 3:28 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:29 A.M.Sunset: 4:57 P.M.Moonrise: 11:23 P.M.Moonset: 1:11 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (47%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

By 5 A.M. local time on November 2, western Leo is more than 50° high in the southeast. The Moon lies just to Mars’ upper right, roughly 1.5° southwest of the Red Planet’s position and 6.3° west-northwest of Jupiter. The gas giant is by far the brightest light here, shining at magnitude –2.0. This morning it lies halfway between the Moon and Regulus to its lower left (east), Leo’s alpha star and the base of the Sickle asterism.

This view offers a great opportunity to see just how far the Moon travels through our sky in a day. By tomorrow morning at the same time, Luna will have moved some 14° to the east, passing close to Regulus and standing southeast of the star in the early-morning sky at the same time. Make sure to check out the view tomorrow for comparison.

#6365. 12 Years Ago, This Jumbo Jet Vanished Without a Trace. New High-Tech Ocean Robots May Finally Reveal What Happened.

The 2014 disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 remains one of aviation’s greatest unsolved mysteries. Inside the latest high-stakes search to find the missing Boeing 777.

On January 2, 2018, from the port city of Durban in eastern South Africa, a ship departed at dusk. This was no vessel outfitted for a nighttime pleasure cruise. In fact, it looked downright strange. Its hull was a shade of prison-jumpsuit orange. Its bow was adorned with a large, flat platform resembling a helipad. Antennas, some pointy, some contained in two white domes, covered its superstructure. A crane was mounted on the ship’s stern. Belowdecks sat eight autonomous submersibles, each weighing about 4,000 pounds, or the equivalent of a Ford F-150. This ship was heading east, bound for a section of the southern Indian Ocean about 1,500 miles west of Australia. Its mission? To find the notorious Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

When MH370 took off from Kuala Lumpur on March 8, 2014, shortly before 1 a.m. local time, there was no indication it wouldn’t be a routine flight. But the Boeing 777-200ER never reached its destination, Beijing. Instead, after 39 minutes in the air, the jetliner disappeared from radar; about seven hours after that, it vanished altogether. Satellite communications analyzed afterward showed that MH370 had turned southward and continued on that course until it presumably exhausted its fuel supply and crashed in the Indian Ocean off the western seaboard of Australia.

An expansive search was quickly mounted, the largest ever for a missing plane. Some 60 ships and 50 aircraft from 26 countries participated, at a cost of more than $150 million. More than 46,000 square miles of Indian Ocean seabed were scanned over a three-year period.

But the plane was never located, and the question of MH370’s whereabouts set off a freneticism rivaled perhaps only by the mystery of Amelia Earhart’s fate on her final flight. In the decade-plus since the plane vanished, numerous and varied hypotheses have surfaced. The aircraft crashed somewhere else, some suggested. Others insisted the plane was shot out of the sky. So vexing was MH370’s disappearance that it even spawned a Netflix docuseries in 2023. Still others contend that, without a doubt, MH370 is on the bottom of the southern Indian Ocean.

Which explains the odd-looking ship that set off on its easterly course in 2018. The craft, a Norwegian-built research vessel named Seabed Constructor, was leased to Ocean Infinity, a deep-sea exploration firm with offices in Europe, Canada, Australia, and the United States. The Malaysian government contracted the company on a no-find, no-fee basis to look for MH370—a mission that promised a reward of up to $70 million. Over several months, Ocean Infinity used its autonomous subs to scan a grid of 9,600 square miles just north of the location where the original underwater search took place. By May of that year, having found nothing, the company suspended its mission.

Bringing the story of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 to a definitive close has been equal parts confounding and elusive. A fool’s errand, one might say. But in spring 2025, the government of Malaysia again contracted the firm—now equipped with new vessels of its own design, as well as advanced underwater robots—to mount a fresh search for MH370. In taking up the search again, in one of the toughest marine environments in the world, Ocean Infinity would be risking money and its reputation in the process. What if, for the second time, it failed to find a debris field of MH370 under the waters of the southern Indian Ocean? What if the black boxes couldn’t be located? What if we never get a definitive answer to how Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 went missing without a trace?

After its 12:42 a.m. takeoff from Kuala Lumpur, with 227 passengers and 10 flight attendants on board, Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 quickly reached its cruising altitude of 35,000 feet and steered toward Beijing. Flying the plane were first officer Fariq Abdul Hamid, 27, and pilot in command Zaharie Ahmad Shah, 53. For Hamid, this was his final training flight before becoming a fully certified pilot. He was in good hands. Zaharie (who was known by his first name) was one of the most senior captains at Malaysia Airlines. He also owned a sophisticated Microsoft flight simulator that he used frequently at home.

At 1:08 a.m., MH370 flew out over the Malaysian coastline, soaring above the South China Sea toward Vietnam. Just 11 minutes later, when the handoff from Kuala Lumpur controllers to Vietnam’s air traffic jurisdiction was about to take place, air traffic control in Kuala Lumpur radioed MH370 one final time.

“Malaysian three-seven-zero, contact Ho Chi Minh one-two-zero-decimal-nine. Good night,” they said.

“Good night. Malaysian three-seven-zero,” came the reply from the cockpit.

Those were the last words ever heard from the plane.

Soon the Vietnamese controllers saw MH370 cross into its airspace. But then something unexpected happened. Air traffic relies on secondary radar, whereby a transponder on an airplane sends a signal that contains information identifying the plane and its cruising altitude. This flight, instead, disappeared entirely from air traffic radar at 1:21 a.m. It wasn’t until four hours later, at around 5:30 a.m., that any sort of emergency response commenced.

The simple fact was that at 6:30 a.m. on March 8, MH370—carrying passengers from China, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan, India, Australia, New Zealand, France, Canada, the U.S., Ukraine, Russia, Iran, and the Netherlands—should have landed in Beijing. It didn’t.

Making sense of how an object as large as a Boeing 777 goes poof in the night is hard to fathom in our modern age. And for the human mind, which craves order and explanation, it is downright maddening—which might explain the bevy of individuals, with no connection to the flight whatsoever, who jumped in eager to provide answers. Over the many years since MH370’s disappearance, a variety of theories emerged about what happened to the plane. One scenario involves MH370 traveling toward Diego Garcia, a small atoll in the Indian Ocean where the U.S. has an army base, before being shot down. Another scenario claims the plane landed in the jungles of Cambodia. Other theories as to what happened to the flight received major airtime in 2023 during Netflix’s three-part docuseries MH370: The Plane That Disappeared. The plane, one person speculated, was hijacked by Russian agents and rerouted to Kazakhstan. Another person claimed the U.S. Air Force shot down MH370 over the South China Sea.

Whether the U.S. Air Force was really responsible was never seriously considered by Malaysia. But officials had suspected that the plane crashed in the South China Sea en route to Beijing. Accident investigators from Europe, Australia, and the U.S. teamed up with the Malaysian government and began searching the sea’s surface for any floating debris. That search was called off in April 2014 when nothing was found.

Yet within a week after MH370 apparently flew off the map, another theory surfaced in the Wall Street Journal. The article contains, to this day, the most plausible and reasonable explanation, one agreed upon by experts in aviation, satellite communications, and government: MH370 continued flying for hours after it disappeared from radar, turned west, away from its expected destination in Beijing, and then southward, ultimately meeting its demise in the waters of the southern Indian Ocean.

After the article was published, the Malaysian government eventually admitted that the account was true—which meant it had carried on a pointless search in the South China Sea for weeks. (In a comprehensive article for The Atlantic written in 2019, the late author and pilot William Langewiesche noted that autocratic bureaucracies with government-owned airlines generally want bad press to go away. It would be better, in other words, not to solve the puzzle, but to make the matter fade into memory as quickly as possible.)

To arrive at such a conclusion, the WSJ relied on an analysis of technical data from Inmarsat, a company that provides satellite services on land, at sea, and in the air. Although MH370 disappeared from air traffic radar screens, a feat easily achieved by whomever was manning the cockpit controls, it continued to link up every so often to a geostationary Inmarsat satellite over the Indian Ocean. Called “handshakes,” these linkups are electronic blips that, while tiny, yielded the most information about what happened to the plane. There were seven handshakes altogether: two that came automatically from the plane, and five others initiated automatically from an Inmarsat ground station in Perth, Australia.

The Inmarsat linkups provided two critical values. The first value is the burst timing offset, or BTO. It’s a measure of the round-trip time it takes for a blip to go from a ground station to a satellite to (in this case) an aircraft, then back up to the satellite and back to the ground station. It’s essentially the distance between the plane and the satellite, and that information gets processed as a series of rings, or arcs, of all possible locations. When it comes to MH370, the most important arc is the last one, the seventh, which the plane crossed at 8:19 a.m. Kuala Lumpur time. What’s important to note is that the seventh arc contains two location possibilities: If MH370 turned north, it may have ended up in Kazakhstan. If it went south, its location is in the southern Indian Ocean.

Determining the direction comes down to the second value: burst frequency offset, or BFO. It shows the difference between the expected frequency from a transmitter and the frequency ultimately received. As Langewiesche explained, the BFO is “a measure of radio-frequency Doppler shifts associated with high-speed movement in relation to satellite position.” Think about it and it makes sense: Neither planes nor satellites are stationary objects, so expected signals won’t match signals that actually get transmitted between the two. (That’s the Doppler effect, that change in frequency of radio waves.) Measuring BFO is a way to determine a plane’s speed and heading. During their investigation into the satellite data, Inmarsat technicians in London picked up on a distortion in the BFO value that suggested MH370 turned south at 2:40 a.m. Further analysis showed that MH370 entered a steep descent, as much as 15,000 feet per minute, just before crossing the seventh arc, which presumably happened after the plane ran out of fuel and both of its engines failed. From there it would have plunged violently into the ocean and shattered into millions of confetti-like pieces, to use Langewiesche’s analogy.

And it’s the satellite data, too, that paints a picture of MH370’s deviated flight path. Once the plane disappeared from secondary radar, it did an about-face over the South China Sea, flew back across Malaysia, over the Strait of Malacca separating Malaysia to the northeast and Indonesia to the southwest, and then, very suddenly, made a sharp turn to the southwest, away from the Andaman Sea to the west of Thailand. Accident investigators later determined that this turn was so tight there was no way the plane was still operating on autopilot. Someone was actively steering it.

What the satellite data doesn’t explain is why this happened—or who might have been flying the plane. Was it a potential hijacker? The available evidence says no: Malaysian and Chinese investigators, aided by American FBI agents, ran background checks on all passengers and flight attendants and cleared them of suspicion.

That left the pilots. Fariq Abdul Hamid was a young man with a fresh career as a prestigious Malaysia Airlines pilot ahead of him. Meanwhile, pilot in command Zaharie Ahmad Shah was portrayed in official reports as “someone beyond reproach.” Just a simple family man. Yet as Langewiesche discovered during his reporting in Malaysia, the official depiction of Zaharie did not align with the man’s private life: His wife had moved out, and he was “often lonely and sad.” He admitted to his own friends that he spent his off-hours “pacing empty rooms waiting for the days between flights to go by.” Among aviation investigators, there was strong suspicion, Langewiesche wrote, that Zaharie was clinically depressed.

And then there’s his flight simulator. Most times, Zaharie let simulated flights play out, from wheels up to wheels down. But a forensic investigation of his simulator showed that Zaharie had done a dry run of a flight profile that eerily mirrored MH370’s final flight path. What’s more, Langewiesche reported, “he advanced the flight manually in multiple stages, repeatedly jumping the flight forward and subtracting the fuel as necessary until it was gone.”

Was it Zaharie? One of the pilot’s lifelong friends, another Boeing 777 captain, told Langewiesche he believed it could have been. It’s not like such an event is without precedent: In 1999, for example, the copilot of EgyptAir Flight 990 intentionally crashed the plane into the ocean just south of Nantucket, Massachusetts. In 2015, the copilot of a Germanwings airliner deliberately crashed that plane into the French Alps. In a report published in 2014, the Federal Aviation Administration cites eight different examples of pilot suicides. And surveys conducted of pilots show that 4 percent have thought about taking their own lives.

As the search pressed on over the years, a group of researchers called the Independent Group emerged, made up of engineers and satellite experts who had found one another online as they simultaneously researched the MH370 crash. One of them, an engineer from Virginia named Victor Iannello, was the person who analyzed Zaharie’s simulated flight, coming to the conclusion that the simulation wasn’t some random event, but rather a potentially pivotal clue as to what happened on MH370’s final flight.

“Until MH370 is found and the reason for its disappearance is known, we will be bombarded with conspiracy theories, false leads, books, and movies which will provide nothing but conjecture,” said Prahlad Shirsath three months after the crash. His wife, Kranti, had been on board. “We need to find the truth,” he continued, “and ensure this never happens again.”

Where is that truth? Perhaps at the bottom of the Indian Ocean, the suspected location of the flight’s data recorder and cockpit voice recorder. Recovering the black boxes might help investigators resolve what happened to MH370. But we have to find them first.

The ocean is vast, and the ocean is scary. The deep ocean especially. Consider, for a moment, the possibility that we know more about Earth’s immediate orbit than we know about its oceans. In space, more than 9,000 satellites roam. On Earth, barely one-quarter of the planet’s oceans are mapped in any coherent way so as to make them discernible for underwater exploration.

In May 2014, the governments of Malaysia and China agreed that the Australians should lead the search for MH370, under the auspices of the Australian Transport Safety Bureau. Fugro, a Dutch firm, was contracted to do the work, with payment coming from Malaysia, China, and Australia. Given the satellite data that suggested splashdown on or about the seventh arc, an area of roughly 11,500 square miles across the arc was selected for exploration. This put the search area between 930 and 1,700 miles away from Australia’s western coast.

“Unforgivable” is perhaps the best word for describing the conditions of the Indian Ocean where search efforts were concentrated. The area saw ripping winds as high as 50 miles an hour, sudden powerful storms marked by 30-foot-high swells, and dense rain and fog. These were the least ideal conditions for sending ships out to sea for long periods of time, far from the closest ports, in a search for the maritime equivalent of a needle in a haystack.

When the underwater search for the remains of MH370 finally kicked off, the depths of the southern Indian Ocean were a mystery. An impressive level of surveying was conducted between May and December of 2014—with further mapping through early 2017—to even understand the topography of the deep ocean floor in this part of the world. It had never been mapped before. Fugro deployed three ships: the Equator, equipped with a hull-mounted echo sounder (to measure depth); the Discovery, with side-scan sonar; and the Supporter, which deployed a single autonomous underwater vehicle with side scanners, sonar, and an echo sounder. In all, close to 275,000 square miles of the deep ocean was surveyed, an area much larger than the search zone but valuable nonetheless for understanding the terrain.

Ridges, peaks, valleys, even underwater volcanoes covered the seabed. Most concerning was a deep underwater canyon that sliced horizontally through the seventh arc, believed by some to be the area where the remains of MH370 would be found. Dubbed Broken Ridge, it was formed by tectonic plate shifts more than 40 million years ago. Its depths reached between 2,000 and 20,000 feet beneath the ocean’s surface; sections of its topography were covered in sediment as thick as 1,000 feet.

“It’s like trying to imagine the Rocky Mountains underwater,” says Mike Exner, another member of the Independent Group. Exner is a retired entrepreneur from Colorado with a background in electrical engineering and satellite communications, having founded several of his own companies. He has also been a licensed pilot for more than 50 years. Exner was the person who studied Inmarsat data and civilian radar—primary radar scans resulting from simple pings about objects in the sky—to conclude that in MH370’s final hours, a flight to the seventh arc would not have been possible if there had been some sort of computer glitch or other systems failure.

“All those turns had to be done manually,” Exner says. “I think we’re about 99 percent sure Zaharie did it.” He adds that he can’t be 100 percent sure but says that once you consider the backgrounds of his copilot, the cabin crew, and the passengers, many of the signs point to him.

For almost three years, Fugro’s ships looked across areas on or near the seventh arc for any signs of the plane. Admittedly, there was a technological element working against them. Autonomous underwater vehicles have been game changers in underwater search and rescue, but they still come with certain drawbacks. Traditional radio waves with meaningful data rates don’t penetrate seawater at even paltry depths of six inches. Communication from ship or shore to a vehicle relies instead on sound waves. But even those become useless once the vehicle is roughly five miles away from its launch point.

“You have more contact with the Mars rover than you do [with] . . . a deep survey vehicle,” says J. Carl Hartsfield, director and senior program manager of the Oceanographic Systems Lab at the nonprofit Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in Massachusetts.

So we humans have to place a great deal of trust in technology that we can’t control once it gets out into the ocean. What’s more, Fugro had only one autonomous underwater vehicle at its disposal, and its maximum diving depth was 13,000 feet, which meant it wasn’t reaching the seabed most of the time. As the years went on, the search zone was expanded from the original 23,000 square miles to an area surpassing 46,000 square miles. But not a scrap of the plane was found, and on January 17, 2017, the Australian-led search was suspended, pending further evidence of the plane’s location.

Could it be that MH370 really isn’t near the seventh arc? Could it have ended up somewhere else? David Mearns, a marine scientist who has led several deep-ocean explorations, says there are only two ways to explain why any piece of the aircraft wasn’t found underwater.

“One, they haven’t looked in the right place. Or two, they’ve looked in the right place, but they missed it,” he says. “Anybody who comes up with anything else doesn’t know what they’re talking about.”

By the time Ocean Infinity arrived at the scene of the crash in January 2018, much more had been deduced about MH370’s probable location. While the initial underwater search took place, an amateur campaign to search for debris from the missing plane began. At the center of this was Blaine Gibson, a Seattle-based lawyer with a penchant for wearing a fedora. (The connection to Indiana Jones isn’t lost on him. By his own admission, Gibson is fascinated by mysteries and archaeology. According to him, he once went searching for the Ark of the Covenant, the gold-plated chest containing the tablets on which the Ten Commandments were inscribed.)

“I was astonished to learn that there was no organized search of beaches and shorelines,” he says. “It always seemed to me that the first piece of debris from this plane was probably just going to be found washed to shore by someone walking on the beach.”

He was right. In July 2015, a flaperon, an airfoil that attaches to a plane wing next to the flap, was discovered by a beach cleaning crew on the French island of Réunion, more than 3,500 miles west of Australia. A right wing flap was found on Pemba Island off the coast of Tanzania, in East Africa, in June 2016. And about four months earlier that same year, Gibson located a honeycomb object broken off from a plane’s horizontal stabilizer with the words “No Step” written on it, a piece that was confirmed to be “almost certainly from MH370 by matching part number, stencil, paint, and composition,” says Gibson. In all, more than 50 pieces of debris have been found so far, much of it on Africa’s eastern coast. (The currents in the Southern Hemisphere move in a counterclockwise swirl: east to west when they’re close to the equator; the opposite direction farther south.)

The significance of the physical evidence can’t be overstated. It appears to confirm that the plane crashed in the southern Indian Ocean, that it shattered on impact, and that there should still be more debris left on the ocean floor. The discoveries also refined the search area: Drift analysis conducted by the University of Western Australia put the crash site at a latitude somewhere between 28.3 degrees south and 33.2 degrees south.

In other words, the evidence provided Ocean Infinity a tighter target. In 2018, Seabed Constructor started its search grid at about 35 degrees south and some 1,300 miles to the southwest of Australia’s west coast. It was also better equipped this time, having brought eight autonomous free-swimming submersibles called HUGINs. These robot crafts, designed and manufactured by Norway-based Kongsberg Discovery, are able to reach depths of 20,000 feet. Each comes with a lithium-polymer battery pack weighing 660 pounds; that allows for around 60 hours of uninterrupted search time. Each is also equipped with a downward-pointing sonar system as well as side-mounted sonars to send out pings to objects on the ocean floor. Onboard magnetometers on every HUGIN can confirm whether a return ping indicates something metallic in nature.

Back in January 2018, The Economist reported that Seabed Constructor was “the most advanced civilian survey vessel,” and predicted that if it couldn’t find MH370, it was “likely that nothing will, and that the mystery of MH370 will remain unsolved.” In May, Ocean Infinity turned back to port, having found nothing on the ocean floor.

That two underwater searches proved fruitless has led to differing views as to where, exactly, the plane landed in the southern Indian Ocean. Richard Godfrey, a retired British aerospace engineer and a founding member of the Independent Group, believes the plane is farther north on the seventh arc. His conclusion largely rests on an analysis he’s conducted of data from WSPR, or Weak Signal Propagation Reporter. Amateur radio operators constantly send test signals and record the data that comes back. Godfrey says that when an aircraft flies through such a signal, it creates a disruption that can be used to track that craft. His results put MH370 inside an 18-mile circle at 29.128 degrees south latitude, approximately 970 miles west of Perth.

“It will only take one more search of this area,” Godfrey told the BBC in 2024, “and we will find MH370.”

Meanwhile, other research groups think differently. One contends MH370 is farther east of the seventh arc, in a 20,000-foot-deep hole that lies along the longitudinal line of Penang Island just off Malaysia’s western coast. Two separate groups believe that MH370 did not dive into the ocean and shatter; they think MH370 came to a controlled, guided landing, and then sank. Part of their argument rests on anomalies in the BFO data, those radio-frequency Doppler shifts. The predicted BFO came in at a much higher frequency than what was observed, possibly indicating that initial thoughts of where the aircraft came to rest are wrong.

One of those pushing this interpretation is Vincent Lyne, a former researcher at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania. He laid out his argument in a paper published in December 2024 and called special attention to the two large-scale searches along the seventh arc.

“A significant positive outcome for ocean research was the huge volume of seafloor data collected across [about 46,000 square miles],” he wrote. “It still remains the most intensely mapped seafloor area of our planet. MH370 was simply not there!”

How these interpretations factored into Ocean Infinity’s new search was unclear. The company is tight-lipped and declined an interview for this article, but CEO Oliver Plunkett did acknowledge Godfrey’s WSPR research in a 2022 teleconference with relatives who lost people on Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

If there’s a new dispute over the fate of MH370, it rests largely on where the plane will be found in the southern Indian Ocean, and not that the plane is somewhere under the seas in that part of the world. Gibson, who discovered part of the plane’s horizontal stabilizer, maintains that there’s no way a controlled landing took place. He cites the more than 50 pieces of debris that have been recovered since MH370 went down. “It’s not intact under water,” he tells me.

Exner, for his part, thinks the WSPR data is no substitute for the Inmarsat satellite communications. “Focus strictly on the seventh arc between 32 and 36 degrees south latitude,” he says. “[MH370 is] probably within 50 miles of that arc. Even though [Ocean Infinity] didn’t find it in the first search, that doesn’t mean it isn’t there.”

When Ocean Infinity ultimately resumed its quest for MH370, it was going back with even newer technology. In the time since its 2018 search, the company had built a fleet of more than 15 ships, ranging from vessels as short as 46 feet and as long as 282 feet. While small crews could climb aboard these ships, all of the vessels were nonetheless designed for remote operation from Ocean Infinity’s control centers at company locations. Ocean Infinity had also developed a line of proprietary underwater autonomous vehicles and acquired additional HUGIN submersibles to aid in its efforts.

The company had also accrued a solid track record of successful searches. Just under six months after Ocean Infinity suspended its search for MH370 in 2018, it discovered the lost Argentine Navy submarine San Juan in the Atlantic Ocean. The following year, it located the remains of the South Korean supertanker Stellar Daisy, which sank in the South Atlantic in 2017. In 2024, Ocean Infinity discovered the wreck of a U.S. World War II destroyer, USS Stewart, that the U.S. Navy had sunk deliberately for target practice in the waters of the Pacific Ocean off San Francisco.

Despite all that, Ocean Infinity trawled the unforgiving waters of the southern Indian Ocean for a few days in March 2025 until rough seas forced it back to port. It resumed searching in late December 2025 and kept at it through January 23, 2026, before departing the search area empty-handed.

“The scale of the challenge both geographically and technologically is almost impossible to comprehend,” said Ocean Infinity’s Plunkett in a March 2026 press release. “If nothing else, we can say with confidence that it isn’t where we looked. That matters—it brings clarity, and it will help those continuing to study the evidence refine their thinking and shape future search strategies.”

Underwater searches, obviously, are not easy or cheap endeavors. When Air France Flight 447 bound for Paris from Rio de Janeiro crashed and sank in the Atlantic Ocean off the northeastern coast of Brazil in 2009, the search team that was dispatched knew where to look for the Airbus jet. And despite it resting at a depth of only about 13,000 feet, the searchers still took almost two years to find it.

Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution’s Hartsfield, whose lab helped facilitate that search, can’t remember the exact figures but estimates that the ships deployed in the search operate at a cost of around $65,000 a day. The Remus 6000 Autonomous Underwater Vehicle used to locate the Airbus cost about another $15,000 a day (in 2026 dollars).

“Although this phase of the search has concluded, our commitment has not,” said Plunkett. “We’re continuing to work with the Malaysian government in the hope of being able to return when circumstances allow.” Ocean Infinity’s current contract runs until June 2026, which means if it hasn’t happened, it’s unlikely that a new search will get underway this year.

But as technology continues to advance, maybe someday an armada of vessels will hit the rough seas near the seventh arc once again—probing the depths, scanning the seabed, sending sonar scans into the darkness—and unearth the newest blips of hope in this maddening unsolved mystery.

Andrew Zaleski, a writer based near Washington, D.C., covers science, technology, and business.

#6364. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

J.M. Young et al. Permafrost detachment slides: a distinct high‐magnitude permafrost mass wasting process. Geophysical Research Letters. 2026. doi: 10.1029/2026GL124103

J.M. Young et al. Recent intensification (2004 – 2020) of permafrost mass‐wasting in the central Mackenzie Valley foothills is a legacy of past forest fire disturbances. Geophysical Research Letters. 2022. doi: 10.1029/2022GL100559

#6363. The Sky Today on Monday, November 2: The Moon passes Jupiter and Mars

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

The Moon slides 1.1° south of Mars at 9 A.M. EST, then passes 0.5° south of Jupiter at 6 P.M. EST. Some parts of the world will see these planets disappear behind the Moon, although this is not visible from North America. Instead, we’ll focus on the trio’s appearance before this in the early-morning sky, where they dominate in the hours before sunrise.

By 5 A.M. local time, western Leo is more than 50° high in the southeast. The Moon lies just to Mars’ upper right, roughly 1.5° southwest of the Red Planet’s position and 6.3° west-northwest of Jupiter. The gas giant is by far the brightest light here, shining at magnitude –2.0. This morning it lies halfway between the Moon and Regulus to its lower left (east), Leo’s alpha star and the base of the Sickle asterism.

This view offers a great opportunity to see just how far the Moon travels through our sky in a day. By tomorrow morning at the same time, Luna will have moved some 14° to the east, passing close to Regulus and standing southeast of the star in the early-morning sky at the same time. Make sure to check out the view tomorrow for comparison.

Sunrise: 6:30 A.M.Sunset: 4:56 P.M.Moonrise: —Moonset: 1:41 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (36%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

The Moon passes 0.8° south of the bright star Regulus in Leo at 4 A.M. EST on November 3. Some regions of the world will see our satellite pass in front of Regulus in an occultation, but again, the event is not visible from North America.

The pair rises together shortly after midnight on the 2nd, following Jupiter and Mars by roughly an hour. By 5 A.M. local time on the 3rd, the Moon-star pair is nearly 50° high in the southeast. Despite its brightness (it is ranked as the 21st brightest star in the sky), magnitude 1.4 Regulus will be the faintest object in this region, as magnitude 0.8 Mars and magnitude –2.0 Jupiter to its west (upper right) far outshine it.

The waning Moon has shrunk from roughly 43% lit yesterday morning to 33% lit today. It is just under a week from New phase, which occurs on the 9th. Between now and then, the phase will continue to diminish and the Moon will rise later in the morning each day, until it travels across the sky in tandem with the Sun when it is New.

Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual Of Mental Disorders", which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.

But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.

Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.

Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.

Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?

Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.

An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.

The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.

It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.

KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?

AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."

The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.

For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.

In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.

And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.

A neuron, in blue, is surrounded by a plaque of amyloid-beta protein, in yellow, which causes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. Tests can be used to detect biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.

I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.

Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.

But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.

With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.

So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."

It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.

KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?

AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.

Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.

It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.

Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.

That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.

KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?

AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.

There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.

That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.

For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.

Patients with anxiety may also be diagnosed with a mood disorder.

I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.

So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.

KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?

AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.

Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.

It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.

It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6361. Your Genes May Already Know Who You’ll Fall in Love With

Observable traits often determined by genetics may attract us to someone who shares them.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Besides the clichéd “must love dogs” and “likes long walks on the beach at sunset,” what do people actually look for when seeking a partner? Dating profiles barely touch on the qualities someone might imagine in their ideal match, and bathroom selfies aren’t doing us any favors. Sometimes the answer is so subconscious, it can only be found in our genes.

Trying to find the person who’s right for us is less random than we might think. When individuals with similar traits find each other, it’s known as assortative mating, which continues shaping the genetic makeup of human populations and is intentional—in a way—whether those couples realize it or not. In the back of our minds are criteria, such as education or certain behaviors, that potential matches have to meet. This can partly explain why some families have been known for certain traits for generations. Researcher Gretchen Saunders of the University of Minnesota decided to find out just how prevalent this phenomenon is by comparing genetic signatures in couples and across generations.

“Understanding mate choice, including how it is changing over time, is critical for both social science and genetics research, as it informs patterns of social homogamy and inequality while also affecting key assumptions in quantitative genetic and genetic epidemiological models,” Saunders, who specializes in statistical genetics and psychology, said in a study recently published in Behavior Genetics.

When partners carry similar traits that can be inherited, their children are also highly likely to be born with them, which can affect how those traits end up being distributed throughout a population. This doesn’t necessarily mean people explicitly choose each other based on those traits alone. It’s more likely that they already associate with groups that share the traits, and through those social and professional connections, they may eventually find a partner in such a group. Saunders based her research on eight specific traits ranging from physical features to education to habits that affect health. These included the visible factors of height and body mass index along with education level. She added five more having to do with drinking and smoking, such as frequency and the start or end of these habits.

Each subject who provided information for the study was given a polygenic score. These are numbers that merge the effects of different DNA variants in the genome to gauge a person’s genetic predisposition to a phenotypic, or observable, trait. Polygenic scores can also predict the likelihood of inherited diseases, which was not a factor in Saunders’ research. She was especially looking for similarities in polygenic scores between spouses and siblings. The phenotypic factor that was most similar between married couples was education level, which wasn’t surprising given that sociocultural variables have been observed in couples with phenotypic similarities for decades. Education was followed closely by alcoholic drinks per week. Less obvious links were body mass index, smoking initiation, and smoking cessation.

Seemingly unrelated traits were often found together. Those who had completed a higher level of education were often found to prefer partners who were taller, had a lower body mass index, and lower likelihood of smoking. Heavy smokers and drinkers tended to be attracted to those with similar habits and a higher body mass index. Polygenic scores based on this data revealed that while spousal genetic correlations were not as strong, they were still substantial. Traits already determined before these subjects became couples, such as height and body mass index, were the most correlated, while traits that were subject to change over time, such as cigarettes or drinks per day and smoking cessation, showed less of a connection. Comparing siblings showed evidence for partner matching based on these traits in earlier generations.

“Apparent differences in genetic architecture across cohorts may reflect not only temporal changes in assortative mating within populations, but also cross-cohort differences in underlying social structure, opportunity, and behavioral norms that shape mating patterns and phenotype distributions,” Saunders said.

So while DNA isn’t necessarily destiny, it may be, at the very least, pointing you in the right direction.

#6359. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

#6358. A Startup Wants to Put 50,000 Mirrors in Space. The Goal: Make Sunlight Available at Night.

For $5,000 an hour, Reflect Orbital will bring you the power of the sun no matter what time of night it is. Astronomers are sounding the alarm.

With the launch of Sputnik in October 1957, humanity officially entered the satellite era, and in the ensuing decades, the thousands of satellites sent into space have drastically changed life on the ground. These sprawling networks of orbital spacecraft provide us with constant GPS navigation, communication, weather forecasting, and an unprecedented level of scientific surveys. But for ground-based astronomers, satellites have been a steadily growing headache.

Problems really started back in 2019 when SpaceX launched the first cadre of Starlink satellites, and almost immediately their immense number and brightness disrupted ground-based observations of space. Today, there are more than 11,000 Starlink satellites, and scientists worry about their impact on next-generation telescopes, including the new Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile.

Now astronomers may have an even bigger problem on their hands: Reflect Orbital. If you haven’t heard of this company, that’s not surprising. Unlike SpaceX, they currently don’t have any satellites in orbit at all, but what they plan to do with those satellites once they’re nestled within Earth’s orbit has astrophysicists begging for the federal government to intervene.

“This is not a ‘concern’—this is like a bullet in your head,” Princeton University astrophysicist Gaspar Bakos told Sky & Telescope. “It’s the end of ground-based astronomy.”

So what exactly has astronomers like Bakos up in arms? Well, Reflect Orbital bills itself as a “sunlight-as-a-service” company whose constellation of 50,000 satellites, each armed with massive mirrors, directs sunlight toward dark areas of the planet. The company says users could conceivably call for sunlight on demand to power solar panels or aid in nighttime search-and-rescue operations. But this altruistic vision likely obscures more lucrative use-cases for the military. That seems especially likely given the going rate for sunlight: $5,000 an hour, according to Sky & Telescope. That price is well beyond the budget of most search-and-rescue groups.

Then there’s life on the ground. Plants and animals, humans included, depend on a day-night cycle that’s existed since Earth formed in the fiery cauldron of our star’s protoplanetary disk. Artificial sunlight could throw that rhythm off. Reflect Orbital CEO Ben Nowack dismissed these fears to the outlet Payload by saying that some people once feared light bulbs.

“I think a lot of people are scared of new things,” Nowack told Payload. “Similar concerns and fears were brought up when light bulbs were introduced to the world, and people were worried about circadian rhythm and like, is this godly?…I think it’s a sign that we’re doing something that’s really new and really important.”

On October 10, Reflect Orbital conducted a test of its technology near the town of Independence, California. As previously noted, the company doesn’t have any satellites in space yet, so instead they used giant, angled flood lights to mimic what the beam would look like from space and invited search-and-rescue groups to the demonstration. For astronomers, the blinding light confirmed their worst fears. Those fears have only grown since mid-July, when the Federal Communications Commission approved the company’s request to build a demonstration satellite called Earendil-1. The name continues the annoying trend of startups borrowing from The Lord of the Rings for their technologies.

“You might think a space mirror could illuminate a customer’s solar farm or a rescue site while leaving everything else untouched,” Macquarie University astrophysicist Richard de Grijs wrote for The Conversation. “That’s not quite how it works, because Earth’s atmosphere doesn’t respect sharp boundaries.”

A study in The Astrophysical Journal of Letters showed how molecules and aerosols would scatter this reflected sunlight, and another study detailed how a satellite with a 54-meter mirror (which is the operational goal) would still be brighter than our planet’s lone satellite if you were eight miles away from the beam. Within the beam, light would appear 40 times brighter than the moon, and the sky would be as luminous as after-sunset twilight. If Reflect Orbital reaches its planned 50,000-satellite constellation, the night sky would become three to four times brighter overall, according to the European Southern Observatory.

For now, the company is forging ahead with its plan to launch its first satellites with India’s Skyroot Aerospace, which will require authorization with the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre. This means the company could technically sidestep U.S. regulatory approval entirely.

“This whole question we have is: Who owns the night sky?” University of Alabama astronomer Michelle Wooten told Sky & Telescope. “I really feel that people should have a say on what their night sky looks like.”

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6357. What is the physical size of a 1-billion-solar-mass black hole compared to the Sun?

When a supermassive black hole is measured as 1 billion solar masses, what would be its actual physical size relative to the size of our Sun?

The size of a black hole is generally taken to be the size of its event horizon. The event horizon is a mathematical boundary around the black hole that marks the “point of no return” — anything that crosses this boundary is trapped inside and becomes part of the black hole forever.

The size of the event horizon can be calculated from Einstein’s field equations, and it depends on (1) the mass of the black hole, and (2) how fast the black hole is spinning. For a nonspinning black hole that has the same mass as our Sun, the radius of the event horizon (also called the Schwarzschild radius) would be about 1.8 miles (3 kilometers). A nonspinning supermassive black hole that is a billion times more massive than our Sun would have an event horizon radius that is a billion times larger, or 1.8 billion miles (3 billion km). This is 4,300 times larger than the radius of the Sun, or about the typical distance between the Sun and Uranus. However, if a billion-solar-mass black hole is spinning very rapidly, then the radius of the event horizon would shrink by about 30% (to around 1.3 billion miles or 2 billion km) because of the way the black hole distorts and drags space around it.

It is important to note, however, that while the event horizon is considered the outer boundary of the black hole, the mass inside the black hole has likely collapsed into a much smaller size under its own self-gravity, often referred to as a singularity. But we don’t actually know if the mass has collapsed into an infinitely small point in space, and, unfortunately, we can’t really say more than that because our understanding of physics breaks down under the extreme conditions that are present inside a black hole. So we use the event horizon as a convenient reference for the black hole’s size, because everything inside the event horizon is part of the black hole.

Misty BentzProfessor of Physics and Astronomy, Georgia State University, Atlanta

Satellite radar and underground electrical scans have revealed a 2,600-year-old structure at Buto, one of ancient Egypt's most sacred cities. The real surprise wasn't the walls — but what was underneath them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself.

The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians, it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape.

Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. Kom C itself rises above the surface as a visible mound, but earlier excavations had reached only the Ptolemaic and Roman layers before hitting the water table.

Now, researchers have turned to noninvasive tools, including satellite imagery, to delve into the mysterious subterranean layers.

First, they turned to the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellite, which can produce radar images by beaming down microwave pulses from orbit and then measuring how they reflect back; the returning signals can reveal subtle differences in surface moisture, elevation and reflectivity that can hint at buried structures beneath the ground. After looking at these radar images, the team spotted a large oval-shaped anomaly buried beneath Kom C that was 420 feet long and 203 feet wide (128 by 62 meters).

The geological profile of Tell el-Fara'in (ancient Buto) and the surrounding Nile Delta, showing the layered sequence of river sands and flood-plain clays from the last ice age and the settlement mound above.

To learn more without disturbing the site, the team ran 15 parallel lines of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) across an area of roughly 58,100 square feet (5,400 square meters). This technique reveals the underground landscape by passing electrical currents through the earth, measuring how they travel and creating a map that archaeologists can read.

The picture that came back was layered. Between the surface and 10 feet (3 m) down, the team found scattered Ptolemaic and Roman debris, including displaced mudbricks, pottery shards and broken limestone, which point to centuries of continued occupation and rebuilding on the site. Later residents dismantled older structures for reuse and left a scatter of displaced material behind.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment.

Deeper still, between 10 and 20 feet (3 and 6 m), the researchers found a large mudbrick structure from the 26th dynasty (688 to 525 B.C.), also known as the Saite period. They were able to date this discovery based on its layer, the unique shape of the mudbricks and other artifacts such as pottery, which the team dated by style and their archaeological layer, with carbon-14 dating applied to associated organic material. The large structure may be a tomb, a house for priests or a religious shrine, the team wrote in the study, published in March in the journal Acta Geophysica.

And below that, at 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) underground, the researchers unexpectedly found a thick, clean layer of sand.

That sand is the discovery within the discovery, the team wrote in the study.

The Nile Delta's clay is notoriously treacherous to build on. It absorbs moisture and swells, and then contracts and shifts as it dries — posing a slow-motion threat to anything heavy sitting on top of it. The Saite builders, it seems, knew this. Before laying the foundations to their structure, they packed a cushion of clean sand beneath it. This sand would have spread the building's weight, let groundwater drain through, and stopped the clay from creeping. It is the same logic behind modern load-distributing foundations — applied here more than two and a half millennia ago.

A 2D electrical resistivity scan aligned with a partially exposed mudbrick wall — the colored subsurface anomaly matches the location of the visible structure above ground.

"By combining satellite radar with deep ERT profiles, we didn't just map the walls of this massive Saite-era structure — we were also able to analyze the subsurface layers," study co-author author Abdelaziz Elfadaly, an associate research professor at Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences, told Live Science. "The detection of a significant, clean sand foundation layer beneath the mudbrick walls explains how these heavy structures survived the high water table and shifting clayey soil of Buto."

The sand layer, in effect, acts as a barrier; it stops groundwater from wicking upward into the mudbrick, which would soften and dissolve it. The sand also lets water drain sideways instead of pooling against the foundation, according to Elfadaly.

A 3-by-3 foot (10 by 10 m) excavation trench that was around 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) deep confirmed the presence of thick mudbrick walls resting on that sand layer, and nearby, a spread of objects that hint at the site's sacred function. According to Elfadaly, these finds included ushabti and shawabti figurines — small servant statues typically placed in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife — and a limestone altar whose carved channels bore dried residues consistent with animal blood, pointing to offering rituals performed at the site. The study also noted a rarer find: a faience baboon figurine, the kind associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

Layout of the ERT (electrical resistivity tomography) survey at Kom C. The blue lines mark one first set of profiles, and the red lines mark the second. Insets show the electrodes and cables deployed in the field, and a large mudbrick wall dating to the Late Roman period.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

A selection of artifacts recovered from the excavated square at Kom C, including small figurines and worked stone fragments from the Saite-era structure.

The Saite period was a moment of cultural revival. After generations of Assyrian and Libyan domination, Egyptian pharaohs retook the throne and poured resources into restoring Egypt's religious landscape, particularly in the Nile Delta, which had been their power base. Buto, with its deep ties to Lower Egyptian identity, was a natural focus. The Saite kings ruled from the nearby delta city of Sais, so restoring Buto reinforced their roots and their claim to the throne.

"A monumental building of this scale underscores the Saite pharaohs' intense commitment to glorifying the Delta region," Hussein Bassir, director of the Antiquities Museum at a cultural research center known as Bibliotheca Alexandrina who wasn't involved with the study, told Live Science in a WhatsApp message. "Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment."

The team is planning a return visit, this time using wider-spaced electrical resistivity surveys to reach deeper layers, along with specialists who study ancient plants and also understand how geological features changed over time, which may help reconstruct what the landscape around Buto looked like when these walls were first laid.

Abouarab, M. a. R., Elfadaly, A., Elbehery, W., Wafa, O., Aboalkassim, I., Younes, A., Hiekl, A. M. A., Saada, S. A., Wilson, P., & Ibrahim, A. (2026). Multi-scale detection of buried archaeological elements across different occupation phases: an integrated approach using radar satellite imagery and electric resistivity tomography at Buto, northwestern Nile Delta of Egypt. Acta Geophysica, 74(2). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11600-026-01809-4
