#6320. Faye Travel Insurance: The Best New Company Out there

We may receive compensation from Faye as an advertising partner. However, this does not influence our evaluations. Our opinions are our own.

I’ve been writing about travel for nearly two decades and, in that time, I’ve watched the travel insurance industry change at roughly the speed of a glacier. For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. After all, you should never, ever, ever, EVER travel without travel insurance. You don’t want to end up needing a GoFundMe to pay your bills and get home if something goes wrong. (You can’t predict the future!)

Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance company that launched coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty new to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

Faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

Faye has one plan for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. A lot of travel insurance companies have lots of plans and you end up squinting at coverage tables trying to figure out which one isn’t going to leave you stranded and has the coverage minimums you need. Faye built a single comprehensive plan that covers most of what travelers actually need:

These limits are pretty standard, especially on the medical coverage. If you want to add stuff on, they have a few optional addons that I think are really good and unique:

The CFAR insurance is really useful and I’ve rarely seen a company allow you to add it on to a policy. Usually, it’s already incorporated at a higher fee but this creates an affordable add on. I also love the pet care add on as more and more people travel with their pets.

Here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Get real-time flight tracking and alerts – You’ll get delay info, gate changes, or baggage carousel numbers when you land! A lot of apps do this but this is a nice add on.

Telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. If you wake up with food poisoning in a town where you don’t speak the language and don’t trust the local hospital reviews, you can talk to a doctor from your hotel bed. (As someone who has had to find doctors in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. (As someone who has had to do this in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u     pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Check destination essentials before you go – Visa requirements, plug adapter types, local emergency numbers, weather, currency conversion, even local apps worth downloading.

Chat with real humans, 24/7 – Actual customer experience specialists, available every day of the year, including weekends and holidays.

Buy an eSIM – The app also enables you to purchase an eSIM meaning you can avoid pesky physical SIM swaps and get connected to the internet right when you land.

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. If it’s a qualifying issue like a baggage delay or flight delay, you may get reimbursed almost instantly. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a new outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

For larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

The combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

If you’re heading out on a trip soon, check it out at withfaye.com, get a quote, and see for yourself.

#6319. Can You Pack Power Banks in Checked Luggage? 2026 Airline Battery Rules Travellers Need to Know

Most travellers now fly with several battery-powered items: a phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones, smartwatch, portable charger or vape. But packing one of them in the wrong bag can cause real problems at the airport.

In 2026, aviation safety authorities are warning travellers to pay closer attention to lithium batteries after reports that millions of batteries are still being packed incorrectly. The biggest mistake is simple: power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not go in checked luggage.

They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat, smoke or catch fire. This matters even more when your carry-on gets taken away at the gate and sent underneath the plane.

No. Power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not be packed in checked luggage. They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat.The same goes for loose camera batteries, spare laptop batteries, rechargeable battery packs, vape devices and phone battery charging cases. If your carry-on bag is taken away at the gate and checked underneath the plane, remove all power banks and spare batteries before handing it over.Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras with batteries installed are treated differently from spare batteries, but the safest habit is still to keep valuable battery-powered electronics in the cabin whenever possible. If an airline allows a device to be checked, it should be completely powered off, protected from damage and prevented from turning on accidentally.

The safest habit is simple: power banks, spare batteries and removable batteries stay with you. Valuable electronics are usually better in the cabin too.

Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage because they contain lithium batteries that can overheat if damaged, poorly packed, overcharged, exposed to heat or affected by a defect.

In rare cases, lithium batteries can enter thermal runaway. That means the battery heats faster than it can cool itself down. It may swell, smoke, burn or ignite.

If that happens in the cabin, passengers and crew can spot the problem quickly. Cabin crews are trained to respond to battery incidents. If the battery is hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold, it is much harder to access.

That is why this rule is not just airport red tape. A small charger in the wrong bag can become a serious safety issue.

Before you check a suitcase, look for anything with a loose, spare or removable lithium battery.

These items should stay in your carry-on or personal item:

You should also think carefully before checking valuable electronics with installed batteries, including:

Some airlines may allow certain devices with batteries installed in checked luggage if they are completely powered off and protected from damage. But for most travellers, the smarter choice is to keep electronics in the cabin.

Checked bags get dropped, delayed, searched and occasionally sent on their own little vacation. Your laptop does not need that character-building experience.

This is where the rules confuse a lot of travellers.

A spare battery is any battery that is not installed inside the device it powers. A power bank also counts because it is an external battery used to charge other devices.

A battery installed in a device is different. This includes the battery built into your phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones or smartwatch.

If the battery is loose, removable or used to charge something else, do not check it. The FAA’s lithium battery guidance says power banks and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage.

Gate-checking is one of the easiest ways to accidentally break the battery rule.

You may pack your power bank correctly in your carry-on at home. Then you reach the gate, the overhead bins are full and the agent tags your carry-on to go underneath the plane.

At that moment, your carry-on has become checked luggage.

The easiest system is to keep all power banks and spare batteries in one small pouch inside your personal item. If your roller bag gets gate-checked, you can remove the pouch in seconds instead of digging through your suitcase while the boarding line gives you the collective death stare.

Airlines measure lithium-ion battery size in watt-hours, written as Wh.

Most standard phone power banks are under 100 Wh and are usually allowed in carry-on baggage. Larger batteries may require airline approval, and very large batteries are generally not allowed in normal passenger baggage.

The 100 Wh rule matters most for large laptop power banks, professional camera gear, video equipment and drone batteries.

A typical 10,000 mAh power bank is often around 37 Wh. A 20,000 mAh power bank is often around 74 Wh. Larger power banks can get close to the limit, so check before you pack.

According to CATSA’s battery packing guidelines, travellers should keep batteries and electronic devices containing batteries in their carry-on baggage, avoid damaged or recalled batteries, and protect spare batteries from short-circuiting.

Look for the Wh rating printed on the back, bottom or side of the power bank. Newer batteries often show this number clearly.

If the label only shows mAh and volts, you can calculate watt-hours with this formula:

Since 1,000 mAh equals 1 Ah, a 20,000 mAh power bank is 20 Ah.

That would usually fall under the 100 Wh carry-on limit.

If the label has rubbed off and the airline cannot confirm the battery rating, the item may be refused. Do not rely on guessing at the airport.

Laptops, phones and tablets have batteries installed inside the device, so they are not treated the same way as loose spare batteries or power banks.

However, airline rules vary. If an airline allows these devices in checked luggage, they should be completely powered off, protected from damage and packed so they cannot accidentally turn on.

That means fully powered off, not sleeping, hibernating or sitting there quietly planning to wake up mid-flight.

In practice, keep phones, laptops and tablets in the cabin whenever possible. They are valuable, easy to damage and often essential if your checked bag is delayed.

No. Vapes and e-cigarettes should not be packed in checked luggage because they contain batteries. They should travel in the cabin and must not be used or charged during the flight.

Rules for vaping products also vary by destination, and some countries restrict or ban them. If an adult is legally travelling with one, it still needs to follow airline battery rules.

If you are packing for someone else, check for these before closing a checked suitcase. A vape tossed into checked luggage can create the same battery issue as other lithium-powered devices.

Smart luggage can usually be checked only if the battery can be removed.

A smart bag is luggage with built-in charging, tracking or other battery-powered features. If the bag is going into the cabin and meets carry-on size limits, it may be accepted as a carry-on. If it has to be checked, the battery must usually be removed and brought into the cabin.

If the battery cannot be removed, the airline may refuse to accept the bag as checked luggage.

Before travelling with smart luggage, find the battery compartment at home. Do not wait until the check-in counter to discover that the “removable” battery requires a tiny screwdriver, a prayer and the patience of a saint.

The drone or camera body may be allowed in checked luggage by some airlines, but spare lithium batteries should be removed and carried in the cabin.

Spare camera batteries and drone batteries should be individually protected so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. Use the original packaging, a battery case, a protective pouch or tape over exposed terminals.

If you travel with several batteries for photography or video work, check your airline’s quantity limits before you fly. Battery rules can be stricter for professional video gear and larger drone batteries.

Loose batteries should never be thrown into a bag with coins, keys, jewellery, cables or other metal objects. Battery terminals can short-circuit if they touch metal.

This is especially important for camera batteries, drone batteries and loose rechargeable cells.

Do not travel with a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, damaged or recalled.

A swollen power bank is not “probably fine.” It is a damaged battery and should be taken to an appropriate recycling or disposal location.

Before flying with an older power bank, check the model number and look for current recall notices from the manufacturer or your government recall site. Some recalled power banks may be prohibited onboard entirely.

If a battery looks questionable, leave it at home. Replacing a charger is cheaper than dealing with a safety incident at the airport.

If a battery or device becomes hot, starts swelling, smokes, sparks or smells strange during a flight, tell the cabin crew immediately.

Do not put it in the overhead bin. Do not hide it in a bag. Do not take it to the washroom. Cabin crew are trained to respond to battery incidents, but they need to know right away.

The goal is not to handle the problem yourself. The goal is to alert the people trained to deal with it.

Before leaving for the airport, do this quick check:

This takes less than two minutes and can prevent a pulled bag, confiscated item or airport delay.

Before you check a suitcase or hand over a carry-on at the gate, make sure:

Before you check any bag, open it and look for batteries.

Power banks, portable chargers, spare batteries and removable lithium batteries stay with you in the cabin. Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras are usually safer in your carry-on. If your carry-on gets taken at the gate, remove your battery pouch before the bag goes underneath the plane.

The goal is not to stop travelling with electronics. The goal is to stop packing them on autopilot.

A two-minute battery check before every flight can save your bag, your gear and possibly your travel day.

#6318. The Key to Stress-Free Travel Is the Right Gear—These Travel Accessories Pull Their Weight

The secret to a seamless travel journey is having the right travel accessories at your side. Whether you're boarding an early flight, hopping on a cruise ship, or catching a cross-country train, it pays to be prepared with smart gadgets and gear that make all the difference. From the packing cubes and laundry bags that help me fit the excessive amount of clothes I insist on bringing to the eye mask and neck pillow that make getting sleep at 30,000 feet possible, the best travel accessories pull their weight every time. After more than six years as a travel editor, I've figured out which essentials are worth bringing along. My lineup of foolproof travel accessories keeps me comfortable on long-haul flights, protects my suitcase from getting lost in transit, and ensures all my things are exactly where they should be.

To help every trip you take be a smoother one, I've put together a list of the very best travel accessories to pack on your next vacation. From in-flight necessities and organization hacks to tracking devices that deliver even the most anxious travelers peace of mind, these are the essentials I recommend most.

A tote bag is the ideal personal item—it's roomy enough to store all of your in-flight essentials and is usually pretty pliable, meaning you can squeeze it under the seat without taking up all of your foot room. Look for one with comfortable shoulder straps, a zipper or magnetic snap closure, and a few interior pockets to store your phone and passport. A trolley sleeve is a nice feature, too, so you can slide it over your suitcase while cruising through the airport. My personal favorite is MZ Wallace's Metro Tote—it's got more pockets than I know what to do with, and its super-soft straps never dig in to my shoulders. Cuyana's sleek System tote, L.L.Bean's iconic Boat and Tote, and Calpak's expandable Luka tote all come highly recommended by my fellow editors too.

A good toiletry bag keeps your products organized and your suitcase spill-free. These smaller options from Dagne Dover and Away offer enough space for your skincare essentials without taking up a ton of space in your suitcase. If you're going on a longer vacation or want to keep all of your products in one place (skincare, makeup, shower essentials, etc.), you might want to opt for Bagsmart's hanging toiletry bag that can be hooked onto the back of the bathroom door at the hotel. It keeps the counter clutter-free, and makes finding exactly what you need a breeze. Peak Design's best-selling wash pouch is another smart pick for longer journeys—commerce director Madison Flager has used hers for over five years and it's still in good shape.

Browse more toiletry bag recommendations.

A rule to live by: Never check your valuables, especially jewelry. Keep necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and rings safe and neatly organized inside a jewelry case that gets stowed in your carry-on luggage or personal item. These durable, compact cases have enough room to store a few different jewelry options. Mark and Graham's case is on the larger side, making it ideal for destination weddings, special events, or longer vacations.

Browse more jewelry case recommendations.

Rather than buy plastic minis every time you travel, get yourself a set of leakproof travel bottles to hold your at-home favorites on the go. My holy grail product, the Cadence capsules, are great for storing toiletries and beauty products, as well as small loose items like vitamins and bobby pins. I also regularly travel with a few of these silicone bottles from Amazon to hold shampoo, conditioner, and body wash. They're leakproof, easy to refill, and aren't super bulky in my toiletry bag.

Browse more toiletry bottle recommendations.

Instead of bringing entire bottles of medication or vitamins, pack a compact pill case that holds only as much as you'll need for the length of your trip. No matter where I'm headed, I always pack the Holii pill organizer—it's small enough to fit in my Dopp kit and has enough compartments to separate what I'll need for each day. Dosey's seven-day pill case is a nice pick for weeklong trips—and it looks so cute on any hotel bathroom counter.

I've recommended Afform's makeup bag to my mom, my sisters, my friends, and even strangers in the airport bathroom. It really is that good! The standout feature is its foldable shape: After you unzip the bag, each side can be pulled down to lie flat, allowing you to see all of your products at once. It's designed to keep each product secured in an upright position, reducing the risk of any spills. The bag's structured silhouette and flat base offer the stability and durability I want all of my breakable—and pricey—beauty products to have while in transit. For something less expensive, Eachy's best-selling makeup bag has a lot to offer—with plenty of room for full-size blushes and bronzers, as well separate compartments and multiple pockets to hold smaller products.

For years, I tossed my makeup brushes in a cosmetic pouch when I traveled—and I suffered the consequences. Not only did it make finding the right brush I need difficult, it also meant the rest of my makeup products ended up covered in leftover powder, blush, and bronzer. This all changed when I finally caved and tried out a dedicated brush holder a few years ago. With this $15 Amazon find, all of my makeup brushes stay in one place and can lay flat in the same direction, keeping them organized and away from other products. It’s large enough to hold several long, thin eyeshadow brushes and thick, dense foundation brushes (and a Beauty Blender too). The case's magnetic flap keeps my brushes secure and the soft silicone material means I can wash it off with ease.

All of those tech items you're bringing along mean you're going to have plenty of charging cubes and cables to keep track of. Save space in your backpack by keeping everything wrapped up in a travel organizer designed specifically for your electronic accessories, like the ones below from Peak Design and Bellroy. These are especially great for long flights where you're more likely to switch between devices.

Browse more travel tech organizer recommendations.

There's no sense in bringing your full-size day-to-day wallet on vacation—chances are, you only need a few cards and some cash. A slim travel wallet allows you to carry just those essentials, and makes it less of headache if it gets lost or stolen. Bellroy's RFID-blocking wallet is a smart choice for travelers, while Coach's sleek leather card holder fits in even your tiniest purses.

Browse more travel wallet recommendations.

A crossbody bag makes the most sense for travel—whether you're sightseeing around London or exploring the Disney parks, you want something to keep you hands-free and ready to go no matter what's on the agenda. These lightweight bags take up little suitcase space and have enough room for your daily essentials: wallet, keys, sunnies, lip balm, and hand sanitizer. Senior features editor Megan Spurrell swears by Baggu's nylon Crescent bag for its versatility and roominess, while commerce director Madison Flager's go-to crossbody is this sleek convertible style from Lo & Sons (you can remove the long strap and re-clip the sides to make it a shoulder bag whenever you need!).

Browse more crossbody bag recommendations.

Some instances call for a slim bag that holds your phone and little else. Whether you're headed to dinner on a cruise ship, down to the hotel pool, or to an outdoor concert, these tiny bags will keep your phone and a few cards secure, without the extra bulk that comes with carrying around a larger purse or tote. Senior commerce editor Hannah Chubb is a big fan of the Hailey crossbody phone case from Bandolier—she's had it for over four years and it's still going strong.

Browse more slim phone bag recommendations.

Also handy: a high-quality passport case (bonus points if it has space to hold your credit cards) to keep your most important document protected. Made of genuine Italian leather, Mark & Graham's sleek passport case is a thoughtful gift for any traveler in your life (especially since it can be monogrammed).

Browse more passport holder recommendations.

Is there anything more humbling that trying to fit a floppy sunhat into your suitcase? It takes up so much space and often leaves your favorite hat completely squished. Last summer, Chubb shared her top tip on how to pack the bulkiest thing in your vacation wardrobe: Use a hat clip. With one, your hat can hang securely from your personal item or suitcase without any fuss. Chubb's favorite one, the Toptote, fits in the palm of your hand. Its design is simple: Stick the brim of your hat between the two magnets, and it gets locked in place, letting your bag do all the heavy lifting.

For a comfortable journey at 30,000 feet—especially long trips where you’re hoping to get some shut-eye—an eye mask is crucial. The 100% silk option from Zimasilk and the soft, sculpted eye mask from MZoo are two highly rated Amazon finds. Both mold to fit to your face, provide total darkness, and stay in place.

Another comfort essential: a travel pillow. It can take some time to find the style you like best, and your pick might vary depending on whether you're in-flight or in a car or on a train. Cabeau's Evolution S3 and Ostrichpillow's Go memory foam pillow are among our editors' go-to's. They offer great head and neck support and are soft on the skin.

Alright, alright, a pair of foldable slippers isn't exactly a necessity for travel, but it is a simple in-flight luxury that makes your time in the clouds a little bit cozier. This one is for the travelers out there who insist on taking off their shoes on the plane (leave your socks on, please!), but still want to be kind to their neighbors. As you prepare for takeoff, slide on a pair of these lightweight slippers. They're not too structured, meaning you can fold them back up and tuck them into a small compartment of your personal item.

Frequent fliers who run cold would be wise to invest in a travel blanket—it'll keep you warm, and if you're on a red-eye, may help you actually get some sleep. Go for something lightweight that can be packed into a small pouch when you're not using it.

Browse more travel blanket recommendations.

We love a good pair of compression socks to fight that pins-and-needles feeling that comes from sitting still for too long, be it on a long-haul flight or a road trip. Our editors swear by socks from Bombas and Comrad—they're comfortable, stay in place, and help reduce swelling.

Browse more compression sock recommendations.

Even if you're not the type of person with a multistep in-flight skincare routine, a few basics can go a long way in keeping your skin happy and healthy after a long day of travel (just make sure all your products are in a TSA-approved size). For a quick dose of hydration, spray Summer Friday's Jet Lag mist before or after takeoff. I also love the brand's lip butter balm to keep my lips moisturized without feeling sticky. For some serious hydration, commerce producer ElleAnna Revell recommends Dieux's lipid-rich face moisturizer. And don't forget your hands—a shea butter cream will do the trick.

A few years ago, I slipped on a set of eye patches before takeoff—and I've never looked back. Now I always travel with a few under-eye patches stashed in my toiletry bag. I do it for the first-class feeling it gives me, but also for the much-needed dose of hydration and brightening it offers my dark circles. All of these options are great, but I recommend Peter Thomas Roth's if you have dry skin; if you hate the slipping and sliding eye patches tend to do, try Rhode's, these bad boys don't budge.

This $30 airplane tray table cover is one of my favorite in-flight travel accessories. It slides onto your tray table like a pillowcase, and completely covers the surface—so you can eat and work off of it without worrying about all those germs. Another bonus: It features four pockets to store essentials like your tablet, passport, water bottle, and phone. This means you won't accidentally leave your most important documents or electronics in the seat's safety manual compartment.

When you need some peace and quiet, swap your noise-canceling headphones in for earplugs. Traveler editor Jamie Spain is a big fan of Loop's earplugs for all kinds of situations—planes, crowded coffee shops, and nightclubs alike. They block out unwanted noise and are comfortable enough to wear for hours at a time.

Another must for general wellness: hand sanitizer. Buy a set and drop one in all your most-used totes and crossbody bags so you're never without. Wet Ones wipes are nice to have on hand too, especially if you're traveling with little ones.

If you’re prone to overpacking like I am, give yourself some added peace of mind with a digital luggage scale; it’ll let you know how much damage your souvenirs did before arriving at the check-in counter on the way home. I recently used this one from Etekcity on a trip to Charleston, South Carolina, and it gave me a nice warning that my bag was nearly overweight (no extra fees here!).

Browse more luggage scale recommendations.

Speaking of luggage, it's a good idea to attach a smart tag to your checked bag so you can easily track it. You'll have peace of mind knowing your personal belongings have made it safely to the right destination, and are right where you left them when you venture outside your accommodations.

Whether you're traveling solo or with kids, using a luggage connector to keep your suitcases looped together makes navigating through the airport a breeze. This three-piece set of luggage straps allow you to attach multiple suitcases together—and it's super simple to attach to any carry-on or checked bag.

Always travel with a luggage tag on your suitcase. It's helpful if your bag is lost and makes spotting your suitcase on a luggage carousel easier. If you want to make your luggage tag even easier to spot, I recommend personalizing it with your initials or snagging one in a bright color.

There's nothing like a dead battery to slow down a trip. Whenever my phone battery is running low, I pull out my tiny portable charger from iWalk. It charges my phone quickly and is only about the size of a lipstick. Both of the options below are compact enough to fit in a small fanny pack or crossbody bag.

Browse more portable charger recommendations.

A power adapter is a must for international travel to make sure you can get devices charged up in the airport and your hotel room. These both offer several different plugs, so you'll be good to go for travel to most anywhere in the world. Plus, you can charge multiple devices at once.

Browse more travel adapter recommendations.

Go cordless with this itty bitty audio transmitter. It plugs into the same jack that corded headphones would, allowing travelers to use their own wireless headphones to watch in-flight entertainment. I always slip this into my carry-on so I can watch movies with my over-ear noise-canceling headphones.

Another gadget I love: This handy phone mount, which lets you position your phone at eye level rather than having to lean it on your tray table or hold it in your lap.

Whether the plan is to listen to music, watch a movie, or just drown out noisy neighbors, most of us won't board a plane without headphones—especially a pair that are noise-canceling. Make sure you have your go-to on hand, plus a pair of corded earbuds (if you forego the aforementioned Bluetooth adapter).

Browse more noise-canceling headphone recommendations.

Even travelers with a library full of books at home have to admit it: E-readers are an essential travel accessory for bookworms. I love bringing my Kindle Paperwhite with me when I travel—it's lighter than even one paperback book, and lets me bring as many options as I want along for the ride.

This isn't a must for every trip, but a portable speaker is a nice addition to your packing list for beach vacations, bachelorette parties, or any time you're staying in a rental home. JBL's Go 4 portable speaker is small enough to slip into a fanny pack, while this Turtlebox option offers some serious sound.

Browse more portable speaker recommendations.

If you're traveling to a wedding or heading out on a business trip, you may want to bring a portable steamer along to make sure your formalwear looks its best after you take it out of your suitcase. These editor-tested steamers are lightweight, packable, and actually get the job done.

Browse more travel steamer recommendations.

Don't underestimate the power of a good packing cube. As a chronic overpacker, compression packing cubes save me every single time. They're designed to press clothing items down tightly so you can fit more inside my suitcase. Packing cubes also help keep me organized; you can sort them by outfit or by clothing type. I usually put bulky items like jeans and dresses in the larger cubes and socks, underwear, and tees in the small ones. These sets from Amazon Basics and Bagsmart are affordable and work just as well as more expensive options on the market.

Browse more packing cube recommendations.

Laundry bags are the newest addition to my lineup of travel accessories. I used to think it was a little unnecessary to pack a small laundry bag with me on a trip, but don't knock it til you try it. I love having a dedicated spot for my dirty clothes so they stay separate from the clean items in my suitcase. And this way, I don't end up leaving my already-worn outfits on the hotel floor (I hate clutter!). I recently bought this two-pack of laundry bags, and I'm planning to bring them on an upcoming trip to Newport, Rhode Island. They are so teeny tiny when empty, and when I'm back from my trip, I can easily dump the whole thing right into the washing machine—easy peasy!

I can't tell you how many times these on-the-go stain removers have saved me. From destination weddings to formal cruise dinners, it's always a good idea to have a little something to help with accidental spills. For small stains, I typically reach for a Tide To-Go stick. It's easy to discreetly pull out of my purse and is completely mess-free. For larger or tougher stains I really need to work on, I swear by Shout Wipe & Go wipes. I'm convinced they have magical powers.

Browse more stain remover recommendations.

This might seem like a no-brainer, but don't forget to pack a trusty reusable water bottle, so you can stop buying overpriced plastic bottles at the airport. Our editors love Owala—its bottles are durable, easy to hold, and keep water cold for hours. If you're tired of lugging around a 30-ounce water bottle, throw Hydro Flask's Micro Hydro in your tote or shoulder bag. In most situations, a few gulps on the go is really all you need! The brand just launched a new version with a built-in straw, so you don't have to unscrew the cap every time you need a sip.

Browse more water bottle recommendations.

The smoothest travel days start with a healthy dose of caffeine—I don't make the rules! I usually bring Owala's SmoothSip Slider tumbler with me because it's so compact and most importantly, it's actually leakproof. If I need to, I can safely toss it in a backpack or tote without worrying that my coffee might spill all over my laptop or Kindle. Plus, it keeps my coffee hot all day long every single time. Stanley 1913's travel mug with a top handle is another slim, lightweight pick you can trust.

We've all been there: You're fast-walking through the airport, hands full, hurrying to get to your gate on time while juggling your suitcase, phone, and a precarious iced coffee. This $10 travel accessory is here to lend a helping hand when you need it most. Simply slide it onto the handle of your suitcase and you'll have two cup holders, one for a coffee and one for a water bottle, as well as a hidden pocket for your phone and wallet, giving you the hands-free moment you need while navigating through the airport.

Time changes, long-haul flights, and jam-packed days can leave us feeling more run-down than we might like on vacation. LMNT electrolytes and Nuun Sport tablets are great at keeping you hydrated on long, active days in warm climates. Plus, they're easy to slip into any bag you're traveling with.

Do yourself a favor and pack a portable fan. A lightweight, handheld option will give you the breeze you need, whether you're in the back of a crowded bus or van, standing in line at Disneyland, or kicking back in a beach chair. Flager praises her Jisulife mini fan for its impressive battery life—it truly lasts all day long. I, on the other hand, love my small Gaiatop portable fan; it's simple to use, works really well, and has three different speed settings.

Browse more portable fan recommendations.

Depending on your destination, a travel-size umbrella might be worth the space in your suitcase. And if you're driving, tossing one in the backseat is a no-brainer. Weatherman's travel umbrella is by far the best model I've ever tried and it's super lightweight. For something slightly more affordable, Repel's windproof travel umbrella is a great alternative.

#6317. Sea to Sky Highway Named One of the Best EV Road Trips in the World

Most people know the Sea to Sky Highway as one of Canada’s most beautiful drives. It winds from the edge of Vancouver along Howe Sound, climbs past waterfalls and mountain viewpoints, and continues toward Whistler and Pemberton.

Now, it has another reason to be on your road trip list: it has been named one of the best EV road trips in the world.

According to a study by iSelect, British Columbia’s Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally among the world’s most EV-friendly road trips. The study analyzed 48 iconic road trips across six continents and scored each route based on factors such as charging infrastructure, distance, estimated charging cost, and traveller reviews.

For Canadian travellers, that is a big deal. EV road trips are no longer just about whether you can make it from one charger to the next. The best routes now combine scenery, reliable charging access, reasonable costs, and places you actually want to stop along the way.

Yes. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of the best EV road trips in Canada because it is relatively short, scenic, well-travelled, and supported by charging options along the route. iSelect ranked it seventh in the world for EV road trips, with 49 chargers available across its 121-mile route and a road trip score of 88.15 out of 100.

The route is ideal for electric vehicle drivers because it connects major destinations like Vancouver, Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton without requiring a long, remote drive through charging gaps.

Electric vehicles are becoming a bigger part of travel planning. The International Energy Agency expects global electric car sales to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. That means more travellers are thinking about charging stops the same way they used to think about gas stations, rest areas, and coffee breaks.

Charging infrastructure is also expanding. The IEA reported that the worldwide stock of public charging points reached more than 7 million at the end of 2025, with nearly 1.8 million public chargers added in 2025 alone.

That shift matters for road trips. A few years ago, EV travel could feel like a math problem with scenery attached. Now, on the right routes, it can feel much closer to a normal road trip — as long as you plan ahead.

The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally in iSelect’s study. The route stretches from Horseshoe Bay toward Pemberton, passing through some of British Columbia’s most famous scenery, including Howe Sound, Squamish, Whistler, and the Coast Mountains.

Chart idea: create a simple horizontal bar chart titled Top 10 EV Road Trips in the World, using the Road Trip Score column. This would work well just below the table.

One of the most interesting parts of the ranking is that Canada appears twice in the global top 10.

The Kootenay Highway ranked second in the world, with a score of 99.24 out of 100. The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh, with a score of 88.15. That gives Canada two of the highest-rated EV road trip routes in the world according to iSelect’s index.

That should not be surprising to anyone who has road-tripped through British Columbia. Canada’s western mountain routes already offer some of the best scenery in the world. The difference now is that EV infrastructure is starting to make those drives more accessible for electric vehicle owners.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not a long cross-country endurance test. That is part of what makes it such a good EV route.

The drive from Vancouver to Whistler is short enough for many modern EVs to handle comfortably, but scenic enough that you will want to stop anyway. Instead of treating charging as an inconvenience, you can build it into the trip.

Stops like Squamish, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, Whistler Village, and Pemberton give travellers natural breaks along the way. For EV drivers, that means charging can happen while you eat, hike, shop, or take photos instead of sitting around watching a battery percentage crawl upward.

Horseshoe Bay is a great place to start if you are coming from Vancouver. It has waterfront views, ferry traffic, cafes, and a relaxed village feel before the highway begins climbing toward Squamish.

Shannon Falls is one of the easiest scenic stops on the Sea to Sky Highway. The short walk to the waterfall makes it a perfect break on the way to Squamish or Whistler.

Squamish is one of the best stops on the route. It has food, coffee, outdoor shops, hiking access, and views of the Stawamus Chief. It is also a practical place to stop, stretch your legs, and check your charge before continuing north.

The Sea to Sky Gondola is one of the most popular attractions along the route. It offers sweeping views over Howe Sound and the surrounding mountains, making it an easy way to turn the drive into a full day trip.

Brandywine Falls is another easy stop between Squamish and Whistler. The walk is short, the waterfall is impressive, and it is a good reminder that the Sea to Sky Highway is not just about getting to Whistler.

Whistler is the main destination for many Sea to Sky road trips. In summer, it is great for hiking, biking, patios, lakes, and mountain views. In winter, it becomes one of North America’s most famous ski destinations.

Pemberton is a quieter extension of the trip beyond Whistler. It offers mountain scenery, farmland, and a slower pace for travellers who want to continue past the busiest part of the route.

Even on EV-friendly routes, it is still smart to plan your charging stops ahead of time. Check charger locations, charging speeds, plug types, and whether stations are available or out of service before you start driving.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not the place to play battery roulette. Mountain roads, weather, traffic, and detours can all affect range. Keep a buffer so you are not stressed if a charger is busy or unavailable.

EV range can drop in cold weather, heavy rain, strong winds, or mountain driving. The Sea to Sky Highway includes elevation changes, so it is better to plan conservatively.

The best EV road trips are the ones where charging fits naturally into the route. Stop for lunch in Squamish, explore Whistler Village, or take a scenic break while the car charges.

Do not wait until you are in a parking lot with weak signal to download a charging app. Set up your accounts, payment methods, and route planning tools before you leave home.

For an EV road trip, we would use a mix of navigation, charging, and general travel apps.

For more trip-planning tools, see our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

Absolutely. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of Canada’s great scenic drives whether you are driving an electric vehicle, hybrid, or gas-powered car.

The EV ranking simply shows that the route is becoming more accessible for modern travellers. The scenery was already there. The charging infrastructure is what makes it easier for EV drivers to enjoy the route with more confidence.

The Sea to Sky Highway’s global ranking is part of a bigger shift in travel. Sustainable travel is no longer just about choosing trains over planes or staying in eco-lodges. For many travellers, it now includes how they drive, where they charge, and whether road trips can be done with lower emissions.

Canada has the scenery. The challenge has always been distance. As charging infrastructure improves, more Canadian road trips will become realistic for EV drivers.

That is good news for travellers, but it is also good news for smaller communities along the way. EV road trips encourage people to stop longer, spend locally, and build their route around towns, restaurants, viewpoints, parks, and overnight stays.

Before driving the Sea to Sky Highway in an electric vehicle, make sure to:

The Sea to Sky Highway has always been one of Canada’s most spectacular drives. Now it is also being recognized as one of the best EV road trips in the world.

That combination makes sense. The route is scenic, manageable, practical, and packed with places worth stopping. For EV drivers, that is exactly what makes a great road trip. You do not want to plan your entire day around charging. You want charging to fit into a journey you already wanted to take.

From Vancouver to Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton, the Sea to Sky Highway proves that EV travel does not have to mean giving up adventure. It just means planning the route a little smarter.

And honestly, if your charging stop comes with mountain views and a coffee in Squamish, that is not exactly a hardship.

#6316. 9 Best Hotels in Rio de Janeiro for a Taste of the Carioca Lifestyle

“I live where you vacation” takes on a whole other meaning when, like me, you're based in Rio de Janeiro. I live smack in the middle of South America’s two hottest beaches—Copacabana and Ipanema—but it’s not the ocean that keeps me in Brazil's buzziest city. It’s the life that happens around it. It’s the sound of the first coconuts being cut open on the beach in the early morning, the sight of barefoot surfers passing beneath my window, and the honey-like melody of bossa nova flowing from a nearby beach kiosk. Not everyone can live here, of course. But luckily, the best hotels in Rio de Janeiro give you a good taste of what it feels like to be a local in Brazil’s most exciting metropolis.

Over the past six years, I’ve come to appreciate how each neighborhood lets you experience the city differently. Copacabana delivers the high-energy hustle and bustle you’d expect from a place that hosts the biggest Carnival celebration on Earth. In contrast, Leblon offers a quieter, more upscale seaside rhythm. And then there’s Santa Teresa, secluded on the forested hilltops, a tried-and-true bohemian village that’s managed to hold onto its personality despite the city’s rising tourism numbers. The hotels below span these special neighborhoods, with each property offering its own unique take on life in Rio, with Brazilian design, memorable views, and hospitality that’ll make you want to stick around just a little bit longer. Read on for the best hotels in Rio de Janeiro, according to our editors.

For glorious Brazilian beaches, Copacabana is ground zero. But the elegant Copacabana Palace is the hotel that created this place, making this strip of sand famous and helping to conjure the idea of the beach as central to Brazilian identity. When the Copacabana Palace opened over a hundred years ago, it occupied an unheralded neighborhood, amid modest houses and fishermen’s shacks. Until then, Rio de Janeiro had been centered on the old downtown areas of Centro and Castelo, and the 19th-century mansions of leafy Santa Teresa, but a new age of leisure arrived in the post-war years. Sunbathing was suddenly a thing, and Coco Chanel made having a tan fashionable. Designed by French architect Joseph Gire, the Copacabana Palace adopted the elegant Art Deco lines of the grand hotels of the French Riviera. More than a century on, the Copacabana Palace is still a Rio icon, bestriding the Avenida Atlântica on that incomparable bay. The style is classic opulence, with vast chandeliers, acres of marble, and Brazilian hardwoods; a sanctuary among the city’s endless partying. But this is Brazil. The Palace may be grand, but it is also fun. The dining options are fabulous, there is a rooftop tennis court, and, across the avenue on that famous beach, hotel staff attend to guests with umbrellas, loungers, cold towels, and sun lotion. —Stanley Stewart

The modern antidote to the Copacabana Palace’s grand hotel glamour, Philippe Starck’s Brazilian debut—which opened in 2007—has design cred in spades. The 89 all-white rooms have balconies (42 with ocean views), but you’ll want to spend time at the rooftop bar by the infinity pool to gaze at Ipanema, Leblon, the Two Brothers Mountain, and Corcovado; watch the sunset; and sip rum muddled with fresh strawberries, a local fave. Other amenities include a spa, beach service, a fitness center, and bike rentals. Proximity, too, is key: The Fasano is across the street from Ipanema Beach, and a seven-minute walk from General Osório metro and 12 minutes from Copacabana Beach.

The Fairmont Rio de Janeiro Copacabana is a lively beachfront hotel that pairs the comforts of a major luxury brand with the Brazilian energy people come searching for. The 375 rooms and suites are spacious and comfortable, and all come with balconies to enjoy the fabulous views. Speaking of which, the property's signature sixth-floor infinity pool melts into the Copacabana horizon, and everything happens around it: specialty coffee and gelato are served in the roomy lounge, contemporary Brazilian dining is highlighted at the outdoor Marine Restô, and cocktails are enjoyed on loungers and cozy couches around the poolside bar. The pool deck also hosts live music, late-night DJs, and Sunday feijoada (a traditional black bean stew) meals, making this a space where Rio’s visitors and locals collide. Elsewhere, the modern gym has everything you need, and I’d return for the spa alone—the two-hour Fire Ritual treatment is a particular highlight. With ongoing beach activities, weekend yoga, and Ipanema within walking distance, this is a hotel that matches Rio’s upbeat social life.

Think of Hotel Santa Teresa Rio MGallery by Sofitel as a hacienda-style counterpoint to the flashier options on the beach. Part of the mini boutique hotel boom happening in the quiet hilltop neighborhood of Santa Teresa, this former derelict mansion has 44 rooms, all with wood floors and sun-filtering shutters that nod to the tropical surroundings without hitting guests over the head with it. The service can be uneven—veering between over-attentive and indifferent—but the 80-foot pool, with its view over Santa Teresa’s stately villas and the glittering waters of Guanabara Bay, and lush gardens more than make up for it. The spa here is worth checking out, too.

Subtle and modern, in contrast to the go-go party scene of the Fasano, Emiliano was a welcome addition to Rio’s oceanfront Avenida Atlântica when it opened in 2016. A five-star SLH property, the 90 rooms and suites—spread across 12 floors—are large and filled with lovely touches like plants and plump white sofas that make it feel like your own sophisticated beachside apartment, while the bathrooms have huge showers and bathtubs. Plus, beach access is great: It's right across the street from the southern part of Copacabana Beach. Be sure to enjoy the rooftop infinity pool overlooking the ocean.

With 51 rooms, Janeiro has the intimacy of a boutique hotel with the five-star service of a much larger luxury brand. Sitting across the street from Leblon Beach, one of the city’s most beautiful stretches of ocean, the beachy property's interior design reflects the effortlessly chic aesthetic of co-owner Oskar Metsavaht, founder of Brazilian fashion label Osklen. Monochromatic tones, warm wood, and oversized windows keep Rio’s natural surroundings front and center in all rooms. Thoughtful touches like yoga mats, afternoon tea service, exceptionally plush robes, and complimentary Ipanema flip-flops make the stay feel more personal than most. The breakfast service feels like being secretly let into a bakery, with warm pão de queijo (Brazilian cheese bread) promptly delivered directly to your table, and a colorful assortment of bread spread out over the bar. Downstairs, Cedilha draws a cool crowd for New York–style bistro dinners, while the rooftop plunge pool frames the twin-peaked Two Brothers Mountain through a circular window. Beach service, bicycles, and nearby gym access make settling into Rio’s laid-back lifestyle easy.

Form meets function at Ipanema Inn, an independently owned urban hotel just one block from the world-famous Ipanema Beach. This thoughtfully designed property channels Brazilian modernism through midcentury furniture by designer Sergio Rodrigues, natural materials, and rooms that range from compact courtyard-facing doubles to a duplex suite with sweeping mountain vistas and space for the whole family. At ground level, Quitéria, the acclaimed in-house restaurant, spills out onto the mosaic sidewalk of Rua Maria Quitéria, where chef David Cruz serves a refined menu sourced from small Brazilian producers. Breakfast runs until 11:30 a.m., staff is among the warmest you'll encounter anywhere, and complimentary bikes connect you to a segregated coastal path stretching from Leme all the way to Leblon. With the metro two minutes away and three of Brazil's hottest designer boutiques within the same radius, this is Rio at its most stylish and convenient. —Patrick Gray

An effortless oceanside social hub with modernist Brazilian design notes, Hotel Arpoador is known for its cool, carefree style and on-site wellness offerings. I first visited Hotel Arpoador when it reopened in 2019 and noticed its unique setting: Arpoador is on one of the only stretches of coastline in Rio that is traffic-free. Returning several years later, I rediscovered a hotel that has become a modern classic on the Rio scene, and the freshness is a joy to behold. Do as I do and head down to spend your days surrounded by the spectacle of Rio’s famous beach culture. Hotel Arpoador offers a beach service with chairs, umbrellas, towels, and staff that can look after your belongings as you frolic in the frothy, wild Atlantic. Be sure to make time to enjoy the rooftop with its triangular pool and panoramic ocean views, as well as the Maré Spa wellness space with its excellent treatments and steam room. And don't forget to grab a drink at Arp Bar—with its in-the-know crowd that spills out onto the beachfront from dawn to dusk, it has become the beating heart of Rio’s social scene. —P.G.

Set on a hilltop in the historic Santa Teresa neighborhood, Chez Georges is a striking example of Brazilian Brutalism, offering sweeping 360-degree views of Sugarloaf Mountain and Guanabara Bay. Just a 20-minute drive from the vibrant Copacabana Beach, its secluded setting feels like an urban retreat, where time slows down and the morning begins with the gentle sound of birds. Whether lounging by the 50-foot pool, listening to soft Brazilian music from the record player, or watching the sunset, Chez Georges offers a tranquil, almost dreamlike escape. While Chez Georges may be modest in size, with only a handful of suites, the rooms themselves feel anything but small. Each suite is designed with ’70s-inspired minimalism. Inside, you'll find a standard wardrobe, desk, and king-size bed, but it’s the floor-to-ceiling windows that steal the show, opening onto a shared balcony with sweeping views that are perfect for watching the sunrise. —Kayla Brock

What is the best neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro to stay in?

For a first visit, I’d choose Ipanema. You have the beach, excellent restaurants, Brazilian boutiques, and metro stations all within easy reach—and it’s very much a lived-in neighborhood, teeming with locals and businesses around the clock.

What is the nicest hotel in Rio de Janeiro?

For classic luxury, Copacabana Palace gets my vote. The century-long history, grand beachfront setting, celebrated pool, and attentive service make staying here feel like you’re playing a part in Rio's story.

How we choose the best hotels in Rio de Janeiro

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. If you're used to cruising in the Caribbean, shore excursion prices on your Alaska cruise might surprise you.

Want to take a helicopter ride to the top of a glacier to enjoy a dogsled ride? It'll cost upward of $700 per person. Excited about an authentic Alaska fishing experience? That's a more than $400 tour. A nearly three-hour scenic train ride on the White Pass and Yukon Route Railroad starts at more than $150 per traveler.

Not only are tours so pricey because Alaska is a remote destination (where it costs more to fly in goods and materials), but also because Alaska is part of the U.S., where wages and tour insurance costs can be higher than in the islands. Plus, many Alaska excursions involve seaplanes, helicopters, specialized boats and other equipment that only add to the price of your onshore experience.

For many, an Alaska cruise is a once-in-a-lifetime trip, and many tours are worth the splurge. But you don't have to spend money hand over fist in every port. Whether you're trying to balance your budget with a few cheaper days or you simply don't have the resources to spend big every day of your vacation, you'll want to seek out cheap or free things to do in Alaska's cruise ports.

Luckily, you have plenty of options. I know because I've spent many a day exploring independently in Alaska's ports. Plus, I consulted with Alaska's tourism representatives to bring you a comprehensive list of free (and cheap) things to do in Alaska on a cruise.

Skagway is known for its gold rush history, but you don't need a pricey tour to immerse yourself in the town's storied past. Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park has four free museums open to visitors, including the Visitor Center Museum (with interactive exhibits), the Moore House Museum (former home of the first family to live in Skagway, with two restored Victorian-era rooms), the Jeff Smiths Parlour Museum (a former bar with a shady past) and the Mascot Saloon Museum (a restored gold rush saloon).

If you're fully embracing the old-timey vibe, you'll want to belly up to the bar at the Red Onion Saloon. Once, it was Skagway's signature bordello, but now it's the place to sling back an Alaska-brewed beer or snack on apps and pizzas named after former good-time girls. For a reasonable $20 a person, you can sign up for a Quickie Tour of the venue's supposedly haunted brothel museum. Ghost sightings don't cost extra!

One of my favorite things to do in Skagway is stretch my legs on a hike, and there are several trailheads within easy walking distance of your cruise ship. Options include the Upper and Lower Dewey Lake, Reid Falls and Gold Rush Cemetery, and Icy Lake and Upper Reid Falls trails. The National Park Service kindly lists its hikes by distance from Skagway's Historic District, as well as by level of difficulty. No guide is needed, and you don't have to pay to access the trails.

Related: Alaska cruise guide: Best itineraries, planning tips and things to do

Window shopping is a popular activity along the main streets by Juneau's cruise docks, but you might be tempted to blow your budget on souvenirs. (Look for sales, especially during end-of-season sailings, if you want to buy gifts for less.)

Typically, you can pay $60 for an all-day pass up and down Juneau's Goldbelt tram*, or if you're in good shape, you can hike from your ship to the top of the tram on the Mount Roberts Trail for free. I did this hike on my recent Alaska cruise, and while it's not technical, it is steep and can be muddy after a rainstorm. Make lots of noise just in case bears are on the trail.

At the top, you can visit the Chilkat Theater to watch a free movie about the region's Tlingit people. If you're too tired to hike back down, you can get a ride back on the tram for $20.

However, the Goldbelt tram has been closed since late April 2026 for maintenance. Visitors can still go to the base of the tram to watch Tlingit artists carve totem poles, weave ceremonial robes and perform cultural dances for no charge.

Other hikes accessible from your ship include the Gold Creek Flume Trail and the Perseverance Trail.

If a stroll through downtown is more your speed, self-guided tours of Juneau come free of charge. The Juneau Voices project features audio installations at 11 spots around town where you can learn about the city through the stories of Native Alaskans. Or grab a map from a tourist welcome center and follow this walking tour to see the city’s highlights.

You can also find a PDF guide to Juneau’s totem poles online.

If you prefer to get your history and culture indoors (not a bad plan in Alaska, given the temperamental climate), Juneau offers a few museums with modest admission fees that are worth checking out.

The Juneau-Douglas City Museum offers a mix of permanent and temporary exhibits on the area's history and art. Admission is $7, but you might need a cab if you're not up for a 20-minute walk. The museum also runs a free walking tour of the Alaska State Capitol Building.

Also, a 20-minute walk from the port is the Alaska State Museum, where you can learn about the cultures of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples. Admission is $14. For more information on Native Alaskans and their cultures, visit the Sealaska Heritage Institute's Walter Soboleff Building ($10 admission) and its gift shop, which features local art. Don't miss the signature totem pole and handcrafted clan house.

If you’re keen for a scenic uphill walk, head up Basin Road to the Last Chance Mining Museum ($5) to learn about the gold rush in a historic mining building.

*At the time of writing, Goldbelt tram is closed but has plans to reopen soon. Check availability and prices before you plan.

Related: Alaska cruise mistakes you never want to make

Ketchikan is best known for its Creek Street Historic District, built on a wooden boardwalk above the salmon-filled Ketchikan Creek. Stroll for free by its historic buildings, shops and restaurants, or pay $10 to stop into Dolly’s House for a glimpse into the city’s former red-light district.

Not far from Creek Street, the Tongass Historical Museum and Totem Heritage Center immerses you in the area’s history for a modest $6 fee (children and military are free). From there, you can embark on a self-guided, 1 1/2-mile Ketchikan Salmon Walk to learn about the fish’s impact on the town (and maybe even spot some, in season, at the Salmon Ladder). The walk will take you past the Totem Heritage Center (also $6, or get a combo ticket to both museums for $9), with its collection of 19th-century totem poles rescued from nearby islands.

If you’re feeling adventurous, you can skip the tour and head out to the Saxman Native Village on your own. It’s 2 miles south of Ketchikan, so it's walkable — but for a few bucks, you can take a city bus there instead. It costs just $5 to wander the park on your own and see the 25 replica totem poles, as well as Native carvers working on new poles using traditional techniques.

Icy Strait Point is a manufactured cruise port near the town of Hoonah. It was created to offer everything cruisers could possibly want in a port, so all the activities are planned to get you to part ways with your hard-earned cash. That said, there are still plenty of things to do in Icy Strait Point for free or cheap.

A free gondola ride transports visitors from one cruise pier area to the other, but if the line is long or you’re afraid of heights, you can walk the same path on nature trails instead. Keep your eyes out for wildlife.

The port has tons of beach access, so you can wander Icy Strait’s shores, stop for scenic photos and look for marine life free of charge. At the Hoonah Cannery building, you can browse the Hoonah Packing Co. Cannery Museum exhibits interspersed among the shops, or get tickets to the Native dance show for $20 per person at the on-site ticket booth.

From the cannery, it’s a 1 1/2-mile (roughly 30-minute) walk to Hoonah, an actual town where many of Icy Strait Point’s workers live and home to Alaska's largest Tlingit village. You can also take an affordable $10 shuttle to town, where you can admire the totem poles and sip a local beer at Icy Strait Brewing.

Related: The best Alaska cruise shore excursions — from heli-hiking to whale watching

Sitka offers a compelling mix of Native Alaskan and Russian history and culture, and a self-guided tour of the key sites in town won't cost you much (if anything at all).

You can get a free tour of the Russian Bishop’s House, an example of 19th-century architecture during Russia’s colonization of Sitka. Baranof Castle State Historic Site (Castle Hill) was occupied throughout the centuries by Tlingit people and later by Russian settlers, and it was the site chosen for the transfer of Alaska from Russia to the U.S. You can check out the views and the informative signs for free.

St. Michael Cathedral National Historic Landmark is an exact replica of the first Russian Orthodox church in the Americas. Because the site has an active congregation, visitors can view its collection of 17th-century religious artifacts for a limited time each day.

Museums with small admission fees include the Sitka History Museum (featuring exhibits on local history) and the Sheldon Jackson Museum (showcasing a collection of Alaska Native artifacts). If exploring old cemeteries is your thing, you’ll want to stop at the more than 200-year-old Sitka Russian Cemetery, with gravestones made from the ballast of Russian ships.

The Sitka National Historical Park’s visitor center and grounds (with walking trails and totem pole installations) are open to all, free of charge. It’s a scenic spot for an easy nature walk, or you can come inside to learn more about Sitka’s Russian and Tlingit cultures or join a ranger program.

You don’t need a tour to gawk at eagles, hawks, owls and falcons at the Alaska Raptor Center. Admission is $16, though it is a bit of a walk from downtown. Watch injured birds relearn how to fly, and take a stroll through the center’s forested grounds.

Finally, you can attend various dance performances at affordable ticket prices. The Alaska Storytellers dance show ($15) celebrates traditional and modern Russian dance, while the New Archangel Dancers' performances highlight Russian folk dances. Or, step into a Tlingit clan house to enjoy the music, costumes and choreography of the Naa Kahidi Tlingit Dancers.

You don’t need to spend a fortune on tours to explore Alaska's culture and history or enjoy its natural splendor. You’ll find plenty of free things to do in port on an Alaska cruise. However, I do encourage you to budget for a few tours, whether it’s to travel beyond the port area into Alaska’s wilderness or to immerse yourself in an activity, such as dog sledding, kayaking, fishing, or whale or bear watching. You won’t regret spending the money on amazing experiences and memories.

#6314. Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs

If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Nomad Citizen covers people under 56 and earning at least $4,000 USD per month. You sign up online, choose your start date, declare that you’re in good health, and confirm you’ll be outside your passport country for more than half the year. You can also add your partner and any children under 18.

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really quickly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the plan can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.
