#6273. We've Tested Dozens of Toiletry Bags—These Are Our Top Picks

If there's one travel truth I live by—and hold dear to my heart—it’s that a dream vacation deserves a dream toiletry bag. After all, what’s a perfectly packed carry-on without a designated home for your favorite lipstick, beloved serums, sunscreen, and all those little beauty essentials that somehow multiply before every trip? The best toiletry bags make room for the whole glam squad, without adding any more suitcase chaos to the packing equation.

On all of our worldly journeys, Condé Nast Traveler editors (myself included) have tested dozens of travel toiletry bags to find the ones worth your precious packing space, from streamlined makeup pouches for the less-is-more crowd to roomy, cleverly compartmentalized cases for those who believe in a 10-step skincare routine. It's no easy job finding the best ones: Some tear after just a few months of use, others have awkwardly sized compartments. Many are too big for a standard carry-on, while others have proven too small to fit the simplest of our travel necessities.

With wipe-clean linings and durable construction, plus smart pockets and ultra chic designs, the carefully selected, editor-tested toiletry bags that earned a spot on this list are the crème de la crème. Read on for our recommendations to keep your essentials organized and your travel beauty routine in check.

Tested by: Jessica Sulima, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? About a year now, and despite how much it’s melded to different parts of my suitcase, the leather has stayed nicely intact.

What is it best for? It's best for longer trips, when you need to carry full-size toiletries. That being said, it also works if you don’t have that much to pack, because the leather folds down however you’d like. I like that the products stay upright for the most part, so you don’t have to worry about bottles squeezing open. The shape makes it so that you can rifle through your things comfortably without dumping everything out.

How much does it hold? My entire skincare routine—cleanser, toner, moisturizer, sunscreen—plus my daily makeup. There’s even room for my vitamins too.

Tested by: Madison Flager, commerce director

How long have you been using it? I've been using this Peak Design toiletry bag for five or six years.

What is it best for? If you're in search of a toiletry bag to keep up with an extended itinerary, this is your solution: It's ideal for longer trips of five days and more. Sometimes I pack it on weekend trips too, but it's a bit bulky, so I find it better suited to checked luggage, or trips where I'll need a good amount of product.

How much does it hold? This is one of the toiletry bag's best features—it truly holds so much. Everything in my routine fits like a glove, each with a dedicated space. I usually bring along shampoo, conditioner, body wash, face wash, moisturizer, eye cream, contact solution, a toothbrush, toothpaste, and floss, plus smaller items like tweezers and nail cutters. There's an exterior pocket sized for a toothbrush, and one inside with a magnetic snap where I store a razor. Plus, there’s a hook on the outside, so you can hang it up in the bathroom.

Tested by: Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? This gem is a newer addition to my travel rotation. I've traveled with it for around two months now—and knew it had to be mine when I saw it came in a glazed dark cherry colorway. (That's now sold out, but there are loads of other fun colors to choose from in the same style.)

What is it best for? Given its spacious yet puffy, cloud-like design, the Luka bag is ideal for any trip where you have some extra room in your carry-on, or are bringing a checked bag. It's a bit bulky for a weekender or duffel bag, though I'd try to squeeze it in if I was packing light. For any of these trips, you can use the hanging clip for easy access.

How much does it hold? It's a bit deceiving just how much this toiletry bag holds—which is much more than it gives off at first glance! I bring all of my beauty products in here, from foundations to lipsticks and moisturizer galore. And though he packs way lighter than me, it can fit my partner's personal care items, too: a face buzzer, hair gel, a toothbrush, and so on. As well as the main pocket with a zippered enclosure, it has two convenient, grab-and-go side pockets as well as an enclosed compartment on the back.

Tested by: Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor How long have you been using it? I’ve had Away's large toiletry bag for just over two years now, and have been obsessed with it ever since.

What is it best for? This is my travel companion for holding my go-to skincare products and toiletries, and it comes with me on every trip. I do also keep all my everyday products in there at home, so it's proven to be always at my ready. It's so chic—especially because it has my initials embroidered on the front—and keeps everything contained. I love that it has so many interior compartments, both zippered and clear, to keep small objects like hair ties, jewelry, and Band-Aids separated from my bigger tubes and bottles.

How much does it hold? Full disclosure: I don’t travel light. But this bag truly holds so much. It fits my entire skincare routine, toothbrush case, deodorant, hair products, body wash, razor, and beyond with ease. The two halves make it easy to find a place for everything.

Tested by: Bridget Knowles, associate social media manager

How long have you been using it? Elizabeth Scarlett’s eponymous label is a London-based luxury accessories brand I discovered during a bout of retail therapy in East London eight years ago. I’ve never looked back since—it’s an unspoken “it-girl” possession.

What is it best for? For longer trips, the Wash Bag is really great to keep everything organized. It has a wipe-clean lining fit for all lotions and potions, and you can personalize it with monograms too, which makes for a great gift. For shorter trips and everyday use, I use the Everyday Pouch—which I strongly suggest adding to your cart. (It’s my life companion in many ways.)

How much does it hold? I put everything in the Wash Bag: daytime makeup, going out makeup (you get me), my nighttime routine, and my morning routine. It’s lined with pockets so you can easily organize brushes, and—I mean—my electric toothbrush even fits in it. That’s how good it is.

Tested by: Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor

How long have you been using it? I've been using—and in love with—this toiletry bag for around two years now.

What is it best for? I promise, my adoration of this bag comes from more than just its good looks. I've been reaching for it nonstop to carry my very extensive skincare routine with me wherever I go—and it's made packing easier than ever. I think I've finally cracked the code to keeping my toiletries organized and ready to go whenever I am. The extra roomy toiletry bag is designed to be packed in your checked luggage, where you have more suitcase space and no restrictions on the amount of liquids you can have inside.

How much does it hold? I used to keep all of my reusable toiletry bottles and miscellaneous minis in a small storage bin underneath my bed. And when it was time to pack for a trip, I'd sift through it and decide what I needed for a particular trip. I decided to put all of my go-to toiletries inside The Kit, including cleanser, body wash, moisturizer, shampoo and conditioner, dry shampoo, tooth paste, floss, and even contact lenses. Now when it's time to travel I can easily grab the pre-packed kit and throw it right into my personal item. I don't even open it anymore to see what I need—it's already stocked up and ready to go.

Read a full review of the toiletry bag here.

How long have you been using it? I ordered this Calpak train case in unison with the aforementioned Luka toiletry bag—so around two months now.

What is it best for? With its boxy, clear, and haute look, the train case is best for extended trips where a checked bag is obvious. Otherwise, it's a superb makeup bag at home for those who don't love too many compartments, and like to have their ready products in view: The transparent panels let you quickly locate what you need without digging. (Not to mention, it looks super cute with the Luka, given the matching colorways. I'm obsessed!)

How much does it hold? When this bad boy arrived at my apartment, it was (luckily) bigger than I expected. It's tall, so it can easily hold my toner bottles, makeup brushes, and blending sponges.

At home, not only does it store my everyday beauty products, but a stock of my next-on-the-lists and just-in-cases—it's where my unopened moisturizers, different lip shades, and nail care products go. My favorite part? There's a hidden, dedicated interior organization pocket attached to the top compartment, which holds the products I wish to keep separate.

#6272. Livery of the Week: Aer Lingus

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Aer Lingus’ standard livery is centered on the shamrock, a symbol that has represented the Irish carrier for more than 80 years. Although the airline has changed its aircraft appearance several times, the three-leaf emblem remains the most recognizable feature of its fleet.

The current design was unveiled on Jan. 17, 2019, during a ceremony at Dublin Airport. It marked Aer Lingus’ first major aircraft rebranding in more than two decades, replacing the predominantly green-and-white scheme introduced in the 1990s.

The redesign retained the shamrock but introduced a revised version with a slight tilt and more pronounced heart-shaped leaves. According to Aer Lingus, the changes were intended to represent movement and the airline’s Irish heritage while giving the logo a more contemporary appearance.

The most noticeable change was the shift away from the green upper fuselage used on the previous livery. The updated scheme features a predominantly white aircraft with a teal vertical stabilizer and engines. Large teal “Aer Lingus” titles appear along the forward fuselage.

The shamrock appears in several locations beyond the tail. Aer Lingus incorporated the emblem into the airline’s wordmark, near the aircraft’s boarding door and on the wingtips. The airline specifically positioned the wingtip design to make it visible to passengers looking out from the cabin.

The aircraft’s lower fuselage also received a teal treatment, making the color visible from below. The combination of white and teal replaced the darker green that had dominated much of the airline’s branding for decades.

Aer Lingus worked with global design consultancy Lippincott on the rebranding. The airline considered more than 50 shamrock designs before selecting the final version. The updated identity also included a new typeface, redesigned digital platforms and changes to other customer-facing materials.

Two aircraft were presented in the new colors during the January 2019 unveiling: an Airbus A330-300 named St Munchin and an A320 named St Schira. The A330 made its first scheduled flight in the updated livery the following day, operating from Dublin to New York.

Aer Lingus has also retained several connections to its earlier aircraft designs. Its 1960s-inspired retro livery, introduced in 2011 to celebrate the airline’s 75th anniversary, featured a darker green-and-white appearance that contrasted with the newer scheme.

More than seven years after its introduction, the 2019 design remains the standard appearance of Aer Lingus aircraft. The colors and placement of the branding have changed, but the shamrock continues to link the carrier’s modern fleet with its earlier history.

#6271. Eurostar Premier (First Class) Review: Better Than Flying, But Hardly A Luxury Experience

My first Eurostar Premier journey took me from Brussels to Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, where I connected to a KLM flight to Los Angeles. The train itself felt older than I expected, but the quiet carriage and productive journey made it a pleasant alternative to flying.

I sometimes enjoy trying a new travel experience without researching every detail beforehand. There is a certain irony in that, considering how much of this blog is devoted to helping others know what to expect. Eurostar was one of those experiences. I had long wanted to try it, and an award booking provided the opportunity.

I booked Brussels to Los Angeles through Air France/KLM Flying Blue for 60,000 miles in business class (plus $478.13 in taxes and fees). The itinerary included a Eurostar train from Brussels-Midi to Amsterdam Schiphol, followed by KLM World Business Class to Los Angeles. I could have booked a departure from Brussels Airport for the same mileage price, but chose the rail connection to try something different.

The cabin description was confusing. My ticket indicated business class, while KLM’s Air&Rail information referred to a “premium” experience for those connecting in business class. Eurostar’s actual classes are Standard, Plus, and Premier. At check-in, the agent confirmed I was booked into Premier.

Rather than use the actual Eurostar check-in desk, Brussels-Midi has an Air France-KLM ticketing office and rail check-in counter located in the rear of the station.

My train departed at 5:53 am and I showed up at 5:15 am to check-in…where I found a massive line and only one agent on duty. One passenger in the front of the line was traveling on SNCF to Paris but had a ticketing issue which the lone agent was trying to resolve. But time was ticking and the line grew longer.

Finally at 5:30 am I walked to the front of the line to ask for assistance, noting my train departed in 20 minutes. I did not mean to be the ugly American, but it was just what the agent needed to ask the frazzled traveler from Côte d’Ivoire (I noticed her passport) to step aside. Within a few minutes she had cleared the line and I was on my way upstairs to the rail platform.

There was a Eurostar lounge in Brussels, but it did not open until 6:00 am during my visit, so I could not use it…though I would have access to it had my train departed an hour later.  Not that I ended up having a lot of time to spare, but it woudld have been nice to have a cup of coffee there before the train departed.

Stepping onboard, I found my seat in Coach 11, the very last cabin designated as Premier.

Stepping onboard felt more like entering an older TGV first class carriage than the sleek, modern interior I had imagined. Old is, not necessarily a bad thing, but the cabin showed wear. My footrest was broken and the cabin just look tattered and well past its prime.

In the very rear of the cabin was a compartment with seating of four that remained empty throughout the journey.

The bigger advantage on this particular departure was how quiet it was: there was only one other passenger in my carriage and even as we neared Amsterdam there was never more than five in the cabin.

A nearly empty premium cabin is not something you can count in Premier, but it made this an especially pleasant setting to work ahead of a long flight in which I did not want to open my computer.

The lavatories in the Premier cabin were very typical European train toilets with metal toilets, a small sink, but fairly spacious.

We departed on time, and an attendant welcomed us and offered me breakfast menu shortly after pushback, along with a packaged moist towelette.

Sandwich IGP Bayonne ham, AOP Comté cheese, with dill picked cucumbers

Fruit Kampot pepper and verbena apples, gala melon, watermelon

Both were accompanied by yogurt, a croissant, juice, and coffee. I chose the fruit, though I would have liked both (and my request for both was politely declined).

It was a modest meal, but I enjoyed it. The fruit was good and the coffee was decent, as was the croissant.

I preferred this breakfast to the catering KLM serves on its short intra-European flights and the presentation was far nicer. It did not need to be elaborate to be satisfying at that hour and I had a second cup of coffee and some cold pressed berry juice prior to arrival at AMS.

The onboard internet worked well, allowing me to be productive during the ride. For this trip, I valued that more than a particularly luxurious cabin, though I was initially concerned that I would be capped at 500 MB of data.

Thankfully, even though I quickly exceeded the cap the internet continued working…

In-seat power was also available so I arrived in AMS with my devices fully charged.

The attendant’s welcome and breakfast service provided a pleasant start to the morning. Sure, it would have been nice to have the sandwich as well (I was still hungry and the cabin was empty), but she denied my request in a very kind way!

At one point I took a walk through the train to check out the Café Car which offers food and drinks for purchase.

Looking at the menu, I’d say I would have been fine with a falafel wrap and Lavazza coffee had I been booked in coach.

My destination was Schiphol Airport, not Amsterdam Centraa, whcih thankfully meant no backtracking a regional train to the airport.

Next came my KLM lounge visit and onward flight to Los Angeles.

For my itinerary, I was happy to have Premier included in the Flying Blue award.

Whether I would pay a substantial premium for it separately is another question and the answer is probably not. Eurostar lists extra-spacious seating and lounge access among Premier’s benefits, but I could not use the Brussels lounge on this departure.

It is also important to compare the correct route. Eurostar’s class descriptions distinguish between London services and continental routes. For example, the included meal in Premier on a London-route would have included a multi-course hot meal.

For a separate purchase, I would compare the actual fare difference and the benefits available for the particular trip (like the lounge), probably paying no more than €50 for the upgrade on this particular route.

Eurostar Premier was less polished than I expected, but I enjoyed the journey. The worn interior and broken footrest deserved attention, while breakfast and reliable internet helped make the ride worthwhile. For this Brussels–Schiphol connection, I was glad I chose the train. It gave me a quiet, productive start to the trip home and left me interested in trying Eurostar again.

Good option. Between the age of those seats and the fabric, I feel like an antimacassar would not have been out of place.

For some reason, I pictured something more like a modern Japanese or Chinese high speed rail carriage.

The seating is awful – Regiojet, our local carrier, used these same coaches as a lowest (sub-economy) class.

I take all lines of the Eurostar fairly frequently, and for context you took an older model of what was Thalys – the high speed train connecting Belgium to France and the Netherlands. They merged with Eurostar a few years back, but the experience remains quite distinct. Eurostar to/from London requires going through security and passport control, and is in a completely different part of the train station, and a lot more like getting in a flight. Overall. I’d recommend Plus. The price difference is rarely huge with economy, and you get more or less the same as Premium but without the lounge access or meal. Most routes max out at less than 3 hours, so I’d buy something before or after leaving, or as noted get a coffee on the train. I’ve taken Premium a few times and while it’s a nice upgrade, I’d not spend my own money on it, and the two times I’ve chosen it with the option of Plus were because I had urgent work and needed the lounge as a quiet office space. Overall, it’s a good review and reflective of the experience. Fingers crossed the new rolling stock freshens things up when it arrives, and I’m glad you could try things in this part of Europe.

#6270. Alaska Airlines Cuts Jobs As $700 Million Loss Looms, CEO Admits Overhead Costs Grew Too Fast

Alaska Air Group is cutting about 200 jobs as CEO Ben Minicucci warns the company could lose as much as $700 million this year if current conditions persist. Higher fuel prices are the immediate problem, but Minicucci also acknowledged that overhead has grown too quickly. That is a sobering backdrop for an airline pursuing an ambitious international expansion.

According to Reuters, which reviewed Minicucci’s employee memo, the reductions affect non-contract positions, including 125 in Washington and 48 in Hawaii. No frontline, non-management positions are being eliminated. Affected employees will finish working November 13 but continue receiving pay through December 31, with severance and other support.

The cuts represent less than 1% of the group’s roughly 32,500 employees. That makes them relatively small across the company, but certainly not small to the people losing their jobs…

Minicucci warned employees that, if conditions persist, Alaska Air Group could record its first adjusted pretax annual loss outside the pandemic since 2003. That is a warning about a potential full-year result, not a $700 million loss already reported. It also concerns the parent group, which includes Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

In its October 20 earnings release, Alaska forecast a full-year adjusted loss of $5.00–$5.50 per share and said fuel would cost $1.8 billion more than its original annual plan. Its fourth-quarter forecast assumes fuel at $4.65–$4.85 per gallon. Third-quarter revenue rose 14% to $4.3 billion, but that commercial growth has not been enough to deliver the annual profit management expected.

Those numbers help explain why simply selling more tickets is not solving the problem.

There was another revealing part of Minicucci’s message:

“We must return to the financial discipline that has long been a key competitive advantage.”

He also acknowledged that overhead expenses had grown disproportionately to revenue in recent years, adding these costs had “grown at a disproportionate rate to revenue.”

Fuel prices are largely beyond an airline’s control, but the size and cost of its management structure are not. The question is why overhead was allowed to grow that way and whether these reductions address the problem or merely provide some near-term savings. Cutting 200 positions cannot will certainly not offset a fuel bill running $1.8 billion above plan.

It also puts management in the uncomfortable position of asking employees to absorb the consequences of spending decisions those employees may have had no role in making.

I have been following Alaska’s efforts to become a more substantial global competitor, including its latest European expansion to Athens and Paris and investment in premium cabins and lounges.

These job cuts do not automatically mean that strategy is wrong, though Alaska cannot cut its way to growth. It needs a product passengers will choose and a network that gives them a reason to return. Pulling back on customer investments when conditions deteriorate could leave Alaska with the costs of expansion but less ability to earn a premium.

Still, growth deserves scrutiny when the company is losing money. Management must be willing to adjust if demand or achievable fares do not justify the investment. Ambition is useful, but it cannot become an excuse to keep spending on something that is not working, though with every investment, it takes time for a sappling to grow into a tree and the “no pain, no gain” mantra certainly applies here too.

Minicucci intends to continue investing in the fleet, customer experience, and network while tightening spending elsewhere. That is a defensible approach…and it could be that these jobs are no longer needed with AI and simply a low-hanging fruit to trim unnecessary expense in order to focus on what is more important.

Alaska Air Group is cutting about 200 jobs while warning of a potential $700 million annual loss. Fuel costs explain much of the pressure, but management’s acknowledgment that overhead grew too quickly deserves attention too.

I want Alaska’s expansion to succeed. Heck, I want JetBlue and Alaska to merge. A stronger competitor is good for passengers. But the company needs to demonstrate that its growth can produce sustainable earnings, and employees losing their jobs should not be the only ones held accountable for restoring financial discipline.

A few years ago, on a damp evening in late March in London, I learned the hard way that countries don’t all change their clocks for daylight saving time simultaneously. After ordering a glass of white wine at a cozy bar in Bermondsey, I mindlessly scrolled on my phone while the bartenders chatted about the clocks jumping forward that coming Sunday. I nearly spit out my Chablis.

Back home in New York City, I had already skipped ahead one hour on the second Sunday in March. As I frantically Googled, I learned that in the United Kingdom, the clocks go forward one hour on the last Sunday in March (and back one hour on the last Sunday in October).

Don’t be like me and lose two hours of sleep in one month. When you travel, remember the following to avoid daylight saving time-related snafus and other time zone mistakes — and if you're in the U.S., most states fell back one hour on Sunday, Nov. 1.

The U.K. isn’t the only country that changes its clocks on a different weekend than we do in the U.S. For example, most European countries follow the same calendar as the U.K., moving clocks forward one hour on the last Sunday in March and back one hour on the last Sunday in October.

Generally, when traveling in the spring and fall, it’s always best to check when the country you’re going to falls forward or backward — and also whether that country observes daylight saving time at all. In fact, according to the Pew Research Center, about 66% of the world doesn’t.

Though daylight saving time is commonly observed in North America and Europe, many non-European Union countries in Europe — including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Iceland, Russia and Turkey — stay on standard time year-round.

In 2023, Egypt became the only country in Africa to change its clocks when it reintroduced daylight saving time for the first time in seven years. Now, each year, its clocks move forward one hour on the last Friday in April and backward one hour on the last Thursday in October.

It’s also worth double-checking these things even if you're traveling within the U.S. In 48 states, daylight saving time runs from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November. Arizona and Hawaii are the outliers that stay on standard time year-round. While it’s less of an issue on an island like Hawaii, Arizona shares enough borders with other states that do observe daylight saving time that it can be problematic.

“Always double-check timing when flying in/out and on road trips through the state,” Becky Blaine, TPG’s newsletter managing editor and former Arizona resident, said. Otherwise, you can risk missing a flight or a reservation.

To keep it simple, remember that Arizona is in the Pacific Daylight Time zone from mid-March to early November, and the rest of the year it’s in the same time zone as other states in Mountain Standard Time.

It’s a similar situation in Canada. Generally, Canada follows the same daylight saving schedule as the U.S., but most of Saskatchewan, the Yukon and some parts of Quebec and British Columbia stay on standard time year-round.

In Australia, daylight saving time starts the first Sunday in October and ends the first Sunday in April in the Australian Capital Territory, New South Wales, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria; meanwhile, the Northern Territory, Queensland and Western Australia don’t observe it.

Outside of daylight saving time changes, there are some general time zone issues to be aware of while traveling.

In countries as large as the U.S., Canada and Australia, it’s easy to see why there are so many time zones. But Eric Rosen, TPG’s director of travel content, also pointed out that the airport in the Maldives is in a different time zone than some resorts in the tiny island nation.

Technically, the Maldives has only one official time zone: Maldives Time, which is five hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). However, some of the archipelago's private island resorts add an hour to Maldives Time to maximize their guests' evening light.

For example, The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Resort sets its clock one hour ahead of the official clock to what it calls "Island Time," but also provides guests with butlers who coordinate transfers to and from the airport so nobody accidentally misses a flight.

Before you go to the Maldives, be sure to check if your resort also does this.

Due to its geographic location, the Canadian island of Newfoundland is 90 minutes ahead of Eastern Time instead of just 60 minutes ahead, as in the rest of Atlantic Canada. On a July trip, Nick Ewen, TPG’s editor-in-chief, found this challenging for calendar purposes.

While traveling in Newfoundland, he received an Outlook invitation to a 7:30 p.m. dinner meeting the following week and accepted it without much thought. However, the actual dinner back home in the U.S. started at 6 p.m. — a detail he completely missed until the reminder popped up 15 minutes before. At that point, he realized he would be late.

Other places offset from UTC by 30 minutes include India, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Iran and some states in Australia. Want to be confused even more? Nepal's time zone is offset by 45 minutes due to its geography.

Even when not dealing with half-hour time zones, it can be easy to make similar mistakes when adding events back home to your digital calendar while traveling in a different time zone.

"Last year, I brought my middle son to a birthday party. We were running a few minutes late, but when we arrived, it seemed like the party was almost over," Tarah Chieffi, a senior writer at TPG, said. "While the kids were eating cake, I double-checked my calendar to make sure we had gotten the time right, and it seemed like we had. But then I went to check the invitation, and we had, in fact, arrived one hour late."

Her mistake? When she entered the party into her calendar while traveling, her calendar app defaulted to the time zone she was in and showed her the incorrect time back home.

"Now, I always toggle the time zone to my home time zone if I enter appointments into my calendar while I'm traveling," she said.

"Outlook lets you have up to three time zones showing on the calendar," Madison Blancaflor, a managing editor at TPG, said.

Go to "Settings," then "Calendar," then "Time zones." Then, check the box for "Show second time zone in Day and Week view" underneath your default time zone. If you need a third one, you can also check that box.

It's also important to remember that it's possible to quickly encounter multiple time zones on cruises — especially on transoceanic cruises, where you'll change time zones daily or almost daily. And if you're on a cruise traversing the Pacific Ocean, you could lose an entire day if you cross the international date line, like Clint Henderson, TPG's principal spokesperson, did when he sailed from Seward, Alaska, to Tokyo last year.

Related: I made a rookie travel mistake that nearly cost me $4,000 — here's how I fixed it

Even on shorter cruises, check if you'll have to change time zones. When I was on a five-day Alaska cruise earlier this summer, I changed time zones twice as we moved in and out of Alaska Daylight Time on a round-trip sailing from Vancouver (which was one hour ahead, on Pacific Daylight Time).

Cabin stewards usually leave notes on your bed at turndown to remind you of upcoming time changes. Clint said he had to set his clocks back between one and two hours each night on his cruise. But you can't always rely on your cellphone to display the correct time when it’s in airplane mode and using satellite-based internet. Bring an analog watch or an alarm clock to ground you if you're unsure whether your device will update properly.

However, some cruise ships may ignore time changes at select ports. "I've had that happen on Royal Caribbean ships in the Caribbean, for example, to avoid the ship time changing three days in a row," said Christine Gallipeau, a senior editor on TPG's points and loyalty team. "So if you're doing shore excursions, make sure you know what time the ship is following, as it may not necessarily match the local time."

Related: Can a cruise help with jet lag? The answer might surprise you

When traveling, don’t assume every country or state follows the same daylight-saving-time rules and schedules as where you live, and be mindful of time zone anomalies. Losing or gaining an unexpected hour can lead to lost sleep, arriving late to an event and, worst of all, missed flights.

#6268. easyJet Launches 7 New UK Routes In 3 Days: See Map & List Now

easyJet is one of the UK's largest airlines. It offers more than 62 million seats annually on flights to and from the country. But for this winter season, the low-cost carrier has cut around 1.3 million to 1.4 million seats across its network, reportedly due to rising jet fuel prices. Several of its routes from the UK have also been affected.

But, of course, it is not all about route cuts. The budget airline has also introduced several new services from the UK, including flights to popular winter destinations and cities known for their Christmas markets, such as Copenhagen, Nuremberg, and Kraków. In fact, seven new routes have launched in just three days.

In just the last couple of days, easyJet has launched two new routes from Newcastle Airport (NCL), connecting the city to John Paul II International Airport Kraków-Balice Airport (KRK) in Poland and Marrakesh Menara Airport (RAK) in Morocco. From November 5, it is also starting a new service to Copenhagen Airport (CPH) in Denmark, operating twice weekly.

However, easyJet will face competition on all three routes. Elsewhere, the budget airline has introduced a new service between Liverpool John Lennon Airport (LPL) and Iceland's Keflavik International Airport (KEF).

Kraków: joins Ryanair (5x weekly) and Jet2 (2x weekly);

Marrakesh: Winter only; will face competition from Jet2; Ryanair will return on the route next summer;

Copenhagen: will join Jet2 and Norwegian Air Sweden

Belfast City, Northern Ireland; 3x weekly

Brand-new service; restoring the connection to Northern Ireland from the Essex airport after 12 years

Brand-new service; only airline flying to Morocco from Luton (although it does face competition from other London airports)

It has also started flying from Manchester Airport (MAN) to Nuremberg Airport (NUE) in Germany, which is Europe’s one of the oldest and most popular Christmas markets. The Manchester–Nuremberg route had been without nonstop flights for several years. According to historical scheduling data from aviation analytics company Cirium, Ryanair was the last airline to operate the route in 2019.

Two of the new routes are between city pairs that have never previously had nonstop flights. As noted above in the table, one of these is easyJet's new service between London Southend Airport (SEN) and George Best Belfast City Airport (BHD), which launched on November 2. The new year-round route operates three times weekly, on Mondays, Fridays and Sundays. Notably, this is not the airline's first connection between Southend and Belfast.

It previously flew to Belfast International Airport (BFS), offering up to two daily flights between April 2012 and January 2014. Another addition is the new service between London Luton Airport (LTN) and Rabat–Salé Airport (RBA), which serves the Moroccan capital. The route is scheduled to launch on November 5, with two weekly flights

The new service will join the two other Moroccan destinations the low-cost carrier currently serves from London Southend: Marrakesh, with five weekly flights, and Agadir, with three. It is the only airline offering direct flights to Morocco from the airport. Overall, this winter, according to Cirium data, it is offering about 33 weekly flights to Morocco from London area airports.

They involve multiple airports across the country. Find out more here!

Looking ahead, the low-cost carrier has several more additions planned from the UK, including new city pairs such as Edinburgh Airport (EDI) to Tromsø Airport (TOS) in Norway, which is a popular destination for seeing the Northern Lights and enjoying winter activities, and SEN to Sharm el-Sheikh International Airport (SSH) in Egypt.

The airline is also expanding its UK network to Budapest, Hungary, with three new routes scheduled to launch later this month. From November 17, it is launching twice-weekly flights from Bristol and Belfast International, followed by twice-weekly services from Liverpool from November 19. Further ahead, easyJet will launch its first international service from the Isle of Man Airport (IOM) on December 19, connecting the island to Geneva Airport (GVA) in Switzerland.

The new route will operate once weekly on Saturdays, and will be the only direct connection between the Isle of Man and Switzerland. The British Crown Dependency has previously had scheduled flights to the city. According to historical schedules, the now-defunct Flybe last operated the route in 2020 using its De Havilland Canada Dash 8-Q400s.

#6267. United Airlines CEO Insists He Runs The “World’s Best” Airline. Does That Title Even Matter?

Scott Kirby believes United Airlines is the best airline in the world (he has for quite some time). I understand his argument, and there are aspects of United that compare favorably with just about any competitor. But the claim raises a more interesting question: what actually makes an airline the best? The answer depends on much more than the seat or the route map or any other single quality…and maybe that’s asking the wrong question anyway.

In his recent Cheeky Pint interview with John Collison and Ben Thompson, Kirby made a case for United that deserves more than an eye roll.

His argument is not that United serves the best food or offers the most luxurious seats. He acknowledges that Asian and Middle Eastern competitors do better on the physical product and probably service. He also identifies schedule as the primary reason people choose an airline. But he believes United’s technology changes the overall assessment:

“I say schedule is the number one reason people pick an airline. But, everything else matters for brand-loyal customers. It’s service, product, reliability, and technology. The Asian and Middle East carriers do better than the US airlines on product for sure, and probably service too. I think we do a really good job, but they have different cultures for service, so they do better on that. But I think technology is the differentiator.

“United, that’s why I now believe that United in totality is the best airline in the world, and it’s because of technology. It’s exponentially getting better. Things like being able to do this for customers when there’s a delay and tell them what’s going on. We started it this summer. AI allows us to institutionalize this. But if you’re going to have a delay, like sending customers weather radar maps. In Chicago, there was a day where the weather was over the horizon, but you had to fly. It was sunny at the airport, but you had to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and so the routes were closed. You couldn’t—

“We sent half the people the normal weather delay, which they think you’re lying… Because it’s sunny outside. You must be lying to me. We sent half a picture with the radar map, and you have to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and the routes are closed because of outside. The people with a 1-hour delay, I think the numbers were negative 60 NPS on the normal way of sending it, plus 60 when we send a picture of the map. A 120-point difference.”

His case for United rests on technology: better tools for managing travel, clearer communication during disruptions, and connectivity that makes time onboard more useful. For example, he describes sending passengers radar maps to explain why distant thunderstorms were delaying flights even though the weather at their airport looked fine. His point is that passengers respond much better when they understand what is happening.

Thus, Kirby is acknowledging that competitors outperform it in some traditional measures of onboard quality, but arguing that United’s technological advantages outweigh those shortcomings.

I think he is right that these things matter. I am less convinced that they settle the question.

Start with the most obvious consideration: an airline is not particularly useful if it cannot conveniently take you where you need to go. I love trying new products and will sometimes take an absurd routing to do so. Most travelers understandably do not approach their trips that way.

A nonstop flight at a convenient time can be more valuable than a better seat reached through a connection. Frequency matters too. An airline with several flights a day gives you more options, particularly when something goes wrong.

This is a substantial part of United’s appeal. Its network gives me reasons to fly it that have nothing to do with whether another airline serves better Champagne.

But the best network for me may be largely irrelevant to someone living elsewhere. A traveler in Taipei and a traveler in Chicago are starting with very different choices. There is no universal route map that works best for everyone.

Emirates is a good example of why an airline’s reputation may need to be separated from the particular experience you are buying.

Mention Emirates and many people think of luxury (massive first class suites, showers, and bars onboard with beautiful flight attendants serving you extensive food and beverage offerings). That “halo effect” reputation is understandable.

But someone booking business class on an older Boeing 777 may encounter a product that falls well short of that image. The retrofitted 777s improve the situation with a 1-2-1 layout and direct aisle access, but I would not put that seat ahead of the leading business class products elsewhere.

Singapore Airlines illustrates this as well. Its reputation for service, built in part around the Singapore Girl branding, is extraordinary. Yet some travelers strongly dislike its longhaul business class seats, particularly their sleeping position.

A beautifully presented meal and gracious service cannot entirely compensate for a bed in which you struggle to get comfortable. Singapore’s new cabin reveal on Friday, November 6, will be particularly interesting for that reason.

My recent Emirates 777 first class flight demonstrated the reverse problem: a superb suite paired with service that did not live up to it. I loved the space, but the experience still fell short.

So what about Kirby’s argument that technology is most important?

We sometimes talk about technology as if it is separate from the passenger experience. But an app that lets you solve a problem without standing in line is providing service. A clear explanation of a delay is providing service. Working internet can determine whether a long daytime flight is productive or frustrating.

US airlines deserve credit here. Their digital tools can be excellent, and United’s app is absolutely the best in the business, no question about it. But even the Alaska, American, and Delta apps are–comparatively speaking–much better than their non-US peers.

To be clear, that does not mean every American airline leads every foreign airline or that an attractive app excuses indifferent employees. It does mean that evaluating service solely by how someone pours your wine misses a large part of what an airline does for its customers.

Connectivity is especially important to me. Extra legroom and a better meal are welcome, but painfully slow or non-functioning Wi-Fi can materially change how I feel about a flight. For someone hoping to disconnect and sleep, it may barely register. The features can be measured. The importance each passenger assigns to them cannot be universal.

I also recognize the limitations of my own perspective. Much of my coverage focuses on premium cabins, and those experiences influence my preferences. But what does the airline offer someone in economy?

Some Asian carriers offer a more appealing combination of legroom, meals, and attentive service than their US counterparts. That deserves weight, even if the business class cabin lacks the latest suite.

At the same time, the aircraft still matters. So do the fare restrictions, baggage allowance, and cost of choosing a seat. A generous meal does not tell us whether the ticket represents good value.

For a family paying for several tickets, the best airline may be the one offering a tolerable nonstop journey at an affordable total price. For a tall passenger, a little more legroom may matter far more than the entertainment selection.

An airline cannot claim superiority for everyone based on what it provides a small number of passengers at the front of the aircraft.

A great airline should operate reliably and treat passengers well when it fails.

Those are related, but separate, expectations. I want to arrive on time. When that is impossible, I want an honest explanation and practical assistance.

No airline can prevent every weather delay or mechanical problem. But how it prepares, communicates, and recovers tells me much more than a polished promotional video.

American Airlines is a useful example from my own flying. I would argue that some of my recent meals on American have been the best among the US network carriers. Its free Wi-Fi has also tends to work very well for me. Those are real strengths.

Nevertheless, my experiences with inconsistent service and operational problems place American well below Delta and United in my overall assessment. That is not a claim that every American flight is bad or every Delta flight is good. It is the cumulative effect of repeated experiences. A carrier earns my confidence over time, and it can lose it the same way.

The loyalty program belongs in this discussion too.

Award availability, redemption prices, and the usefulness of elite benefits all affect how much value I receive from an airline. A good program can persuade me to choose one carrier when the alternatives are otherwise similar.

But I try to separate the airline I enjoy most from the program in which I find the most value.

An excellent redemption does not make an uncomfortable seat comfortable. Status does not make a canceled flight depart. Conversely, a wonderful airline can have a loyalty program that gives me little reason to engage with it. Ideally, the program reinforces a relationship the airline has already earned through its service.

Qatar Airways and STARLUX are among my favorites because I have found their overall experiences so compelling. The appeal extends beyond a seat or a meal: I look forward to flying them because of the reliable Wi-Fi, excellent service, and quality in everything.

Air France has also come such a long way. Its newer business class seat is excellent, and the addition of Starlink on equipped aircraft addresses something that matters greatly to me. Combined with the food and service I enjoy, that makes it an increasingly attractive choice.

Yet I still have many reasons to fly United. Its network and technology have practical value in my life that an exceptional flight on another carrier cannot always replace.

That is why my favorite airline and the airline I choose for a particular trip need not be the same…maybe the point is that talking about which carrier is “best” is ultimately futile and our focus instead should be rewarding carriers who do things well and not patronizing those that continually disappoint.

Kirby’s claim is worth discussing because he recognizes that being the best involves more than having the fanciest cabin. Technology and network utility deserve more credit than they sometimes receive.

But I would not crown United the best airline in the world on that basis alone. The seat still matters. So does the person serving you, the reliability of the operation, and what happens when your plans unravel.

For me, the best airlines are the ones that bring those elements together consistently, but at the same time I realize how arbitrary my own evaluation can be. Thus, I tend to think asking “who is best” is the wrong question versus asking “who does X,Y, and Z well?”

What makes an airline the best for you—and which airline comes closest?

Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

In Kirby’s world, as long it is said with enough superlatives it must be true

I mean a lot of people in the comments are about to say “Kirby is wrong and has his head up his own ass” but go ask any airline CEO what the best airline in the world is and 90% will say their own airline. It is literally their job as CEO to be championing their own airline. I don’t know why it is a surprise to anyone that Kirby says his airline is the best in the world.

Also there is no objective measure of the best airline in the world. What matters is what works for you personally. I live near a United hub so of course United gives me the greatest access to destinations. If I lived near an American hub then American might be the best airline for me. Its a throwaway comment, made by a CEO doing his job. His broader point is that just having the best first class seat doesn’t make you the best airline and he’s right on that.

#6266. Air Fares Still ‘Quite Low,’ A4A CEO Says

Air fares have risen about 22% year-over-year, largely due to the surge in jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

But considering the very low-cost environment that prevailed prior to 2026, tickets are still relatively inexpensive, Airlines For America CEO Chris Sununu said this week.

“Airline costs are actually quite low,” Sununu told CBS’ The Takeout. “They’ve risen 22 percent in the last year because of the Iran war, but from all-time lows. So no, overall, flying in the United States is still incredibly affordable.”

“If you want that premium seat, that first class seat, obviously you pay a little more for that,” he continued. “That economy seat is still very affordable.”

Airline ticket prices have risen since February, when the conflict began. The collapse of ultra-low-cost Spirit Airlines in May and major carriers’ shift toward premiumization could also be playing a role.

When pressed by host Major Garrett on reports that U.S. airlines are letting seats go empty instead of lowering prices to effectively discipline the market, Sununu said that was “100 percent” false.

“If a flight is not making money, believe me, it’s been pulled off because jet fuel is so high,” he said. “Instead of three flights a day from Wichita to Green Bay, there’s two flights. So, no, when you get on a flight now, it’s going to be more often than not very very crowded.”

Asked about the FAA’s sweeping air traffic control modernization effort, Sununu was positive and credited Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford with launching the first serious system-wide upgrade in decades.

“For forty years they’ve done nothing,” he said. “And they’ve done more in the last twelve months than they have in the previous forty years. And that is coming as a cynic of Washington, who has seen the political landscape littered with failed infrastructure projects.”

The main benefit for customers, Sununu added, will be efficiency.

“It’s always going to be safe,” he said. “But over the past few years they’ve had to slow the system down, because it is so antiquated, to ensure the safety. But now we get that efficiency back.”

Is airline elite status worth it anymore? It’s an age-old question that’s back on plenty of travelers’ minds — especially after two of the four largest U.S. carriers overhauled their loyalty programs this month.

And one theme is becoming clear: To get the best rewards, members are going to have to spend ... a lot.

Starting in 2027, taking the most United Airlines flights won’t necessarily translate to the highest United MileagePlus status.

Instead, the airline's top elite members will be the customers who spend the most money — either on flights or the airline’s cobranded credit cards.

Top-tier 1K status will also be harder to earn.

Meanwhile, Southwest Airlines took its biggest step yet toward nudging flyers toward its lineup of credit cards.

Beginning next year, every dollar its members charge to their Southwest Rapid Rewards cards will count toward status.

Southwest also closed a key shortcut to its most alluring perk: the Companion Pass. Going forward, members hoping to score the "buy-one, get-one" flight pass will have to spend their way to the airline’s top status tier (or take 100 flights in a year).

These changes weren’t entirely surprising.

Over the past decade, airline status has become less about the time you spend in the sky and more about the cash you’re willing to spend.

For years, American Airlines and Delta Air Lines have awarded status based purely on the money their frequent flyers spend.

And across the industry, carriers have become more agnostic about whether those dollars come in the form of a flight booking or card swipe at the grocery store.

On some airlines, you can now technically swipe your way to status without ever setting foot on a plane.

Here’s how much you’d need to pay for top-tier airline status in 2027 — if you went exclusively by credit card spending.

*Note: American has not announced what its status thresholds will be in 2027.

Note: United requires a minimum of four United-operated flights for members to be Premier-eligible.

Note: Cardholders earn a one-time 10,000 TQP boost upon hitting 130,000 TQPs in 2027.

Note: Elite credit earned by flying or other eligible spending reduces the card spending needed to qualify for elite status. Southwest still also offers elite qualification via flight segments.

It’s not just the eye-popping dollar amounts travelers must now spend to reach status.

Airlines have also made carrying a credit card a more important part of the overall loyalty experience.

United and Delta cardholders now get access to better mileage redemptions than members who don’t carry a card.

JetBlue will soon offer exclusive elite perks to JetBlue TrueBlue loyalty members who carry its top-tier card.

And even more airlines offer cardholders shortcuts to elite status.

Delta this month said it’s on track to pull in a record $9 billion through its banking partnership with American Express.

American expects to make $8 billion this year through its tie-up with Citibank.

Those are eye-popping numbers, of course.

Beyond the raw cash flow, though, airlines also see turning flyers into cardholders as one of the best ways to become part of customers’ day-to-day lives, even when they’re not on a trip.

“It really is about making sure that we are top of mind for our members every single day, whether or not they’re able to be on board our aircraft," Jarad Fisher, United’s president of MileagePlus, said in a recent interview.

On one hand, airline status still offers a host of ways to save money, get better seats and travel with more flexible policies.

And, in some ways, qualify has become more realistic for travelers who aren’t true “road warriors," since everyday spending counts toward status.

At the same time, free first-class upgrades have gotten harder to score and status benchmarks keep getting pricier to earn.

It's created a real dilemma for travelers who fly a lot — but only have so much money they're willing to put toward earning status: Is it worth dumping tens (or hundreds) of thousands of dollars onto your favorite airline’s credit card to reach your status goal?

Think about what you’re getting out of status, and whether it’s worth the investment.

If not, you could be a candidate to hop off the status "hamster wheel" and be an airline "free agent."

But if you've crunched the numbers and decided status is still worth it, you may need to double down on your favorite airline.

And that might mean prioritizing credit card spending on that carrier's card. Because in 2026, that is almost as important as flying when it comes to unlocking the best perks.

Here’s how much you’d need to pay for entry-tier airline status in 2027 if you went exclusively by credit card spending.

*Note: American has not announced what its status thresholds will be in 2027.

$25,000 with the Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® (see )

Assumes 12 flight segments on American to fully unlock the card’s “Flight Streak” benefit.

$25,000 with the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card

Note: United requires a minimum of four United-operated flights for members to be Premier-eligible.

Of course, the most efficient way to earn status is by combining your card spending with flying.

Spending on flights does typically earn you more elite credit (and points) than you'd get with typical credit card spending.

While airline credit cards can offer strong value with that carrier, other cards may offer a stronger return for your spending.

For instance, there's basically no airline card that truly competes with the American Express® Gold Card on rewards for dining worldwide and grocery purchases.

And some Capital One credit cards offer 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase.

Most of us only have so many dollars to dole out, and sometimes the best rewards to earn are the flexible points you can transfer to a wide range of partners.

Plus, as a frequent traveler, I also carry hotel cards that are key to unlocking perks once I arrive at my destination.

If you're rethinking your loyalty with a particular airline, there are status matches you can take advantage of to effectively “change airlines.”

Just remember: Most U.S. carriers are now playing the “spending to status” game in some form. So, you may encounter similar sticker shock with your new carrier of choice.

Plus, even after matching, you’ll likely have to hit an ambitious challenge goal to keep your status for the entire year.

While United and Southwest announced major overhauls to their loyalty and status programs, Delta opted to stay the course for next year.

Its Medallion qualification requirements will not change in 2027.

Delta’s last major shake-up to its Delta SkyMiles program came in 2023, which led to significant backlash among its SkyMiles members.

American likely won’t update its AAdvantage members for a few months since its loyalty year technically doesn’t begin until March 1.

So, it remains to be seen whether the status game will continue getting harder for more flyers in the new year.

#6264. United Boeing 757 Declares Mayday As Fuel Runs Low After Aborted Landing At San Francisco

This article was updated on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, to include additional context on the FAA's rules on Mayday declarations. It was originally published on Sunday, November 1, 2026.

A United Airlines Boeing 757 declared a Mayday on Friday morning due to low fuel after aborting its landing at San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and going around. The aircraft — operating flight UA1023 from Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) — was on final approach to Runway 28R when it suddenly went around due to an unstable approach.

Moments later, the flight crew declared "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, fuel emergency," before climbing to 5,000 feet and reporting 5,200 lbs of fuel remaining. The flight, which had 97 people onboard, ultimately landed safely around 14 minutes after the go-around, with no injuries reported.

The Boeing 757-200 (registration N19117) was operating the transcontinental service on the morning of Friday, October 30. Air traffic control (ATC) audio from Flight Follower shows that the controller cleared the aircraft to land on Runway 28R. ATC also warned the crew about wake turbulence from a Boeing 787 Dreamliner that had landed ahead of it, as well as a slight tailwind of five knots.

The 757 then attempted to land at 11:11 AM local time — however, ADS-B data shows it started climbing at around 75 feet as the pilot initiated a go-around, later clarifying it was due to an unstable approach. The crew then declared a Mayday due to the fuel emergency and was cleared to land on Runway 28R for a second time, touching down safely at 11:24 AM. It is not clear whether the wind or wake turbulence from the preceding 787 played any part in the go-around.

Simple Flying contacted United Airlines for comment on this incident. A spokesperson responded that "the crew did not declare an emergency," while confirming that the flight had 91 passengers and six crew members onboard. The crew can be heard using the word "Mayday" when communicating with ATC, but the aircraft did not change its transponder squawk code.

While a change to an emergency squawk code is standard protocol during emergencies, it is not necessarily required when the crew has already communicated the situation by radio. The 5,200 lbs of fuel remaining is close to the minimum threshold for a Boeing 757-200, although it is up to the discretion of the pilots whether to declare an emergency.

Under FAA rules, US airlines on domestic flights must carry enough fuel to reach their destination and an alternate airport where required, plus a further 45 minutes of flying. The incident occurred just five days after another United flight reported critically low fuel levels — on Sunday, October 25, United flight 1854 from Grand Cayman (GCM) to Houston (IAH) declared an emergency after its right main landing gear failed to extend, with the pilots later reporting having just 10 to 12 minutes of fuel remaining.

A late-night security incident prompted multiple diversions and long holds as one jet declared a fuel emergency.

United says its crew did not declare an emergency, but the FAA's guidance for pilots and controllers raises questions about that claim. Under FAA Order JO 7110.65, pilots should declare an emergency by opening their radio call with the word Mayday, ideally repeated three times. For a less serious urgency situation, pilots should use "Pan-Pan" instead.

Controllers are also told to treat a situation as an emergency if they believe one exists, even when the pilot has not declared one, as pilots may be too preoccupied with handling the emergency to use the radio. The incident also shows the distinction between declaring an emergency and simply telling ATC that fuel is running low, known as a minimum-fuel advisory.

The FAA defines a minimum-fuel advisory as a warning that an aircraft has very little room for further delays before its fuel becomes critical. It does not, however, constitute an emergency declaration or guarantee priority handling. If a pilot decides that the remaining fuel needs priority handling to ensure a safe landing, the FAA says an emergency should be declared instead.

Fuel emergencies are among the most serious situations a crew can face, leaving pilots with limited time to reach an airport before fuel levels become critical. However, not every low-fuel situation is automatically an emergency. Pilots can first declare "minimum fuel" to alert ATC that they cannot handle any further delays to landing.

If the situation becomes more urgent, pilots can declare an emergency using the Mayday call. This tells ATC that the aircraft requires immediate assistance, allowing controllers to prioritize its landing and deal with other flights accordingly.

Importantly, a fuel emergency does not necessarily mean that the aircraft is moments away from running out of fuel. It means the crew has reached a point where its remaining fuel requires immediate attention and further delays cannot be accepted. In UA1023's case, the crew reported approximately 5,200 lbs of fuel remaining soon after the aborted landing, but it was able to land safely around 14 minutes later.

An unstable approach occurs when an aircraft is not properly configured or following the required speed, descent rate, or flight path, making it unsafe to continue with the landing. Airlines set specific criteria that aircraft must meet by a certain height to be considered stable.

The Flight Safety Foundation (FSF) recommends reaching this point at 1,000 feet above the airport in poor visibility, or 500 feet in clear conditions. The aircraft should be fully configured for landing and on the correct glide path, while its descent rate should generally stay below around 1,000 feet per minute.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

If any of these conditions are not met, the crew is expected to go around. For a flight that already has little fuel to spare, the extra time of performing a go-around could turn a tight fuel situation into an emergency.

#6263. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Thatched Cottage Tucked Away in the Cotswolds

Choosing the perfect place to hole up for a weekend getaway is not always straightforward. But this spring, the decisions seemed to make themselves. After a relentlessly busy start to the year, I was looking for a place to escape. And the place needed to fit certain criteria: Somewhere my partner and I wouldn't have to speak to anyone but each other; somewhere we could sleep for 12 hours a night and take the days slow and easy without guilt; somewhere within a couple of hours’ drive from our home in northwest London; somewhere rural, where I wouldn’t be woken up by the neighbors’ bathroom light or the sound of the tube; and somewhere we could have the place to ourselves, but still be close to some nice pubs or restaurants, so we wouldn't have to hunt and gather our own dinners, God forbid.

An Airbnb in the Cotswolds was the obvious choice. Luckily, I remembered I’d saved a cozy-looking cottage on Instagram a few months prior to feeling the sudden urge to get away. I revisited my staycation wishlist and found Strawtop Cottages: two 16th-century thatched-roof cottages that sit side by side on a quiet street in the quaint little village of Adderbury. I booked one of them, Strawtop Two, for a long weekend in April.

We checked into Strawtop Two after a speedy drive from London on a Friday night. As we unlocked the front door, we found switched-on lamps casting a cozy glow across the beamed living room; kindling ready to be lit in the wood-burning fire. In the egg-yolk yellow kitchen, a fresh loaf of sourdough was sitting pretty on the chopping board for us; organic eggs and marmalade on the counter; Daylesford butter, bacon, and rosé in the fridge. My partner prepared a simple supper while I nosed around the rest of the cottage, discovering a sweet dining room with floor-to-ceiling windows and an enormous bunch of fresh flowers around the back, as well as a boot room with Barbour jackets, Wellies for stomps across the fields, and umbrellas (likely a requirement, considering we were visiting in April).

I learned that the sister properties are owned by local content creator Josie Irons (@Josieldn on Instagram) and her husband Charlie Irons (who manages the properties), who have been custodians here for just a small part of the cottages’ centuries-long history. Their meticulous renovations have restored the spaces beautifully, preserving all the Grade II-listed original features that make staying here feel like a journey back to a simpler, more peaceful time, while adding plush finishing touches that feel every bit as cosseting as those of the area’s top-of-class hotels.

I originally saved this cottage because of the kitchen, drawn in by sunshiny pictures and clips of its buttery-hued walls, vintage copper pans, and an old-school kettle whistling on the Aga stove. But as I nipped between the two bedrooms—one on the first floor with minty green walls, one folded into the eaves on the top floor with tongue-and-groove woodwork—I found there’s a lot more to love here, like the Bamford pillow mist left next to the beds, and the blackout blinds creating one of the darkest and quietest bedrooms I’ve ever drifted off in. Wrapped up in the bed linens, I snoozed more peacefully than I’d managed to in months.

After homemade coffee sipped while listening to the Roberts Radio on Saturday morning, we headed a few minutes up the road to The Yurt at Nicholsons restaurant. This was one of a handful of recommendations that Charlie had sent us ahead of time. Normally, I’m a stickler for doing my own research (read: a snob and a control freak), but in the name of keeping things as relaxed as possible, I decided to put my faith in his suggestions. I shouldn’t have hesitated: a gooey camembert croissant, cut through with umami bacon, and a full English breakfast with melty pork belly chop and smoky baked beans hit the spot.

Our supper, also recommended (and booked for us) by Charlie, at The Norman Knight was every bit as impressive. I ordered perfectly blushing steak frites and felt smugly like I’d uncovered a hidden gem. Our Sunday lunch at The Duke of Cumberland’s Head, where we shared bowls of cauliflower cheese and crispy potatoes, was one of the tastiest roasts I’ve had in a while. Trust me, having Charlie as a de facto concierge is one of the biggest unsung perks of booking a stay here.

Back at the house, we hibernated on the sofa, reading the paper and watching Netflix in the dinky living room. I took mental notes of my favorite design details: the antique coffee table laden with magazines, the books plopped into recesses in the stone chimney, the deep-green rainfall shower stocked with Bamford products, the Steamery steamer and Dyson hairdryer in the bedroom vanity, and the Soho Home robes. If I could make my London flat one-tenth as comfortable as this little countryside cottage, I’d be thrilled. For now, I’ll bookmark the cottage next door for my next escape.

This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
