It earns 4 points per dollar at U.S. supermarkets on up to $25,000 in purchases each calendar year and at restaurants worldwide on up to $50,000, then 1 point per dollar. If groceries and dining are a large share of your budget, these bonus categories can build your points balance quickly.

The Gold isn't limited to food, either. It earns:

That range makes it my strongest one-card recommendation for someone who wants to earn Membership Rewards points across both everyday spending and travel.

The card has a $325 annual fee (see ), but includes up to $10 monthly Uber Cash for eligible U.S. Uber and Uber Eats orders†, up to $10 monthly dining statement credit with select partners and up to $50 biannual statement credits at U.S. Resy restaurants. (Enrollment is required for select benefits.)

That makes the fee easiest to justify for someone who will use the statement credits naturally and put the earning categories to work. Still, the credits are supporting actors here: The strong bonus categories are why the Gold deserves top billing.

If, like me, you spend about $800 per month at the grocery store, that alone will earn you 38,400 points annually. If you also spend $500 per month on dining, $3,000 per year in flights and $1,000 in prepaid hotels booked through Amex Travel, your annual haul climbs to 76,400 points.

That's worth over $1,500 according to TPG’s October 2026 valuations.

Personally, I'd be tempted to transfer 60,000 of those points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue for a one-way business-class saver award between the U.S. and Europe. Those seats can be difficult to find, but that's the kind of redemption that makes my grocery runs feel more rewarding.

†Uber Cash will only be deposited into one Uber account when you add the Amex Gold as a payment method and redeem with any Amex card.

To learn more, read our full review of the American Express Gold Card.

Airfare is where the American Express Platinum Card gets its chance to flex.

The card earns 5 points per dollar on flights purchased directly from airlines or through American Express Travel®, including through AmexTravel.com and the Amex Travel App, on up to $500,000 in these purchases each calendar year (then 1 point per dollar). It also earns 5 points per dollar on prepaid lodging booked through Amex Travel and 1 point per dollar on all other eligible purchases.

Spending $4,000 on airfare each year would earn 20,000 Membership Rewards points on the Platinum card. That's worth about $400 according to our valuations, compared to just $40 earned on a 1% cash-back credit card. That level of spending isn’t outlandish: A family of four paying $500 per ticket for two trips a year would reach it. I usually travel more than twice a year, so that difference can add up even faster.

Don't overlook the fact that these rewards come from booking flights directly with the airline, either. Buying straight from the source instead of through a travel portal can make it easier to change or cancel your reservation if your plans change, or when you have to make last-minute adjustments due to delays or operational cancellations.

The Platinum carries an $895 annual fee (see ), so it makes the most sense for frequent flyers who can pair the airfare earnings with benefits they'll also use. My favorites are its broad airport lounge access through the American Express Global Lounge Collection, up to $200 in annual airline fee statement credits for incidental charges with one selected qualifying airline and complimentary Hilton Honors Gold status. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

To learn more, read our full review of the American Express Platinum Card.

Every business has expenses that refuse to cooperate with bonus categories. The Blue Business Plus Credit Card from American Express makes sure those purchases still pull their weight.

The card earns 2 points per dollar spent on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar. It also earns 2 points per dollar spent on prepaid hotels and other eligible travel purchases booked through amextravel.com (and those purchases don’t count toward the $50,000 annual threshold). There's also no annual fee (see ).

That makes the Blue Business Plus an excellent catch-all card for eligible business owners. Rather than worrying about whether each purchase falls into the right merchant category, you can use it for general business spending and know you’re earning twice the standard rate until you hit the annual cap.

Maxing out the threshold with $50,000 in business expenses would earn 100,000 Membership Rewards points. If your business values simplicity more than squeezing every last penny out of a redemption, one of the easiest options is to use those points to cover $1,000 in airfare booked through Amex Travel. Transferring your points to travel partners might be worth even more.

It isn’t the flashiest card in the Amex portfolio, but quietly doubling your points on broad business spending is a skill worth having.

To learn more, read our full review of the Blue Business Plus Credit Card.

Related: Who qualifies for a business credit card?

Some businesses spend a little everywhere. Others have two or three expense categories that swallow the budget whole.

The American Express Business Gold Card is built for the latter. It automatically earns 4 points per dollar in the two eligible categories where your business spends the most each billing cycle, on up to $150,000 in combined purchases each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar.

My favorite part: Amex automatically identifies your two highest eligible spending categories each billing cycle, so you don't need a crystal ball to make a selection in advance, and you don't have to analyze your expenses line by line to choose a category after the fact. The strongest categories can even change from month to month, allowing the card to adapt to your business rather than forcing your business to follow the card.

A business putting $50,000 of qualifying expenses on the card would earn 200,000 Membership Rewards points, even without maxing out the full annual bonus threshold. One way I’d put those points to work is by transferring them to Aeroplan. That balance would cover two round-trip tickets from Miami to Rio de Janeiro — in business class.

The card has a $375 annual fee (see ), so its sweet spot is a business with enough qualifying spending to put the 4-point-per-dollar rate to serious use. For smaller or more varied expenses, the Blue Business Plus may be the easier fit.

To learn more, read our full review of the American Express Business Gold Card.

For most customers, holding all four cards is overkill, but pairing two together can supercharge your earnings compared to carrying a single card.

For personal spending, the Gold does most of the earning work on its own with its generous earning rates. Adding the Platinum improves your rewards on flights, but the combination is better evaluated as using the Gold as your primary earner and the Platinum as a way to enhance your experience through its many benefits and statement credits.

The business pairing is much easier to defend. Use the Business Gold for purchases in your two highest eligible bonus categories and the Blue Business Plus for everything else. One handles the obvious expenses; the other cleans up everything left behind.

If you're juggling both personal and business expenses, my pick is for the personal Gold and Blue Business Plus. Between the two, you'll earn 2 to 4 points per dollar on an impressive number of charges while paying only one annual fee.

Welcome offers are exciting, but short-lived. Long-term point maximization comes from paying with the right card.

And the best Amex card for earning Membership Rewards points depends on where you spend the most.

I may dream of an infinite points balance, but the goal isn't to collect every shiny Amex card; it’s to make more of my spending earn 2, 4 or 5 points per dollar.

For personal spending, the Gold is a strong choice for groceries and dining, while the Platinum can provide additional value for frequent flyers who use its premium travel benefits. Business owners may prefer the Blue Business Plus for everyday purchases or the Business Gold for concentrated spending in its bonus categories.

Once your biggest expenses earn more than 1 point per dollar, all that's left is remembering which card to use when it's time to pay and letting the points pile up from spending you were already doing.

#6261. Report: Alaska to Lay Off 200 Employees

Alaska Air Group, the parent company of Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, and Horizon Air, will lay off about 200 workers as financial losses tied to the higher price of jet fuel grow.

The Honolulu Star-Advertiser obtained an email sent to employees Friday morning acknowledging the cuts.

“Despite having the right strategy and strong momentum, fuel prices and geopolitical challenges are putting significant financial pressure on our business,” CEO Ben Minicucci wrote. “If current conditions persist, we could lose as much as $700 million this year, which would be our first adjusted pretax loss outside of the pandemic since 2003.”

According to the Star-Advertiser, 125 workers in Washington state will be laid off, and 48 in Hawaii.

The affected employees will be out of a job Nov. 13, but will continue to receive pay through the end of the year.

Alaska’s leadership said no front-line, non-management positions have been affected, suggesting the eliminated jobs are management-related.

Separately, Hawaiian Airlines CEO Diana Birkett Rakow said in an email to staff that, of the 48 affected positions at Hawaiian, 40 roles will be eliminated entirely, and eight people will be be offered other jobs within the airline.

Birkett Rakow also said that two senior leaders – Jim Landers, head of Hawaii operations, and Shelly Parker, head of guest operations – will retire at the end of the year. Both of their positions will be eliminated following their departure.

#6260. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Cabin on a Vineyard Just 2 Hours From London

I'm always on the hunt for a new cabin stay in the British countryside. Having visited at least two a year since 2020, I'd now dub myself something of an expert. Living in East London, sometimes all I crave is solitude, and I find that a slightly rustic spot, kitted out with all the necessary amenities, can be more restorative than a jam-packed, buzzy hotel stay.

I don't drive (hey, I'm a Londoner), which can be a rather large obstacle when planning cabin stays. But Liba Vineyard, a luxury glamping site made up of three pod-style homes in Porton, just a 15-minute taxi ride from Salisbury station, presents no such problem. The pods are all bookable on Airbnb, and I scooped up the Hawthorn Pod for a stay this autumn, eager to hunker down and work on writing my upcoming book. Door-to-door from London, I managed to reach it in two hours, armed with enough books and food to last two nights.

Once I'd settled into the Hawthorn Pod, I realized the Wi-Fi was excellent, and I wouldn't need to leave at all during my stay. The pods are dotted along winding wood-chip paths, which branch off towards the three cabins: Hawthorn, Beech, and Elder. All sleep four people and have a wood-fired hot tub, although Hawthorn is slightly more snug than the other two and better suited to solo visitors and couples. Beech is best for anyone traveling with children, while for larger groups, renting all three would be a fun way to celebrate a birthday. It's a spot that can be both solitary and social, depending on what you're after.

Inside, the pods are neutral, bright, and cozy. Draped curtains add a sense of grandeur to the French doors, while the bathroom—the biggest test of any cabin—was a welcome sight. A flushing toilet and strong water pressure are unsung luxuries, and things I'm always relieved to find in a cabin. The kitchen has everything you'd need, but there's also an outdoor barbecue firepit, making cooking here a genuine joy.

Nearby, there are plenty of sightseeing opportunities, pubs, day trips, and activities: UNESCO World Heritage Site Stonehenge is just a 15-minute drive away, while Cranborne Chase National Landscape and the New Forest are both under a half-hour drive. The property itself is full of life as well, with alpacas grazing, chickens clucking, and a muster of peacocks running between hedgerows. On Mondays and Wednesdays, you can join a yoga class in a studio above the winemaking barn.

Each morning, I'd wake to the sound of peacocks, open the drapes to soft golden light trickling in, and breathe in the fresh air before lighting a fire to get breakfast started. Since returning home, I've longed for the calm of those mornings and the methodical mindfulness of cooking over a flame.

The owners have big plans in the works. Soon, wine will be available from the vineyard, which is expected to produce up to 10,000 bottles a year over the next few years. Chris Reynolds, who owns the land with his wife, Louise Marshall, gives every pod guest a tour, something that will become an even bigger selling point once wine is available to taste. Ahead of this, visitors can sponsor a vine through a subscription model in exchange for wine, pod stays, and events such as harvest parties. Liba is already certified organic and is working towards biodynamic certification within the next nine months.

Next summer, the 10-acre farm will be bookable for weddings, while early discussions are underway about an on-site café and additional activities to complement the existing yoga studio.

#6259. 55 Thoughtful Gifts for Men Who Love to Travel

The holiday season will be here before we know it, which means it’s time to start thinking about gifts for the ones you love. When you’re shopping for a special guy in your life this year, skip the things he doesn’t actually need and go straight for the ones that count: thoughtful pieces he’ll put to good use on his next trip, upgrades to his everyday essentials, and a few small luxuries that make being on the road that much better. The best gifts for men, after all, aren’t necessarily the flashiest—they’re the ones that become part of his routine, whether that means packing them in a carry-on or enjoying them on a quiet Sunday morning at home.

I’ve hand-selected over 50 gift ideas for men who love to travel, featuring many talked-about favorites with a few less expected additions too. From a timeless leather weekender that’s perfect for a quick getaway to at-home accessories that will enrich any guy’s space, I've got you covered with plenty of options he’ll love. Read on for all of the best travel gifts for men or jump straight to the section you think will interest him most.

At Condé Nast Traveler, editors spend a lot of time debating, researching, testing, and re-testing all things travel accessories and luggage. If you’re looking for the best suitcase to buy your guy this holiday season, look here. But if you want something a little unique that will absolutely rock his travel routine for years to come, check out some of the gift ideas below. To make his next long-haul flight more comfortable, consider gifting him a comfy neck pillow, sleep mask, or a pair of compression socks. A ludicrously capacious leather weekender or a luxurious Italian notebook are smart upgrades he’ll cherish forever. And in case of emergencies, a good ol' fashioned flask will more than do the trick.

Here’s the thing about men: There’s a part of us that will always relish having a new toy to play with. This category is for those who will appreciate a wild card gift and savor the element of surprise. A perfect pair of travel-sized binoculars made from the best optical-grade crystal in the world? Jackpot! The latest generation of AirPods with top-notch noise-canceling technology? Bingo! A smart watch that can track his steps on the go? Perfect!

Clothes are a tough gift for the holidays. Everybody is different, every body is different, and a lot of guys are just downright picky when it comes to what they get dressed in everyday. That being said, there are a few tricks of the trade to consider here—when gifting clothes, don’t go too big, too outré, or too outlandish. The secret is to select timeless, quintessential pieces that travel well, age well, and can be styled into any wardrobe: a Barbour jacket, a crisp white shirt, or a navy suit that packs nicely into a suitcase. When in doubt, a pair of high-quality sunglasses in a classic silhouette is generally a win too.

Lovers of the great outdoors are a funny bunch to shop for. They typically have all of their most treasured gear ready to go already, so this is a demographic for whom you need to be on your A-game. Gifts for outdoorsy types need to be the newest of the new with smart details, category-leading engineering, and unassailable durability. Think a lightweight Norwegian cooler that keeps drinks cold without any ice (that’s right—no ice), or a comfortable running shoe that can handle endless wear and tear. Outdoorsy folks will say that they can never have too many puffy layer-type things—so go ahead and consider a thick blanket or the iconic Arc’teryx Atom insulated hoodie. And if all else fails you can get them a beautiful Stanley bottle to keep their favorite soups and beverages warm in even the most wintry conditions.

I hate to stereotype the genders—but a lot of self-care products out there are marketed more heavily toward women, leaving the average guy in the lurch. He may not know the benefits of investing in a Dr. Barbara Sturm skincare regimen, or how an Omnilux LED mask can help slow visible signs of aging. There’s a whole world of self-care products out there! Here, I’ve gathered some of the best items to kick-start his journey—sometimes all it takes is Dr. Dennis Gross’ miracle-working peel pads.

Food is one of my favorite ways to experience travel. If you’re not quite ready to gift someone a trip to sample authentic panettone straight from the oven in Italy, the good news is that the marvels of modern packing and shipping have made some of the world’s tastiest foods closer than ever. A sampler of high-quality spices will upgrade his at-home cooking. A $60 bag of beans is the perfectly fun gift for a coffee snob who might not buy it for himself. And a perfectly unassailable upgrade to his go-to sauté pan (if he even has one), or the investment of a proper stand mixer, are foolproof.

No matter what the recipient’s sense of style is, there are certain upgrades that are likely to fit into most any home. Beautiful linen sheets are always welcome, as is a great bathrobe or pair of slippers to remind him of a luxury hotel. When in doubt, the flourish of a Flamingo Estate candle hits just the right notes.

If you have a Capital One credit card, you may be able to earn extra rewards on purchases through Capital One Offers.

Similar to Amex Offers and Chase Offers, the program gives eligible cardholders access to shopping deals that can help them save on purchases they were already planning to make.

Here's how Capital One Offers works, how to use it and what to know before shopping.

Capital One Offers is a shopping rewards platform that gives eligible Capital One customers access to special deals at participating merchants. Offers span categories such as clothing, electronics, home goods and travel.

The platform is available to eligible U.S. consumer Capital One credit card holders, including those with cards in the Venture, Savor and Quicksilver families. (Business credit cards are not eligible.)

You can access available offers through your online account or the Capital One mobile app. However, eligibility varies by account, so you'll need to sign in to see which offers are available to you.

Unlike the standard rewards you earn on everyday purchases, Capital One Offers requires you to select an eligible deal and follow its redemption instructions.

For example, if you find an offer for 5% back at a retailer, you could earn that reward on top of the points or miles you'd normally earn with your credit card, as long as your purchase meets the offer's terms.

Capital One Offers is different from Capital One Shopping. Capital One Offers provides deals through eligible Capital One accounts, while Capital One Shopping is a separate shopping tool that helps users find coupon codes, compare prices and track price drops.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

The deals you'll find through Capital One Offers depend on what's available when you sign in. You might see discounts on clothing, electronics or hotel bookings, with participating merchants and reward rates varying.

Some offers apply to most purchases from a retailer, while others are limited to certain products or categories. Keep in mind that rewards may also exclude taxes, shipping and other fees.

You can find Capital One Offers through the issuer's website or mobile app:

From there, you can browse deals or search for a specific merchant.

How you redeem an offer depends on whether you're shopping online or in a physical store.

Keep in mind that for online offers, the link you use matters, as Capital One relies on tracking information to associate your purchase with the offer.

Be sure to confirm which locations, payment methods and purchases qualify. An online offer won't necessarily apply to an in-store transaction, or vice versa.

Related: How to maximize online shopping portals for your purchases

Capital One says rewards typically arrive in about 45 days, although some can take up to three billing cycles. Certain offers may take longer.

For hotel offers, payouts are issued after you complete your stay, and the reservation must be completed within one year of booking.

Related: The best credit cards for online shopping

There are a few things worth keeping in mind before taking advantage of an offer.

I've gotten into the habit of checking Capital One Offers whenever I'm shopping online with my Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card. Sometimes there's a deal worth using, but other times I'll find a better offer through another shopping portal.

That's why it's worth comparing your options before making a purchase. For example, an offer for 5% back through Capital One, for example, might not be as valuable as a higher reward rate elsewhere.

Just keep in mind that you generally can't stack Capital One Offers with other shopping portals or promotional codes. Using another portal or certain coupons could invalidate your reward, so you'll want to decide which offer to use before checking out.

For travel purchases, I'd also recommend comparing the total price and booking conditions rather than focusing solely on the advertised reward.

Each offer has its own terms, including potential spending requirements, expiration dates and usage limits. Some deals may exclude gift cards, certain products or other purchases, while others may be limited to a single transaction.

Look at the terms before shopping, particularly if you're making a large purchase or planning to use an offer more than once.

You can check the status of your Capital One Offers rewards by opening the menu on the right side of the Capital One Offers page and selecting "Shopping Trips." From there, you'll see a tracker showing the status of your purchases and rewards.

It's also worth saving your offer details and order confirmations, especially for purchases with longer payout timelines.

If your reward hasn't arrived when expected, double-check that you met the offer requirements before contacting Capital One.

Related: Capital One miles: How to earn, redeem and transfer rewards

Capital One Offers can be an easy way to earn extra rewards on purchases you're already planning to make.

Before shopping, check your account for available deals, compare your options and follow the offer's instructions to make sure your purchase qualifies.

Just remember that offers and eligibility can vary, so a deal available to one Capital One customer may not be available to another.

Related: Tips and tricks to get maximum value from your Capital One miles

#6257. Cruising to Alaska? Check if Your Next Port, Bus, or Lodge is Indigenous-Owned

The Huna Totem Corporation was featured on Condé Nast Traveler's Bright Ideas in Travel 2026. Read the full list of winners here.

From April to October, cruise ships tower over downtown Juneau’s Marine Way, a coastal path that connects the port zone to downtown. Should a traveler pause for a moment between ship and souvenir store, they’ll notice Kaagwaantaan Kootéeyaa, a tall, intricately carved pole rising against a backdrop of forest and mountains. At its base, a panel explains that the cedar pole depicts five of the Kaagwaantaan Tlingit clan’s crests: a hat, person, orca, eagle and bear. It is an arresting introduction to the long-overlooked human history of this place.

Since 2023, totem poles have adorned this highly trafficked shoreline, part of Kootéeyaa Deiyí (“Totem Pole Trail”)—a city-wide project led by the Sealaska Heritage Institute (SHI) that represents the cultures of the Tlingit people who have inhabited Juneau for at least 10,000 years, as well as the Haida and Tsimshian who arrived a few hundred years ago. Visible evidence of the region’s Indigenous communities was previously limited, says SHI’s Ricardo Worl (Tlingit), who sees the trail as “an opportunity to reestablish our presence on our ancestral lands.” Noting that more than a million cruise ship passengers land in Juneau each year, Worl hopes the trail “is the beginning of their education about our culture.”

Alaska’s cruise industry has long invited travelers to experience the “Last Frontier” while relegating Indigenous peoples to the margins of the tourism economy. Now, a shift is occurring—one that goes beyond simply incorporating Indigenous culture into the cruise experience. Across Alaska, Native corporations are increasingly owning and shaping the tourism infrastructure itself, from cruise docks and terminals to ground transportation, giving them a greater stake in how destinations develop, and how visitors experience them.

I came to Alaska to see how Indigenous ownership is changing the experience on the ground, following a route that took me from whale watching at cruise ports on the coast to bear and moose spotting at a lodge deep in the Interior. At each stop, I saw how Alaska Native corporations are shaping the places that travelers pass through.

Created following passage of the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Alaska Native corporations are for-profit companies run by and for Alaska Native shareholders. For Huna Totem, a Tlingit village corporation representing shareholders with ties to Hoonah and Glacier Bay, tourism is an important part of its economic development strategy. Its best-known development, Icy Strait Point in Hoonah, is Alaska’s first private cruise destination and has become a model for Alaska Native-owned tourism—creating local jobs, keeping economic benefits within the community and making Tlingit culture part of the visitor experience.

When Icy Strait Point opened in 2004, Huna Totem leadership was focused on “providing economic stability for generations, so the culture can be perpetuated,” says Ruth Banaszak, director of marketing and communications. Icy Strait Point has two cruise ship piers located about a half-mile apart and activity areas for 30 different excursions to distribute visitor flow around the site so that it never becomes overwhelming. To get around the vast site, I made use of the forested walking trails and two gondola systems, one of which took me to the summit of Hoonah Mountain, which I quickly and thrillingly descended via the ZipRider, a six-cable zipline. Walking around the museum exhibits housed inside a 1912 salmon cannery that closed when the fishing industry declined, I could connect tourism's present and future with its economic history. The cannery was once a symbol of loss; now it provides new economic opportunities. “We hire around 350 people for the season,” says Banaszak. “So, in a town of 950, anybody who wants to have a job in the community has one.” The model has also allowed local residents to build businesses of their own, including boat tours to Point Adolphus where, in just two hours, I spotted dozens of orcas, a few humpback whales and uncountable numbers of sea lions and sea otters. In each place, instead of being whisked onto an excursion operated by an outside company, I was experiencing a destination that had been shaped by the community whose ancestral home I was visiting.

“We’ve done this for our own community in Hoonah,” says Banaszak, “so now [we’re asking] how can we take what we’ve learned here and help other rural communities do the same thing?”

That thinking has led Huna Totem around Southeast Alaska and beyond. In Whittier, the corporation opened Glacier Gateway cruise terminal in 2024. Huna Totem and Doyon, Limited, another Alaska Native corporation, have also acquired Portage Glacier Cruises and Alaska Coach Tours, creating Native-owned touchpoints that extend from ship to shore and beyond. In Klawock, on Prince of Wales Island, Huna Totem partnered with Doyon and the local Alaska Native village corporation Klawock Heenya to develop a new cruise port in 2024. The destination uses a single-ship model, with development focused on Tlingit culture, local involvement and community values.

Back in downtown Juneau, Huna Totem is developing Áak’w Landing, a cruise dock and waterfront development targeting its first full season in 2028. The project is designed to improve how cruise visitors move through the city—including eliminating the need for tender boats at the site—rather than simply bringing in more ships. Reflecting its approach of being “culturally driven, community-centric, [and] business-focused,” says Banaszak, Huna Totem sees the project as both infrastructure enhancement and an opportunity to incorporate Alaska Native culture into the visitor experience—two poles from SHI’s Kootéeyaa Deiyí will be raised at the site.

The broader ambition is to create a network of Native-owned tourism businesses across Alaska. “So that Alaska Native tourism grows: culturally-led tourism as it should be done, people telling their own story themselves,” Banaszak says.

The cruise industry may seem an odd venture for Doyon, Limited, which is based in Fairbanks and represents the largely Dene people of the Interior, but, says Jordan Sanford, president of Doyon Tourism, “more than 60% of visitors come to Alaska by cruise, so [we realized] if we wanted to grow, we needed to be involved.”

Deep in Denali National Park, Doyon has operated Kantishna Roadhouse, the park’s only Indigenous-owned lodge, for 30 years. Arriving via a small plane from the park entrance—road access, closed for five years due to a landslide, will return in 2027—I spent blissful days backcountry hiking free from cell service. Evenings were spent listening to presentations by staff, such as an introduction to Dene beadwork and regalia; spotting wildlife including grizzly bears, moose, and caribou, then watching the setting sun light up the slopes of mighty Denali. Since 2004, in partnership with Aramark, Doyon has also operated bus tours, transit services, and campgrounds in the park. The partnership with Huna Totem gives Doyon an opportunity to diversify and grow, while responding to a recent shift in cruise passengers’ expectations: “They’re looking for more authentic experiences,” she explains. “We see that as our advantage. We put shareholders to work, and they share their culture,” she says. “There's a lot of businesses here that have been sharing the culture for so long, but from non-Alaska Natives,” she adds.

Next up is the restoration of the 1925 Chatanika Gold Camp near Fairbanks, which is scheduled to open in 2027 as a northern lights experience center, filling a critical infrastructure gap. Aurora viewing in Alaska today typically means pulling off the side of the road and drinking a hot chocolate, says Sanford. With Chatanika, “we're creating a space [with] cultural programming to make it more of an experience.”

It’s another link in an emerging network of Native-owned businesses across the state. The ultimate goal is “an Alaska Native-owned corridor, where [travelers] are visiting Alaska Native-owned businesses along the way,” says Sanford. For cruise passengers, that means more opportunities to encounter Indigenous culture, while knowing that Indigenous people are benefiting from the industry. And it means that your next Alaska cruise itinerary might begin at a Native-owned port, continue aboard a Native-owned bus, lead to a Native-owned excursion, and end at a Native-owned lodge.

#6256. Transfer Chase Points To British Airways, Iberia, Aer Lingus, With 30% Bonus

Chase Ultimate Rewards has just launched its latest airline transfer bonus. Actually, it’s a trio of transfer bonuses, as it’s valid for British Airways Club, Iberia Club, and Aer Lingus AerClub. This is a popular bonus when available, so I think some members will find this to be worthwhile.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is offering a bonus when you transfer points to British Airways Club, Iberia Club, or Aer Lingus AerClub. Between 12AM ET on November 1, 2026, and 11:59PM ET on December 1, 2026, members can receive a 30% bonus when moving points.

A transfer bonus like this seems to be offered an average of once to twice per year, and it’s typically in the range of 20-30%. So the 30% bonus is as good as it gets, and this is the biggest percentage bonus that we’ve seen so far in 2026.

Keep in mind that this bonus covers three different Avios currencies, and on top of that, you can freely transfer Avios between the various “flavors.” When you go to make a transfer, you should immediately see the 30% bonus reflected. Transfers from Ultimate Rewards to these partners are typically instant.

Keep in mind the various Avios currencies also partner with other major transferable points currencies, and we do sometimes see transfer bonuses with other programs as well.

I think there’s value to be had in taking advantage of a 30% bonus on points transfers from Ultimate Rewards to Avios. That’s not because of any one particular redemption opportunity, but rather because of the collective value of the Avios ecosystem.

Back in the day, the best uses of British Airways Avios were for short haul travel on partner airlines, including on Alaska and American. Unfortunately those redemption opportunities have been devalued horribly.

However, lots of great new options using Avios have emerged. For example, I love how Qatar Airways Privilege Club is now an Avios airline, as this opens up some great opportunities:

Anyway, there’s a ton of potential value here, so see my guides to maximizing Avios with British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Aer Lingus Aer Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, and Finnair Plus.

For the next several weeks, you can get a 30% bonus when you convert your Chase Ultimate Rewards points into Avios with British Airways Club, Iberia Club, and Aer Lingus AerClub.

Avios is one of the most useful points currencies out there, especially given across how many airlines you can redeem these rewards. I think for many people, this could be worth a speculative transfer.

#6255. The Very Best Thai Food in New York City

There are several ways to describe delicious food in Thai: Aroy means delicious, while aroy mak takes it a step further to very delicious. But my favorite word is zaab (also spelled zabb or zab; แซ่บ), a term rooted in the Isan region of northeastern Thailand that conveys a bold deliciousness, often associated with the heat. In New York City, we’re spoiled for choice when it comes to food that delivers true zaab.

I’ve spent my life immersed in the world of Thai food. One of the joys of growing up in a Thai restaurant family is participating in one of our favorite hobbies: scoping out other Thai restaurants to see what’s good. Most summers, my aunts would close down their restaurant in Royal Palm Beach for two weeks, and they’d road trip from South Florida up to New York City to check out casinos and taste Thai restaurants along the way—when I was lucky, I got to join them. My grandpa, for his part, used to drive to the city weekly to get products for his grocery store in Washington, DC, and through his firsthand research, old friends, and the Internet, he created detailed restaurant guides to help me find footing when I moved to the city almost five years ago.

As I continue to eat my way through the city’s Thai restaurants, I feel spoiled for choice. More and more chefs are serving regional specialties of their hometowns and maintaining Thai food’s great balancing act between the spice, acid, salt, sweetness, and umami, while incorporating their own signature flair.

While the city’s established Thai spots, particularly out in Elmhurst, Queens, remain beloved, plenty of the most compelling and exciting bites can be found in various parts of the city. There has never been a more exciting time to eat Thai food in NYC, and these 14 restaurants best embody its golden era.

If you want an overview of the best dishes across Thailand without leaving the city, let your first stop in Queen’s Little Thai Town be Ayada. The beloved restaurant has familiar favorites like pad thai and tom yum, but let its expertise in other regional favorites be an excuse to try my dad’s favorite Yen Ta Fo, a bubblegum-pink soup with soft rice noodles and a savory tomato and bean curd sauce.

364 Grand Street, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Any of the fiery curries on the rotating menu

When the news of Ugly Baby’s closure last year hit my WhatsApp chat with my Thai friends, you would’ve thought that someone had died. In a way, it felt like we lost a family member. Ugly Baby was one of the rare spots in the city that didn’t hold back on heat like many in America do to appease Western palates and milder heat tolerances. But all was saved when the beloved restaurant announced its reopening in Williamsburg earlier this fall. It’s now a fun, lively two-floor restaurant with eclectic dishware and recipes from various Thai provinces, including brutally hot curries from Southern Thailand and Northeastern Isan cuisine.

Its menu is sorted from least spicy to most spicy—written out as “the laughs” to “the ugly” (dishes toward the latter end consist of a few menu items that will make you feel like you’re breathing fire). Luckily, waiters are standing by with large jugs of water, ready to refill at the sight of sweat dripping down your forehead.

Bangkok Supper Club makes a convincing case for the arrival of upscale Thai dining.

Order a la carte, or do the $150 tasting menu at Bangkok Supper Club.

641 Hudson St, New York, NY 10014 (Meatpacking District)

With an award-winning cocktail program by Suwincha "Chacha" Singsuwan and a menu from executive chef Max Wittawat, Bangkok Supper Club makes a convincing case for the arrival of upscale Thai dining. The drinks are as much of a draw as the food. I like to start my meal with a fish sauce cocktail, a savory, umami-forward drink that captures the depth of fish sauce while balancing it with sweet notes of floral pear. It’s unexpected, but feels just right, and is a lovely accompaniment to my other must-order: the pork jowl. These deep-fried pork cheeks arrive atop a fragrant, garlic-baked rice.

One of the best parts about eating in Thailand is getting food from restaurants and stalls that specialize in one singular dish. As my dad says, that’s how you know it’s good. Eim Khao Mun Kai is one such place. Its one dish, khao mun gai, is the Thai version of Hainanese chicken rice, served with a spicy, fermented bean sauce.

The $12 set meal includes tender steamed chicken thighs made with halal meat and gizzards, fragrant ginger rice that’s cooked with chicken droppings, and a savory broth-based soup made from the bones, with sides of cilantro and cucumber plus plenty of sauce. It’s a tight shop and cash-only. When my dad comes into town, it’s the first place we go to.

Must-order dish: Northern-style curry noodles

Since 1990, this institution has been serving what my friend calls “old-school auntie energy” with wooden accents, white tablecloths, and a sprawling menu. When I say sprawling, I mean it. You can flip through pages at SriPraPhai and can eat all the fried meats, papaya salads, curries, and noodle dishes your heart desires.

Zaab Zaab specializes in Northeast Isan cuisine, repping where both owners are from.

76-04 Woodside Ave, Queens, NY 11373 (Elmhurst)

208 Grand St, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Zaab Zaab has locations in both Elmhurst and Williamsburg, and specializes in Northeast Isan cuisine from where owner Bryan Chunton and chef Aniwat Khotsopa hail. The restaurant’s signature dish, an herb-packed larb ped udon, features cilantro- and mint-packed ground duck, fried liver, and crispy skin; it’s served with a plethora of fresh lettuce, cabbage, extra herbs, and sticky rice. When I go with a group, though, I also make sure we order the pla neung manow, which comes steamed with a chili, garlic, and lime sauce that’s so flavorful, you’ll want to drink it like soup (luckily it’s served with little bowls so you can).

800 Grand St, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Chor muang for an appetizer; pad kea mao seafood as a main

Focusing on 19th- century recipes from the royal consort court, Kaew Jao Jorm’s (named after the former King Rama V’s favorite flower) serves a regal menu in its intimate, 20-seat restaurant. The exterior is on an unassuming street in Williamsburg, but inside, it is the restaurant incarnation of Mary Poppins' bag: compact, but they manage to pack in far more than you’d expect.

Though the signature dumplings, chor muang—chicken and peanut filling encased in delicate butterfly pea flower dough—are the star, don’t overlook the noodle dishes, which are slurpable, expertly sauced, and so soft as to be almost buttery.

Thai Diner does diner favorites reimagined, like their beloved Thai Disco Fries.

Head to Thai Diner for brunch, lunch, or a vibey dinner.

If you have friends from out of town that you really want to impress and show how fun eating in New York City can be, go to Thai Diner and get an order of the Thai Disco Fries. I find that these crispy, crinkle-cut fries smothered in a peanutty massaman curry sauce are delicious enough to justify to out-of-towners how much you overspend on rent. Reservations can be hard to get, but they do take some walk-ins, so your best bet is to either arrive slightly before opening, or put your name down and wander around Nolita until your name is called.

The restaurant has a tropical dive bar feel, with plenty of diner favorites reimagined like a custardy Thai tea babka, French toast, and a signature Thai Diner egg sandwich made with Isan-style sausage wrapped in a plush roti. Co-owners Ann Redding and Matt Danzer also recently opened Mommy Pai’s, a fast Thai chicken takeout spot on the same block that’s a great lunch spot without the wait.

Dishes are meant to be shared family-style here—like a whole fish drenched in cliantro-lime broth.

661 Driggs Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Steamed fish with Thai herbs

Specializing in seafood dishes, Fish Cheeks focuses on the bright flavors of southern coastal Thailand. Dishes are meant to be shared family-style here, and though the menu features a few poultry, pork, and beef options, your best bet is trusting the name and going straight for fish. I recommend getting a whole steamed fish for the table—your dinnermates will relish in sharing the communal centerpiece and drenching rice in its cilantro-lime broth, or the coconut crab curry, which comes with rice noodles for soaking up every last bit of the creamy sauce.

Though its flagship Noho location can book out quickly, its equally delicious (and newer) spot in Williamsburg is a bit easier to secure a reservation at, for now.

New Flatiron restaurant LenLen is definitively cool.

The menu at LenLen includes crowd-pleasers and bolder dishes like a durian crab curry.

40 E 20th St, New York, NY 10003 (Flatiron)

If I had to describe LenLen in one word, it would be cool. This relatively new spot hit Flatiron earlier this year, bringing a fresh excitement to the Thai food scene in midtown. For me, the standout of the menu is the love-it-or-loathe-it durian crab curry. It’s earthy, fruity, and well worth the visit alone. While you’re there, order the wagyu beef boat noodles, too, which are served in a rich, dark broth that reminds me of the ones I’ve had in Ayutthaya, one of my favorite cities in Thailand (and the birthplace of boat noodles).

There are whispers of a speakeasy opening downstairs in the coming months, which gives the restaurant extra potential to become a go-to dinner spot that seamlessly transitions into a night out.

Ler Lers does classic Bangkok-style fare right.

From pad thai to grilled meats, Ler Lers does it all.

417 Tompkins Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11216 (Bed-Stuy)

Not to be confused with LenLen, Ler Lers is a newer spot in Bed-Stuy and does classic Bangkok-style fare right. Its ambiance is stylish and warm, with a mix of rattan and earthy tones, for a setting that makes sipping on a sweet iced Thai tea feel right even on a cold rainy day.

I’m pretty weary of ordering pad thai out in restaurants, just because the cuisine has so much else to offer. But a friend promised me that the pad thai topped with crispy pork belly was “awesome,” and after trying it for myself, I’ve started saying the same to friends and family. The rest of the menu has a lot of other familiar favorites like fried rice and grilled meats, and if you’re someone who enjoys a sticky tamarind sauce as much as I do, try the branzino, too.

Hommali is stylish in every sense of the word, from the plating to the space.

The Hommali cocktail menu is also expansive—go for the signature tomato option.

28 7th Ave S, New York, NY 10014 (West Village)

A newcomer to the West Village restaurant scene, this design-forward space has some serious pedigree with a menu curated by Bangkok-native Chattchakorn “Benz” Khajornchaisan, formerly of Eleven Madison Park. The restaurant is stylish in every sense of the word, with sage green tiles, oak accents, and warm lighting.

You can’t customize spice level here, so expect to get a little red from dishes like the prik larb beef tartare that comes with crispy tripe chips and is fiery with northern larb spices. The Hommali Five Spice dry-aged duck is also a standout and comes with fragrant rice that’s cooked in duck drippings. My opinion? The best order is getting the panang curry with tender beef cheek. It’s spicy, nutty, and you’ll want to order a side (or two) of roti to soak up that sauce.

The cocktail menu is also expansive—go for the signature tomato cocktail, which is vodka and rice wine-based with tomato extract, poblanos, and tamarind.

Soothr in the East Village specializes in noodles from all across Thailand.

204 E 13th St, New York, NY 10003 (East Village)

25-20 43rd Ave, Long Island City, NY 11101

Must-order dish: Sukhothai-style tom yum noodle soup

Thai noodle shop Soothr specializes in noodles from all across Thailand, and though the stir-fried variety is delicious, the soup noodles are the real standout. The Sukhothai-style tom yum noodle soup is a must-order, and encapsulates the best of Thai noodle soups with a deeply savory-acidic broth topped with bouncy fish cakes, meatballs, and rice noodles. Soothr has a new-ish Long Island City location that’s got a more nightlife vibe to it (and just as great noodles).

Kru in Williamsburg draws on Thailand’s vast culinary history, reimaging regional traditions through a contemporary lens.

90 N 14 St, Brooklyn, NY 11249 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Lamb massaman curry pot pie

Named after the Thai word for “mentor,” chef Ohm Suansilphong honors the many teachers in his life through Kru. Here, he draws on Thailand’s vast culinary history, reimaging regional traditions through a contemporary lens. This looks like a crispy, massaman curry pot pie sprinkled with slow-cooked, pull-apart jackfruit, and tender lamb or tamarind-chili coated calamari that’s sweet, salty, and a little spicy. Chef adds and tweaks the menu seasonally, but I suggest the first thing you eat is always the Ma Hor, a savory bite of seasoned meat atop fresh fruit. The word means galloping horse, and it has enough warmth to open your tastebuds for the rest of the meal. Pay attention to the wine list: the restaurant is just as thoughtful about its award-winning program as it is the rest of the menu. Consider this a go-to as worthy of casual weeknight dinners as it is of special occasions.

#6254. Transfer Capital One Miles To Air France-KLM Flying Blue With 20% Bonus: Worth It?

Capital One has just introduced its latest points transfer promotion, whereby members can receive a 20% bonus when moving rewards to Air France-KLM Flying Blue. This has the potential to be an excellent deal.

Capital One is offering a bonus when you transfer points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue. Between 12AM ET on November 1, 2026, and 11:59PM ET on November 30, 2026, members can receive a 20% bonus when moving points.

The transfer ratio is usually 1:1, so through this promotion you can transfer miles at a 1,000:1,200 ratio. The 20% bonus should post at the same time as the standard rewards. There’s no registration required, and no limit to how many bonus points you can earn. Transfers from Capital One to Flying Blue are generally instant.

We see bonuses from various transferable points currencies to Flying Blue every so often, in the range of 20-30%. So if you’re in the market for earning some Flying Blue miles, this is a good opportunity.

Air France-KLM Flying Blue is a valuable SkyTeam frequent flyer program. The program has attractive award pricing on Air France and KLM, offering many of the best ways to cross the Atlantic. Admittedly saver award availability can be tough to come by, though if you have Flying Blue Platinum status, you get access to more award space, which is an awesome perk.

On top of that, Air France and KLM make more award seats available to members of the Flying Blue program than to members of partner programs. So even when Flying Blue’s pricing isn’t the best, there are situations where it could make sense to book through Flying Blue (though with all of the Delta SkyMiles devaluations we’ve seen, typically you will find the best pricing through Flying Blue).

I should mention that in September 2026 we saw a Flying Blue devaluation, whereby awards now followed a tiered pricing structure. This means that the cheapest awards are now “Light” fares, and if you want the same inclusions as before, you need to buy up to a “Standard” fare, which costs more miles.

There’s always value in having a stash of Flying Blue miles if you think you’ll be traveling transatlantic in the coming months. I redeem through Flying Blue every year (usually multiple times per year), and consistently get value. I find it to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points.

The only other consideration here is that all major transferable points currencies partner with Air France-KLM Flying Blue, and we see transfer bonuses with some frequency. So I’d be strategic with which program you transfer points from, especially based on how you’d otherwise redeem them.

Through November 30, 2026, you can receive a 20% bonus when you transfer miles from Capital One to Air France-KLM Flying Blue. This bonus is being offered on Capital One’s end, so you should see the bonus right away, and can take advantage of this as often as you’d like.

This has the potential to be a good deal for redemptions on Air France-KLM as well as SkyTeam and other airline partners. If I didn’t already have a stash of Flying Blue miles, I’d take advantage of this.

Do you plan on converting Capital One miles into Flying Blue miles with this bonus?

#6253. The Hidden Math Behind Airlines Deciding Who Gets A Last-Minute Bump Up To Business Class

In 2026, AI-driven pricing and real-time flight capacity adjustments have changed how last-minute business class seats are filled. The traditional system relied on rigid 'fare buckets,' but now, even if you are a top-tier elite, you aren't competing against the person behind you on the upgrade list anymore: you are competing with the AI model.

Today, the algorithm continuously recalculates the exact prices to sell as many seats as possible to leave. AI models have become much more effective at attracting cash buyers than older methods. That means the automated priority system, which grants upgrades based on status, has effectively been pushed to the final minutes before pushback.

However, it is still entirely possible to snag a last-minute bump up to business class with a combination of good luck and loyalty status. Comparing the 'big three' in the US shows that American, Delta, and United Airlines all follow similar but slightly varied rankings. If there is more than one frequent flyer potentially eligible for a leftover seat in business class, United and American follow Premier status as the main differentiator.

AA uses total loyalty points as a tiebreaker, as does UA, but with some additional caveats as well. Meanwhile, Delta follows a list with eight criteria to determine who receives the upgrade. DAL prioritizes the original airfare purchased before the flight when assigning upgrades, and basic economy ticket holders are ineligible under virtually all circumstances.

To win the upgrade game on Delta, you have to understand two separate elements: the eight-tier priority hierarchy and inventory management. When ten Delta Diamond Medallion members request the same single seat, status is the cheapest way to sort the list down. Delta publishes every line item.

Medallion status comes first, and the cabin purchased, including any paid upgrades, comes as the second differentiator. Million Miler status is the third deciding factor, then travel experience tier, where extra fares clear ahead of classic ones, according to The Points Guy’s Delta upgrade guide.

Premium economy buyers ahead of main cabin buyers

Extra fares ahead of classic and refundable

If more data is needed to choose the upgrade candidate, the system can also draw on Delta Reserve card membership, corporate traveler status, and Medallion Qualification Dollars. Time of request is the very last tiebreaker at the gate.

When Delta has leftover premium seats, its automated system ranks eligible passengers by running down the checklist first.

The Points Guy reported that Diamond and Platinum members can clear Delta First upgrades 120 hours before departure. Regional and Global Upgrade Certificates and miles upgrades are processed ahead of complimentary ones. A top-tier elite member can therefore be placed in a seat days before Delta considers a lower-tier member’s request. Last-minute passengers compete for whatever is left after that sorting is done in advance.

The United's upgrade system, known as MileagePlus, operates differently from DAL. UA relies on a mix of Elite Status, hidden Fare Class codes, and upgrade points. UA gives Global Services members first claim regardless of fare, according to The Points Guy. Premium Plus passengers booked in the O, A, and R fare classes next, followed by Premier status.

Fare class is the next tiebreaker in the order Y, B, M, E, U, H, Q, V, W, S, T, L, K and G, but Basic Economy is ineligible. United ranks passengers based on how they are trying to upgrade. People using instruments or points leapfrog those waiting for free complimentary upgrades. UA’s upgrade currency is PlusPoints, which go only to Premier Platinum and 1K members, with 40 awarded at Platinum and 280 at 1K.

Since February 1, every Premier member is eligible for complimentary upgrades and PlusPoints on award tickets. If two passengers have the same status and are using the same upgrade method, UA factors in the cost of the original airfare, unlike DAL.

American primarily focuses on loyalty points as the differentiator for upgrade candidates. AA confirms upgrades by status first, then by upgrade type, with systemwide and mileage award upgrades ahead of complimentary ones, then by rolling 12-month Loyalty Points. The booking code and then date and time of the request settle any remaining ties.

Spending history therefore sits closer to the center of AA’s ladder than of UA’s, where fare class does that work. Basic Economy tickets purchased with AA are completely ineligible for upgrades. Furthermore, mid-2026 updates introduced massive changes to how transcontinental and Hawaii flights handle upgrades, a change that covers nine routes.

Complimentary upgrades will only move flyers up to Premium Economy, not Business Class, if they originally purchased a standard economy ticket. AA now requires a premium economy ticket to be eligible for a business class upgrade to Hawaii.

In 2024, Delta stopped ranking upgrades by fare class and began ranking them by the cabin a passenger actually bought. View From The Wing reported that on domestic flights, buyers of premium economy now take priority for the forward cabin. A traveler who paid for premium economy automatically outranks anyone holding a fare in the main cabin.

The system rewards the purchase of a product instead of the direct price of a ticket, pushing demand toward Delta’s premium fares overall. The Legacy upgrade system relied on Ticket cost as the second differentiator for upgrades, but the new system ignores value and only considers cabin class.

If two Diamond Medallion members are competing, the Diamond who bought a Comfort+ ticket will always beat the Diamond who bought a standard Main Cabin ticket. That is true even if the Main Cabin ticket happened to cost more in cash.

The cheapest fares are not even considered on the upgrade ladder at all. Delta Basic fares are ineligible for any upgrade, paid or complimentary, regardless of status. Autopilot reported that the rule now extends to Delta First Basic, Delta Premium Select Basic and Basic Business, which went on sale from July 8. Even the cheapest premium cabin fares carry no upgrade rights.

Premium cabin products like business class have become the main source of profits for legacy carriers like the US' Big Three. Airlines struggled to sell Old-school International First Class suites. They were mostly filled with people using frequent flyer miles or free corporate upgrades. A cabin that is empty or filled with non-revenue passengers doesn't make money. Meanwhile, economy has essentially become a loss-leader or a break-even product for legacy airlines.

Operational upgrades solve a different problem. When the economy is oversold, an airline can move passengers forward to free seats rather than leave someone at the gate, and the move is inventory management rather than reward. At the gate, an unsold seat earns nothing once the door closes, so filling it with an oversold passenger costs the airline very little.

View From The Wing argues that Delta handles gate upgrades poorly and suggests the process creates headaches for travelers even with high status membership. The result is an upgrade that is real but impossible to plan around, because it depends on an oversale that the airline is trying to avoid creating. Operational moves cannot explain the largest gap in the system, which is the near-total absence of free upgrades into long-haul business class.

The steady influx of AI systems into airline operations continues.

Behind the scenes, the Revenue Management System acts as the supreme court of an airline's finances. It is a massive, automated data engine that works 24/7 to solve one specific problem: How do we make sure a high-value customer pays thousands of dollars for a premium seat, rather than giving it away for free to a frequent flyer? The RMS does not care about your elite status or your credit card tier.

Modern revenue management systems use Origin and Destination forecasting powered by machine learning. It builds a mathematical model of the flight based on years of historical data. Historically, the RMS adjusted fares manually or in rigid, stepped intervals. In 2026, systems use Continuous Pricing. Instead of a ticket costing either $400 or $600, the AI can quote $412.54, adjusting the price by pennies in real time based on user interactions.

Instead of letting those seats go to the free upgrade list, the RMS calculates your individual 'willingness to pay' threshold and flashes a dynamic cash upsell: "Upgrade now for $149." If you buy it, the RMS successfully 'monetized' a seat that would have otherwise been handed out as a free perk. The ultimate showdown between the Revenue Management System and the Airport Operational System happens 30 to 45 minutes before departure.

Up until then, the RMS maintains absolute control, hoping for a last-minute cash buyer or an expensive flight change. Once the flight control window closes as boarding begins, the RMS 'surrenders' its inventory. It passes whatever empty premium seats are left over to the Departure Control System at the gate. Only then does the gate computer look at the 8-tier DAL priority list or the AA Loyalty Point tie-breakers to clear the passengers for free.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.
