#6244. Are Marriott Bonvoy Airline Mileage Transfers Worth It? They Could Be, But…

Among hotel loyalty programs, one thing that makes Marriott Bonvoy unique is the ability to (fairly) efficiently convert hotel points into airline miles. While most major hotel loyalty programs allow some sort of opportunity to convert hotel points into airline miles, it typically represents a very bad value.

In this post, I’d like to take a look at the opportunity to convert Marriott points into airline miles. Which airline programs can you move your Marriott points to, what’s the transfer ratio, and is it worth it?

It’s possible to convert Bonvoy points into airline miles, with your choice of nearly 40 different frequent flyer programs. Let’s take a look at which partners Marriott Bonvoy has, what the transfer ratios are, etc.

Marriott points generally convert into airline miles at a 3:1 ratio, and with most partners you get 5,000 bonus miles for every 60,000 Marriott points you transfer.

In other words, 60,000 Bonvoy points will convert into 25,000 airline miles (including the 5,000 bonus miles). You can take advantage of that bonus of 5,000 miles multiple times, meaning that you can convert Bonvoy points into airline miles at a ratio of up to 2.4:1.

Note that you can transfer a minimum of 3,000 Bonvoy points and a maximum of 240,000 Bonvoy points per day. So if you want to transfer more than 240,000 Bonvoy points, you’ll want to do so over multiple days.

Below is a chart with the airline frequent flyer programs you can transfer your Marriott points to, along with the standard transfer ratio, plus the ability to earn a bonus when transferring a minimum of 60,000 points.

While I covered these details above, let me specifically note the exceptions that apply here:

With the major transferable points currencies, converting points into airline miles is typically an instant process. So it’s worth being aware that Marriott points don’t convert into airline miles instantly. Rather, transfers generally take anywhere from a day to a couple of weeks, with transfers for most partners taking anywhere from two to five days.

I’d consider this to be a major weak point of this opportunity. I generally recommend converting points into airline miles in situations where you have a specific use in mind, and that could be a situation where you find award space on a particular flight.

Obviously that’s not exactly useful here, since it could take a couple of weeks for the transfer to happen, and odds are that whatever award availability you were looking at will be gone at that point.

The process of converting Marriott points into airline miles is really straightforward. Just go to the partner transfer page, click the “Transfer Points” button, and then you’ll be asked to enter the information for the account you want to move your points to. There you’ll be able to select how many points you want to transfer, and note that the amounts shown won’t reflect a bonus, if eligible.

It’s important to be sure that the names of the accounts match, as you can only transfer your Marriott points to an airline frequent flyer account that’s also in your name. Also keep in mind that once the miles are in your frequent flyer account, they’ll be subject to the standard airline mileage expiration policies of the program.

While I think converting Marriott points into airline miles could represent a good value, it’s not how I choose to redeem my Bonvoy points.

To briefly crunch some numbers, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each. At a 2.4:1 transfer ratio (60,000 points per 25,000 miles), that’s like “paying” 1.68 cents per airline mile, which is a pretty decent cost.

Why do I choose not to convert Marriott points into airline miles?

I absolutely don’t think anyone is off base for choosing to convert Marriott points into airline miles. For that matter, this could be a good option if you’re in a crunch, and just need to top off an account for a high value redemption. However, it’s not how I choose to redeem my points, and I don’t think the value is there for most.

It’s more of a last resort redemption option, if you’re truly unable to get value elsewhere. In fairness, that might just be the direction the program is headed. While Bonvoy points have been significantly devalued over the years for hotel redemptions, the mileage conversion options have remained mostly consistent.

While the ability to convert Marriott points into airline miles has been around for a long time, we’re increasingly seeing two-way transfers, where you can convert airline miles into Marriott points.

The idea behind this is great — maybe someone has a lot of airline miles, but really wants to redeem for a hotel stay. Is this a good deal, though? Unfortunately the answer is almost always “no.”

Currently the below programs let you convert airline miles to Marriott Bonvoy, with both the transfer ratios and any exceptions listed.

While I suppose more flexibility is always a good thing, these transfers are almost never worth it. As a reminder, I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, and you’re getting at most one Bonvoy point per airline mile.

If you have the same valuation I do, at a 1:1 transfer ratio you’re getting up to 0.7 cents per mile, while at a 2:1 transfer ratio, you’re getting up to 0.35 cents per mile. That’s not a rate at which I’d be happy cashing in miles.

It’s possible to convert Marriott points into airline miles with over three dozen programs. While this is the best hotel points to airline miles transfer ratio that you’ll find with any program, it’s still not how I’d choose to redeem my Bonvoy points.

Yes, I appreciate the “insurance” that this redemption option provides, since it essentially creates a floor value for Bonvoy points. However, Bonvoy points are hard to efficiently earn through anything other than hotel stays, so I prefer to save them for hotel stays. I’d rather convert credit card points currencies into airline miles.

Where do you stand on the value of Marriott Bonvoy airline mileage transfers? Have you ever redeemed Bonvoy points this way?

Generally I agree with this article. The points can be used with Marriott for better value but if you need to just top off for an airline redemption it may be worth doing. Buying Marriott points could be of good value when there is a 50% or 75% bonus offer.

If one looks at Bonvoy point redemption for award stays these days, unfortunately the average appears well below $.007 USD, maybe somewhere between $.004-$.006. Bonvoy-> Airline Transfers are increasingly becoming a more competitive redemption option. Not all FFPs are created equal, just like not all previously referenced Bonvoy transfer partners are equal. There are some good opportunities. Actually, Bonvoy points transferring to the airline FFP of my choice(s) are now my preferred way to use my Bonvoy points.

In terms of converting Marriott points to United miles, neither Marriott nor United should be seen as a “savings bank” for loyalty credits. I move some Marriott points to United miles (enough to get the special bonus) when (1) my supply of United miles is running “low” and I need same for flight(s) in the not too distant future and (2) one of the special bonuses is currently in effect. In general, over the last 30 years I've been accumulating airline miles (remember TWA?) and hotel points (remember SPG?), I've never seen the value of these miles and points increase over time! Devaluations and additional charges (such as so-called “destination fees” or “resort fees”) as well as no real redemption chart for Marriott points hardly make those Marriott points any type of stable currency. For that matter, airline miles are not really any better. 😀 As an aside, the best airline loyalty redemption value I ever got was in 1985 when I redeemed 90,000 miles on TWA for a open-jaw, round trip for two, first class, from SFO to CAI, returning TLV to SFO.

#6243. How To Redeem Alaska Atmos Rewards Points: Rules, Fees, & Sweet Spots

Alaska Atmos Rewards (formerly Alaska Mileage Plan) has long been a favorite points currency among miles & points geeks, given the carrier’s unique array of airline partners, generous stopover policy, and attractive redemption rates.

In this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at how to redeem Atmos Rewards points. How do you earn Atmos Rewards points, what are the rules around redeeming them, and what are the best uses?

There are several different ways to go about earning Alaska Atmos Rewards points, from credit cards, to outright buying points, to transferring them from other cards.

The Atmos Rewards program has three co-branded credit cards, issued by Bank of America, and they all have excellent welcome bonuses with limited eligibility restrictions:

What’s so great is that you can potentially qualify for all of these cards, so that’s an opportunity to earn lots of points. For example, I picked up both the Atmos Rewards Summit Card and Atmos Rewards Business Card on the same day.

The Atmos Rewards program is transfer partners with Bilt Rewards, so you can transfer Bilt Points to Atmos Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This could be a great reason to pick up one of Bilt’s credit cards, with options including the Bilt Blue Card (learn more), Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

You can even pay rent with an Atmos Rewards card and earn 3x points while paying a 3% fee, which could be a useful deal, especially if you’re pursuing elite status.

The program also partners with Marriott Bonvoy®, so you can transfer over Marriott points. The ratio is that 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy® Points convert into 25,000 Atmos Rewards points (if you convert in different increments, it’s a 3:1 ratio).

This can be a solid value, and there are lots of credit cards that can earn you Bonvoy points, including the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more), Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card (learn more), and Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more).

The Atmos Rewards program is pretty aggressive about selling points, and the program seems to offer promotions on purchased points every couple of months. When we see these offers, you can expect bonuses in the range of 90-110%. This is often an opportunity to acquire Atmos Rewards points for under two cents each.

It doesn’t cost anything to join the Atmos Rewards program, so I generally recommend signing up ahead of time — you have to be a member for at least 10 days in order to take advantage of one of these promotions.

Not only are there great ways to earn Atmos Rewards points either through credit cards or by buying them outright, but Atmos Rewards is also a good program to credit flights to.

For one, Atmos Rewards is the last major US frequent flyer program to give members the option to earn points based on distance flown rather than dollars spent. Atmos Rewards allows mileage earning on a variety of airline partners, ranging from Condor to Cathay Pacific. Atmos Rewards lets you earn points for travel on the following airline partners:

The one thing worth mentioning is that you can only earn Atmos Rewards points on Korean Air, Philippine Airlines, and Starlux Airlines, if you book through Alaska, rather than through one of the partners.

Alaska Atmos Rewards has some great redemption opportunities, though there are also quite a few rules to be aware of. Let’s cover some of those basics.

Alaska Airlines belongs to the oneworld alliance, though the airline has an array of partners beyond oneworld. It’s possible to redeem Atmos Rewards points for travel on the following airlines:

All Atmos Rewards award redemption partners can be booked online at alaskaair.com. If you have a complicated itinerary or are having issues with the website, you’ll want to call the Atmos Rewards partner award desk, which can be reached at 800-252-7522.

When it comes to redeeming points, Atmos Rewards has three simple award charts that are a combination of zone and distance based.

There’s the Americas award chart, which covers any travel from the United States to anywhere in the Americas, including North America and South America.

Then there’s the Europe, Middle East, and Africa award chart, which includes travel from the United States to Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, and travel within Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

Lastly, there’s the Asia-Pacific award chart, which includes travel from the United States to Asia-Pacific, within Asia-Pacific, and between Asia-Pacific and Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

The most significant thing to understand here is that the “starting at” prices are actually what you’re going to pay if there’s saver level award availability. All partners have the same award pricing assuming there’s saver award availability.

There are a few other important things to mention:

The Atmos Rewards program awards status points for award travel booked through the program. This applies for travel on Alaska, Hawaiian, and all other partner airlines.

Just book using Atmos Rewards points and have your Atmos Rewards number on the reservation, and you’ll earn one status point per mile flown, regardless of the class of service (this assumes you select to earn Atmos Rewards points based on distance flown).

This is a massive point of differentiation for the program, and if you ask me, it’s a contributing reason that many American loyalists might want to consider Atmos Rewards.

One of my favorite things about the Atmos Rewards program is that you are allowed a stopover on a one-way award ticket when traveling between regions. This is possible regardless of which partner you redeem with.

So if you book a roundtrip as two one-ways, this means you can potentially get two stopovers on a roundtrip ticket. To book a ticket online with a stopover, just use the multi-city function, and you can search each portion of the ticket individually.

Now, admittedly with the program being distance based, you are in some cases potentially paying more for itineraries with stopovers, but it’s still a useful feature.

On the surface, Atmos Rewards should have access to the same award availability as other partner airlines do, though in some cases Atmos Rewards inexplicably doesn’t have access to the same space. Most commonly:

This won’t be consistent, but it is something to be aware of, and it sure can be frustrating. There’s generally not any way to get around this.

When searching award availability on some partner airlines, you may see award pricing that’s way above what the chart suggests. This includes for some flights on Aer Lingus, Icelandair, Qatar Airways, and Starlux Airlines. In those situations, what’s happening is that there’s no saver level award availability, but Atmos Rewards has negotiated to have more award availability at a higher cost.

I know this kind of pricing frustrates some people and makes them think the program doesn’t offer good value. However, in these situations, other partner airlines simply wouldn’t have access to the award space. So I wouldn’t view it as a negative, but rather just as an opportunity you probably don’t want to take advantage of.

Atmos Rewards blocks many many partner awards within 72 hours of departure. I’ve been told that this policy won’t stick around, though I don’t have a timeline for when it will change, and it continues to be live. It’s certainly something to be aware of when it comes to last minute redemption opportunities.

Furthermore, Atmos Rewards doesn’t have access to any nonstop domestic American awards at the saver level within six days of departure. Don’t expect this to change, as it’s presumably a commercial decision on American’s part.

There are a couple of fees associated with redeeming Atmos Rewards points:

Atmos Rewards no longer has any change or cancelation fees for award tickets, which gives you lots of flexibility to speculatively lock in awards, or even change them if a better routing opens up. The only exception is that the $20 partner award booking fee can’t be refunded.

Atmos Rewards passes on carrier imposed surcharges (often referred to as fuel surcharges) for travel on some partner airlines. Specifically, these apply for travel on British Airways, Hainan Airlines, and Icelandair. Fortunately they don’t apply for travel on other partner airlines.

Atmos Rewards doesn’t allow award tickets to be placed on hold. To book an Atmos Rewards award ticket you need to have sufficient points in your account, though you can always cancel it for free.

Atmos Rewards points don’t expire. However, if you don’t have any account activity for over two years, your account may be locked for security reasons, and your points may be accessed by contacting Atmos Rewards and verifying personal details.

We all have different travel goals, so there’s never going to be a one size fits all answer as to what the best use of points is. Broadly speaking, my favorite way to redeem points is for aspirational redemptions in first and business class, since that’s where you’ll get the most outsized value.

However, nowadays I’d argue that the redemption sweet spot with Atmos Rewards is largely for shorter awards, given the distance based pricing. In some way, the Atmos Rewards award charts are almost a competitor to British Airways Club, in terms of the great value of short haul redemptions. Since you can redeem Atmos Rewards points for flights globally, I figured the best way to share some sweet spots would just be to take a look at each award chart individually.

Before I do, let me acknowledge a new reality of the miles & points hobby. The reality is that airlines are getting savvier when it comes to how they release award space, and in many cases, they open fewer award seats to members of partner frequent flyer programs. This is beyond any carrier’s control, but it does limit the arbitrage opportunities by using great frequent flyer programs.

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for the Americas, which applies exclusively if traveling within the Americas (including North and South America).

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Honestly, I think this is the chart with the most consistently good pricing, whether traveling short haul or long haul. So if you can find award availability within the Americas, you should be pretty happy with the pricing. I redeem Atmos Rewards points constantly for travel on American, as it’s a way to get a good deal on domestic flights, especially in a premium cabin. It might not be the most aspirational thing on earth, but it sure is practical.

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for Europe, Middle East, and Africa, which applies if traveling within or between any of those regions, and also applies if traveling between the Americas and any of those regions.

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for Asia-Pacific, which applies if traveling within Asia-Pacific, and between Asia-Pacific and any other regions. Note that Asia includes the Indian subcontinent, since some other award charts put that in the same region as the Middle East.

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Alaska Atmos Rewards is one of the most useful programs for redeeming points. Given the zone and distance based award chart, you’ll generally find the best value with the program for shorter distance itineraries, where pricing can be very attractive.

I’d say Atmos Rewards is a program that has become practical more than aspirational, and that’s something that I don’t mind, at least at this point in history. It’s not like there are many Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, or Qantas, ultra long haul first class awards to snag, so we’re not missing out on that much.

Atmos Rewards is my go-to program for most awards covering a distance of up to 1,500 miles, give or take.

What’s your favorite use of Alaska Atmos Rewards points?

#6242. Singapore Airlines’ New First & Business Class Cabins Will Be Unveiled This Week

In November 2024, Singapore Airlines announced a huge investment into its premium passenger experience, which will see the introduction of all-new cabin products, plus the expansion of first class. These cabins will be retrofitted on dozens of Airbus A350s, and will also be available on newly delivered Boeing 777-9s in the future.

The product was initially supposed to roll out as of the spring of 2026, though as is all too common nowadays, the project was delayed due to supply chain constraints, etc. The good news is that the wait is almost over — the new product will be unveiled on Friday, November 6, 2026, with an entry into service planned for the first quarter of 2027. Let’s recap all the details we know as of now.

Singapore Airlines will be investing 1.1 billion SGD (~835 million USD) to update the interiors of its entire long haul Airbus A350-900 fleet. This consists of a total of 41 jets, and includes the carrier’s seven A350-900ULRs, with the “ULR” standing for “ultra long range,” as these planes operate the world’s longest flights.

The only A350-900s that won’t be reconfigured are the ones that are specifically designed for regional flights, featuring the same cabin products you’ll find onboard Boeing 787-10s.

With this project, we can expect changes across cabins. We’ll see first class added to the carrier’s ultra long range A350s, an all-new business class product, refreshes to premium economy and economy, plus an updated inflight entertainment system and the installation of Starlink Wi-Fi.

How will the layouts of these jets change, once reconfigured? Singapore Airlines’ standard long haul A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines’ ultra long range A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines will be introducing new first and business class products. This isn’t just some new interim product, but rather this is intended to be the carrier’s new premium product in the long run. The same seats that are being installed on the Airbus A350-900s will also be installed on the carrier’s Boeing 777-9s, so these are very much “flagship” cabins.

Singapore Airlines initially intended to debut new premium cabins on its 777-9s, which were first supposed to be delivered in 2020. However, those have now been pushed back to late 2027 at the earliest. So clearly Singapore Airlines decided that it’s finally time to introduce new cabins, even if the 777-9 keeps getting delayed.

Singapore Airlines will introduce a new first class product on its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, which operate the world’s longest flights. This same product will be available on 777-9s in the future, but won’t be available on standard A350-900s. Furthermore, there are no plans to retrofit existing 777s with this product. A350s will have four of these seats, while 777s will have six of these seats.

Below is the first teaser picture of Singapore Airlines’ new first class.

Currently Singapore Airlines only has first class on its A380s and 777-300ERs, so it’s cool to see this product expand.

Official details about the new first class are limited, other than that it’s “designed with increasingly discerning travellers in mind,” and that the first class seats “promise to deliver an unparalleled in-flight experience.”

We have reason to believe that the new cabin will be in a 1-2-1 layout. Why? Well, Singapore Airlines filed a patent some time back, clearly for the carrier’s new first class product. The patent is for the 777-9, where the airline will have a first class cabin with six seats.

The plan seems to be to have individual suites along the windows, plus a double suite in the center. However, the center suite can be used by either one or two people, so if people are traveling separately, there’s a partition that can go up.

As you can see, there’s a bit of staggering with the cabin, to maximize the width of the suite, as the aisle curves a bit.

This looks like a very nice product, though to be perfectly honest, it doesn’t look like anything revolutionary. Nowadays some of the top first class products are in a 1-1-1 configuration, like what you’ll find on Japan Airlines and Emirates. Admittedly the flexibility of the double suite in the middle is great for those traveling with someone, since that’s not something that was really considered with the new Japan Airlines and Emirates products.

For that matter, we have reason to believe that Cathay Pacific may offer the world’s best first class on its 777-9s, as it could very well be in a 1-1 configuration.

This is super exciting. Singapore Airlines is one of the best airlines in the world, with incredible service, food, drinks, and more. However, at this point the carrier’s business class hard product isn’t really cutting edge anymore.

With details being so limited, all we can do is speculate as of now. So I have a few thoughts:

In late 2024, when this project was first announced, Singapore Airlines shared the following timeline for debuting the new first and business class seats:

Unfortunately that timeline didn’t stick. Several months ago we learned how the first retrofitted aircraft wouldn’t enter service until the first quarter of 2027, best case scenario, with the expectation being that some long range A350s would be reconfigured before the first ultra long range A350 gets a makeover.

The revised timeline reflects industry-wide supply chain constraints, as well as delays in the certification of one of the new seats (a common industry problem). The aircraft will be retrofitted by SIA Engineering Company in Singapore.

So, is that still the timeline we’re looking at? It would appear so. Singapore Airlines has confirmed on social media that it will unveiling its all new products on Friday, November 6, 2026.

From the first sketch to the final detail, discover how the new Singapore Airlines travel experience comes together across every cabin class and every part of the journey.Unveiling on 6 November 2026. pic.twitter.com/dTML7QmOXe

This announcement is actually being marketed as being about more than just seats, as it’s described as “the new Singapore Airlines travel experience,” and we’ll learn how it “comes together across every class and every part of the journey.” We’ve already seen the airline tease details of a new dining concept as well as new amenities across cabins, so presumably this will all come together to form the new experience.

Which routes are likely to get the new cabins first? While we’ll see how this plays out, based on historical precedent, it’s likely that Sydney (SYD) and London (LHR) will be the first two destinations, since those are the first destinations where the airline has sent all of its new long haul products.

Singapore Airlines plans to introduce all-new cabins on its Airbus A350-900s, which will also eventually be installed on Boeing 777-9s. Most exciting is an improved new business class product, which is long overdue. Singapore Airlines will also be adding first class to its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, with a boutique cabin having just four seats.

While this product was supposed to enter service as of the second quarter of 2026, the timeline has been pushed back to the first quarter of 2027, due to supply chain constraints and certification issues… a familiar story! The expectation is that the new cabins will be unveiled this week, on November 6, 2026. I’m mighty curious to learn the details, so I’m happy that the wait is finally (almost) over.

What do you make of Singapore Airlines’ plans to introduce new long haul cabins?

#6241. Buy Finnair Plus Avios For 50% Off (1.06 Cents Each): Best-Ever Price Worth It?

The Finnair Plus program has just launched its newest promotion on purchased Avios, offering up to a 50% discount, which is an opportunity to acquire Avios for as little as 1.06 cents each. This is the best offer from the program of the year, and you can use this to acquire any “flavor” of Avios at an advantageous rate.

Strategically buying points for premium travel can be a great value, especially with a specific use in mind, so this is an offer I’d seriously consider.

Between 12:01AM EET on November 2 and 11:59PM EET on November 16, 2026, Finnair Plus is offering a limited time promotion on purchased Avios. If you purchase Finnair Plus Avios, you can receive the following deal:

Beyond the discount, you can also receive tier points toward status equivalent to 10% of the Avios purchased. This is of course useful if you’re going for elite status with Finnair, but otherwise, is of limited value.

Now, here’s where it gets interesting — Finnair lets you select the currency in which you want to buy Avios (you can find the option to switch currencies at the top of the screen), and the price differs:

So based on current exchange rates, you’re best off paying in JPY, followed by USD, followed by EUR. If you maxed out the promotion with a 50% bonus and paid in JPY, the best deal you could get would be to pay $2,110 for 200,000 Avios, which comes out to 1.06 cents per Avios (in USD), inclusive of all taxes and fees.

Note that this offer is only available to Finnair Plus members who joined the program before October 30, 2026, and have a minimum balance of 50 Avios in their account (though those Avios can be transferred from another “flavor” of the currency).

When Finnair Plus offers a promotion on purchased Avios, it’s common to see either a 50% bonus or a 40-50% discount. The 50% discount gives you the absolute best price, so this is definitely the time to buy Avios, if interested.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Finnair Plus Avios purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Since the purchase of Finnair Avios can potentially be billed in a foreign currency, there is one other great option. The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) offers 3x points on foreign purchases, so that’s a fantastic card for this kind of purchase.

What should you expect from Finnair Plus award pricing, and the best ways to redeem to Finnair Plus Avios?

Below you can find the one-way Finnair Plus award redemptions rates for travel on Finnair.

Awards also have surcharges, though they’re at least mild. If you have a connecting itinerary, you’ll only be charged the surcharge correlated to the most expensive segment flown.

When your award booking includes a connecting flight, Avios are charged separately for each flight, except for flights within Finland and Northern Europe. For example, a Frankfurt to Helsinki to New York business class award would cost you 82,500 Avios (20,000 Avios plus 62,500 Avios). One awesome thing is that Finnair Plus has an award seat guarantee, meaning there’s pretty consistently award availability when booking far in advance.

Finnair Plus also allows redemptions on partner airlines, though the pricing isn’t particularly attractive, for the most part. The more important thing to keep in mind is that it’s possible to transfer Avios between the various “flavors” of the currency.

Therefore this promotion is also an opportunity to earn Avios that you can transfer 1:1 to programs like Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, etc. That opens up more redemption opportunities.

Finnair Plus has launched a promotion on purchased Avios. With this, you can receive up to a 50% discount when purchasing Avios, which is an opportunity to buy them for 1.06 cents each (in USD, when paying in JPY). This is the best price of the year from Finnair Plus on purchasing Avios (and the best price for purchasing any current of Avios this year, for that matter).

London routinely ranks among the world’s most-visited cities. It is home to incredible museums, a fabulous theater scene, great restaurants, luxurious hotels and its main airport, Heathrow (LHR), is a hub for multiple airlines, making it a great stopping-over point on a larger trip.

That said, the British capital is well worth visiting on its own for anything from a few days to a few weeks, depending on how much of an Anglophile you are.

Despite the strong U.S. dollar, London is still an expensive destination, so if price points have been putting you off lately, here are some easy strategies to stretch your London trip budget even further using miles and points.

And if you have some strategies of your own to use airline miles, hotel points and credit card rewards to maximize a trip to London, please share those in the comments below!

Where you should stay in London depends on the purpose of your visit. If you are in town for business, you might want to stay near the City of London, while folks who want a quieter neighborhood might like Kensington or Notting Hill. Knightsbridge is best for those who want upscale shopping, while Mayfair has fantastic restaurants and boutiques.

London can get dreary and gray during the winter months and crowded during the summer, so your best bets are fall from September-November and spring from March-May when the temperatures tend to be mild and days will include a mix of sun and rain.

The number of miles you need to fly to London depends on which airline you take and which miles you redeem, as well as the time of year since some mileage programs require more miles during peak travel times. That said, you can find flights on some airlines, like Virgin Atlantic, by redeeming as few as 6,000 miles each way.

American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines all fly to London from various U.S. airports. You’ll also find plenty of flights from over a dozen U.S. cities from the U.K.’s two main carriers, British Airways and Virgin Atlantic.

The cost of a trip to London depends on when you visit, how long your trip is and where you want to stay. The city has options for travelers ranging from budget flights and accommodations to luxury hotels that can cost well over $500 a night. Luckily, many hotels are accessible using credit card rewards and hotel points.

Now that the FAQs are out of the way, here's what else you need to know to start planning your trip to London.

Virgin Atlantic flies to London Heathrow from 11 U.S. cities and using Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points can be a real bargain. Just beware of taxes and fees that can be several hundred dollars, even for economy tickets.

I like using the airline’s Reward Seat Checker tool to price out tickets between city pairs over a month at a time. You can often find economy tickets between the East Coast and London for as few as 6,000 miles each way. Yes, you read that correctly — you can cross the Atlantic for just 6,000 miles. Even better, premium economy starts at just 10,500 miles and Upper Class can require as few as 29,000 miles (though it’s often much higher).

Unfortunately, you’ll be on the hook for anywhere from $450-$1,700 in taxes and fees round-trip depending on your class of service. That’s a lot, but perhaps not so bad considering even some economy flights are costing upwards of $1,400 at the moment, saving a few hundred dollars by redeeming a few thousand miles can be well worth it.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is a 1:1 transfer partner of:

What’s more, some of these partners, including Amex and Bilt, offer limited-time transfer bonuses, so you can score even more of a deal on award tickets.

Related: The best ways to travel to London with points and miles

British Airways is one of the most generous airlines in the world when it comes to releasing award seats in its four classes of long-haul service: economy, premium economy, business class and first class.

The downside is the hefty fuel surcharges and taxes on the airline's flights to and from its London Heathrow hub. There are, however, some ways to mitigate those.

The key is to redeem points and miles from the right programs. The extra charges will still be relatively high, but you can end up saving hundreds of dollars per ticket — each way! To illustrate this most clearly, let's focus on British Airways business class.

While American Airlines AAdvantage would only require 57,500 miles each way in business class for British Airways flights between the U.S. and London, the taxes and fees can cost between $750-$1,000 each way. The same is true if you were to redeem 45,000-70,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points each way – with taxes and fees that can top $1,100.

Instead, you might want to consider redeeming Cathay Pacific Asia Miles. Flights from the East Coast start at 63,000 miles plus $200-$450 in each direction, while those from the West Coast incur the same taxes and fees, but require 93,000 miles.

For its part, British Airways Club would require 88,000-99,000 Avios in each direction depending on which city in the U.S. you’re flying from, plus taxes and fees closer to $400-$500. Yes, that is still a chunk of change, and it’s a lot more Avios or Asia Miles, but it can be well worth it to save close to a thousand dollars per person.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of:

Cathay Pacific Asia Miles is a transfer partner of:

That means that although you’re spending more miles for a ticket than redeeming through AAdvantage or Atmos, you have a lot more transfer partner options to top up your British Airways or Cathay Pacific accounts.

Related: Great award availability but beware the taxes: British Airways business class review

Another way to save on taxes and fees on award tickets as well as sparing yourself a few miles is to redeem United MileagePlus miles for a ticket on United. Not only does United charge far lower taxes and fees than British Airways and Virgin Atlantic, but if you are either a United MileagePlus elite or carry a United cobranded card, you might be eligible for preferential redemption rates on award tickets booked through MileagePlus.

You’ll pay just $5.60 flying from the U.S. to London, in any class of service, and around $200-$400 on the return, depending on which cabin you’re in.

Plus, you can save on the mileage portion of your ticket if you’re an elite or a credit cardholder. Take these flights from London to Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), for instance. Regular MileagePlus members would have to redeem 40,000 miles for coach, 50,000 for premium economy and 80,000 for United Polaris business class. But if you have access to preferential rates, you’ll save at least 10% of the miles and need just 36,000 for coach, 45,000 for premium economy and 72,000 for business class.

If you don’t currently carry a United credit card, consider the United℠ Explorer Card (see ) or the United Quest℠ Card (see ).

United is also a 1:1 transfer partner of Chase Ultimate Rewards if you carry one of the following cards:

Finally, don’t forget that United has a special partnership with Marriott. Normally, when you transfer 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points to one of its airline partners, you end up with 20,000 airline miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus for 25,000 miles total.

With United, however, you get a 10,000-mile bonus, so 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points convert to 30,000 United miles. That’s probably a special-circumstance use for most folks, but still something to consider if you’re swimming in Marriott points.

Related: The best times to apply for Chase’s United cards based on offer history

As you might expect, London is lousy with points hotels, and more are on the way. I’m most excited about the Waldorf Astoria London – Admiralty Arch and the St. Regis London, both of which should open in early 2027.

I’d suggest picking the area you want to stay in and then doing a search with your preferred hotel programs around there. In the meantime, here are some of my top picks with each program.

The swanky NoMad London opened in 2021 and immediately gained a following thanks to its maximalist decor and popular bars and restaurants, not to mention its central Covent Garden location. It’s now part of Hilton, so you can redeem points for stays. Nights start at $550 or 100,000 Hilton Honors points.

I also love the colorful BoTree Hotel, which is part of Hilton’s Curio Collection. It opened in a quiet pocket of Mayfair in 2023 and has bright but sophisticated rooms and is home to an outpost of the see-and-be-seen Italian eatery Lavo. Rates start at $400 or 108,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

I love Mayfair, so my top Hyatt pick for the city is Hyatt Regency London – The Churchill, which sits right on stately Portman Square and is turning 50 years old next year. The room decor is not exactly overawing, but the public spaces are grand indeed and the service is impeccable. Nights start at $440 or 25,000-55,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

TPG staffers also love the Great Scotland Yard Hotel, which is part of Hyatt’s Unbound Collection. Rooms are on the small side, but you can’t beat the history since it’s in a heritage-listed building that was once the Metropolitan Police headquarters. Rates start at $380 or 20,000-40,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

For something a bit hipper as well as budget-friendlier, try the Standard. It’s in a very busy area right near Kings Cross, but chic, 70s-inspired room decor and several buzzy bars and restaurants will make your time here feel like an upscale city experience. Rates start at $305 or 20,000-40,000 points per night.

Related: Which credit cards should you use for Hyatt stays?

Even among quirky Kimptons, the Kimpton Fitzroy is a standout thanks to the magnificent 1900 landmark building that houses it and its central Bloomsbury location. Make time for afternoon tea in Palm Court, which is a veritable London institution. Rates start at $319 or 66,000 IHG One Rewards points per night.

The InterContinental London Park Lane has an utterly convenient location at Hyde Park Corner and features spacious rooms, specialty drinks inspired by the royal family at Arch Bar and an expansive spa and fitness center. Rates start at $433 or 83,000 points per night.

Related: Which credit card should you use for IHG stays?

It might occupy a heritage-listed building from 1910, but the London Edition feels utterly of the moment (even though it opened over 13 years ago). Rooms have Edition’s signature look of white textiles, wood paneling and minimalist bathrooms. It’s worth spending an evening admiring the sculpted ceiling at Berners Tavern while enjoying dishes from chef Jason Atherton’s menu. Rates start at $485 or 70,400 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

Formerly a Renaissance hotel, St. Pancras has since joined Marriott’s Autograph Collection and is a favorite among train enthusiasts thanks to its location in a landmark neo-Gothic edifice attached to the train station of the same name. Rooms feel opulent in a Victorian way, and its Moorish-inspired spa is a treat. Rates start at $280 or 52,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

While hotel points come in handy for saving bundles of money on otherwise expensive stays, if you are looking to splurge while in London, there are still ways to save on luxury hotels.

Travelers with either the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express should check American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, which sometimes has third- or fourth-night free packages at some of the city’s finest hotels. These bookings also come with perks like free daily breakfast for two, a $100 on-property credit, availability-based upgrades and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout.

There are plenty to choose from, but my personal favorite London hotels that participate in Amex FHR include:

Remember, if you have the American Express Platinum Card or The Business Platinum Card from American Express you are also eligible for up to $300 in statement credits biannually for up to a total of $600 per year on prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection or Airbnb Luxe bookings (of two nights or more for THC and Airbnb) through American Express Travel® or the Amex Travel App™. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, those FHR bookings will require two nights or more to be eligible for this credit.

You might also consider booking a luxury hotel through the Capital One Premier Collection if you have the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card or the Capital One Venture X Business for valuable benefits like free daily breakfast for two, up to $100 in on-property experience credits and room upgrades (if available).

Likewise, if you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve or the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business you can book a hotel that is part of The Edit by Chase Travel℠. Cardholders are eligible for two statement credits of up to $250 each (for a total of $500) this calendar year to put toward stays of two nights or more booked through The Edit. During your stay, you are also eligible for availability-based upgrades, complimentary daily breakfast and a $100 on-property credit.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve’s The Edit credit: What to know

Although British food was long a punchline, the city has become one of the world’s premier dining destinations in the past two decades or so. These days, you can find everything from Sri Lankan hoppers and Scandinavian smoked fish to French haute cuisine and sustainable farm-to-table fare.

Prices are high, though, so it’s best to maximize rewards on your spending and any statement credits your credit cards might afford you.

Another favorite tip of mine: You can often find discounts of up to 50% at some restaurants by booking reservations via The Fork. Then, just show your reservation details at check in, enjoy your meal, and the savings will be automatically applied to your bill.

Related: The best credit cards for dining

Taxis and Ubers are easy to come by in London, though rides can be expensive. So if you do go this route, so to speak, make sure to use a card that earns bonus points on ride-hailing services.

It’s also easy to hop on the city’s Tube lines and buses, both of which are easy to navigate and affordable, by simply tapping on with your credit card. If you decide to do so, keep a card that earns bonus points on public transportation at the top of your wallet.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (see ) earns 2 points per dollar on local transit and commuting, for example, and the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card earns 2 points per dollar on local transit purchases.

You might be able to use the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s $300 in annual travel statement credits toward transit purchases as well as taxis and Ubers since these charges often code as “travel.”

Related: The best credit cards for commuting expenses

No matter whether you spell it “theater” or “theatre,” no trip to London would be complete without seeing a production in one of the West End’s magnificent venues. Ticket prices tend to be more reasonable than in the U.S. but can still put a dent in your budget. Luckily, you can take advantage of the Chase Sapphire Reserve Stubhub credit to offset some of that cost.

Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders receive up to $300 per year to use on purchases made through StubHub or its sister site, Viagogo. The credit is split into two biannual credits of up to $150 (activation required; through Dec. 31, 2027).

Among the productions currently available through Stubhub in London are “Paddington: The Musical” (just beware it’s mostly sold out except for last-minute tickets) and “Oh, Mary!”.

A few years ago, Capital One partnered with The Cultivist, a service that grants members free, priority access to dozens of museums around the world. Eligible Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card holders can register for half-price membership that costs $220 per year instead of $440. This auto-renews at the discounted rate for the second year and then is full price after that.

While $220 is a lot, if you visit museums frequently, you can end up saving far more than that on tickets since The Cultivist Enthusiast-level membership available with the Venture X includes priority admission for the cardholder plus a guest. In London, the participating museums include:

Finally, some credit cards levy foreign exchange fees on purchases you make outside the U.S. They tend to add 1-3% to your purchase price, which can add up quickly. Instead, use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees, of which there are many to choose from.

If you travel abroad frequently, you might also want to consider the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card. In addition to waiving foreign transaction fees, the card actually earns 3 points per dollar on foreign transactions, in any category. It’s almost too good to be true, and that makes it one of the best credit cards for trips abroad.

#6239. BermudAir Completes Move to New Florida Airport

BermudAir transferred flight operations to Orlando Sanford on Saturday after almost three years serving Orlando International.

The carrier now flies between Orlando Sanford and Hamilton, Bermuda. A second route, to Belize, will commence Dec. 21.

BermudAir announced the switch from MCO to SFB in June, saying Sanford is a more convenient and efficient gateway for flights to and from Bermuda, the Caribbean, and Central America.

The inaugural flight received a water cannon salute at Sanford on Saturday.

#6238. Save On Air France-KLM Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Air France-KLM flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel. We’ve seen this offer in the past, and I’m happy to see it return, as I always get significant value from it. However, this offer isn’t quite as lucrative as past ones.

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500 or more with Air France-KLM by December 15, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 25,000 bonus points rather than a $250 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 25,000 points at $425.

For what it’s worth, in the past when I’ve purchased sustainable aviation fuel with Air France in order to earn XP (the metric by which you qualify for status), that triggered an Amex Offers deal. So at least anecdotally, that seems to work. Furthermore, taxes and carrier imposed surcharges on award tickets also seem to qualify.

I’m always happy to see this offer available, though let me note that this isn’t as lucrative as in the past. In past situations we’ve seen a $200 statement credit or 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000+, so as a percentage return, this definitely isn’t as good.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines on up to $500,000 per calendar year and then 1x.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $2,500 ticket, you’d receive a $250 statement credit plus 12,500 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $462.50 on $2,500 of spending, which comes out to an 18.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500+ on an Air France-KLM ticket. If you’re planning travel on Air France or KLM, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

Were you targeted for this Amex Offers deal, and if so, do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6237. Everyone On US-Bound Flights, Including Crew, Must Now Declare They Haven’t Been In Congo In The Last 21 Days

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued an order on travel for the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) which has now come into effect. It requires all air travelers, including crew, flying into or connecting through the United States to sign that they haven't been present in the DRC in the last 21 days.

The order comes into effect at 11:59 PM EST on November 3. It will be applied to all flights that depart for the US at or after this time. The order comes in response to the outbreak of the Ebola disease in some remote areas of the DRC. Simple Flying has contacted the CDC for further comment.

An attestation order is a requirement for a traveler to confirm something before they come to the United States. The CDC initially issued the order on October 2. It was clarified on October 28, confirming that it applies to crew and passengers on any aircraft, including cargo services. The order also applies to crew on "deadhead" status, meaning that they are onboard a flight but not carrying out duties. Despite the severity of these new restrictions, the CDC insists that "The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low."

The 21-day restriction has been chosen because that is the maximum incubation period for the disease. Being present in the DRC means physically entering or traveling through the country, either by land, air or sea. It still applies even if someone doesn't leave the airport or aircraft. Day zero of the period is when the individual leaves the DRC, with day one being the first full day outside the DRC. Impacted people can only enter the US from day 22.

Airlines are responsible for collecting and retaining the attestations. The CDC then has the right to request any attestations to confirm compliance and assist with public health investigations should there be any Ebola cases within the US. The required retention time for carriers is at least 42 days.

When you fly to America, you'll be asked to sign the attestation prior to boarding. One authorized individual, such as a parent or guardian, may sign individual attestations on behalf of each member of a travel party. Anybody refusing to sign the document will be denied boarding. You can also be prosecuted and fined if you submit false information.

The current plan is for the order to run until December 18 unless the CDC changes the rules before then. The regulator may also extend the order should the DRC Ebola outbreak worsen or continue.

The flight was forced to land in Montreal after US authorities identified a passenger from Ebola-stricken Congo.

Airlines have a degree of freedom to decide how they will deal with the attestation process. Make sure to check before you travel as processes will vary between carriers. The Travel has reported that Delta Air Lines' guidance states the following:

"Travelers may complete the attestation upon check in via the app or Delta.com. Travelers will also receive a link to the attestation via the check-in reminder sent 24-hours before departure."

Meanwhile, if you are flying with American Airlines, you can complete the attestation during check-in on the carrier's website, on the app, at the airport or with a printable PDF. United Airlines has fewer options, with the process only available as a confirmation step during check-in. Things are easier for large groups flying with JetBlue, as one person can complete the form for multiple passengers in their party so long as they are flying under the same booking.

#6236. El-Sayed's silence over mom's FBI questioning raises transparency concerns

Fox News contributors Karl Rove and Melissa DeRosa discuss Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s response to questions about his family’s alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood on ‘The Story.’

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is facing renewed scrutiny from Republican critics over his mother's questioning by federal investigators more than two decades ago as part of an investigation into an Islamic charity where she worked.

El-Sayed's Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., accused the Democratic candidate of misleading Michigan voters about his views on the Muslim Brotherhood, pointing to reported associations involving members of El-Sayed's family.

El-Sayed previously told Fox News that he has "never been" and will "never be" a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. Fox News Digital is not aware of any direct ties between El-Sayed and the organization.

El-Sayed's campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

CONTROVERSY OVER ABDUL EL-SAYED'S FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD IGNORED, DOWNPLAYED BY LIBERAL MEDIA

Former Vice President Kamala Harris joins Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for a roundtable discussion at Birth Detroit. (David Guralnick/Pool/Getty Images)

"Michiganders cannot trust Abdul El-Sayed. He lies about his physician credentials, his family life, and about how much his disastrous policies will cost Michigan's families," a spokesperson for Rogers told Fox News Digital. "Tell the truth, Abdul."

El-Sayed has not publicly addressed the details of his mother's questioning by federal investigators or the raid on the offices of the Islamic charity where she worked since the Washington Free Beacon resurfaced the reports last month.

Federal authorities raided the Missouri office of the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA), where El-Sayed's mother, Fatten Elkomy, worked in 2004, according to the Columbia Daily Tribune. The newspaper reported that federal agents questioned Elkomy for approximately three hours during the investigation.

In 2008, IARA was shut down by the federal government in connection with alleged violations of federal sanctions and terrorism-related financing restrictions, including allegations involving funding for Islamic militants in Afghanistan and terrorist groups such as the Taliban and al Qaeda.

Elkomy was not charged in connection with the investigation, according to multiple reports. Fox News Digital has found no evidence that she facilitated transfers of funds to terrorist organizations.

The U.S. Treasury Department did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment about the government's findings concerning IARA's alleged connections to the Muslim Brotherhood or why Elkomy was questioned by federal investigators.

TRUMP LINKS MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD: 'HE'S A CON MAN'

During his Senate campaign, El-Sayed has sought to distance himself from his mother's reported political associations, emphasizing that she did not raise him.

El-Sayed was raised in Michigan by his father and stepmother after his parents divorced when he was 3.

"I have no ties. We have no ties," El-Sayed told NBC's Tom Llamas in October. "I have never had these conversations with my mother, I wasn't raised by my mother."

The scrutiny of El-Sayed extended to the candidate's fundraisers and campaign events with Islamic leaders, some of whom have reported ties to the Muslim Brotherhood or have been accused of making antisemitic or hateful remarks. The controversy has also included El-Sayed's campaign appearances with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker.

His former Democratic primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Rogers on Sunday, citing concerns about El-Sayed's approach to the safety of Michigan's Jewish community and his repeated campaign appearances with Piker, who previously said, "America deserved 9/11."

"I don't like a democratic nominee for U.S. senate campaigning and standing with someone who's saying that America deserved 9/11," Stevens said during a CNN interview Sunday night.

El-Sayed declined to comment on Piker's remarks during an April interview with POLITICO but later disavowed them during an August appearance on NBC's "Meet the Press."

EL-SAYED ERUPTS AT GOP RIVAL OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ACCUSATIONS IN FIERY SENATE DEBATE

Democratic nominee for Senate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during a campaign event on Oct. 14, 2026, in Detroit. (Paul Sancya/AP Photo)

Amy Mek, founder of the RAIR Foundation, a nonprofit organization focused on investigating groups it identifies as connected to terrorism, echoed Rogers' concerns about national security and El-Sayed's silence in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Mek, who previously testified before Congress about terrorism-related threats in the United States, told Fox News Digital that she believes El-Sayed's silence on his mother's questioning reflects political considerations.

She also pointed to social media posts by El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, who wrote on X in 2012 that members of their family have "long been" members of the Muslim Brotherhood.

In a separate 2013 post that remains publicly available on her account, Abdelhadi said she was "praying for all my family that supports the #MB."

Abdelhadi later recalled her family's fear of FBI surveillance in a 2016 article titled, "Queer, Muslim, and Unwelcome at the 'New Stonewall.'"

El-Sayed has not publicly addressed his half-sister's statements in detail but called the tweets "not serious" during his NBC interview, accusing Llamas of "using hearsay evidence from a tweet" to question him about his family's reported connections to the Muslim Brotherhood.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines.

#6234. Denver Air Connection Plans First Florida Service

Denver Air Connection will launch its first-ever service to Florida, and it will be outside the scope of any Essential Air Service (EAS) contract. The only other place in the carrier’s network that isn’t directly part of an EAS contract is its service to Telluride, Colorado, from both Denver and Phoenix.

Beginning January 9, 2027, DAC will begin nonstop flights from Muskegon, Michigan, to Orlando Sanford, with service operating on Saturdays using the 50-seat Embraer E145XR.

While Muskegon itself only has one other destination, Chicago O’Hare, which is also operated by DAC under the EAS contract, DAC will compete indirectly with Allegiant, as it has a sizable operation and a base in Grand Rapids, Michigan, which is located only about 45 minutes east of Muskegon.

The 1,030-mile route from Muskegon to Orlando Sanford on the E145 will become the longest at-risk flight operated by any EAS carrier, and one of the longest commercial airline flights operated by an Embraer E145 in the country, overtaking the current record holder, United’s 830-mile route from Washington Dulles to Mobile, Alabama, by almost 200 miles.

That record for the E145 is a little bit of a technicality, as JSX does operate a handful of flights over 1,000 miles with its Embraer E145s, but the carrier is not considered a commercial airline, and is instead classified as a “public charter operation.”

Muskegon Airport director Ken Efting did have something to say about this new service: “This is a historic milestone for MKG and the communities we serve…This is exactly the kind of opportunity we’ve been working toward, and it’s a testament to our growing community support and strong partnership with Denver Air Connection.”

This isn’t the first time an EAS carrier has operated at-risk service to the state of Florida from an EAS community. These smaller carriers sometimes begin flights to leisure destinations like Florida and other leisure-heavy destinations to entice higher passenger numbers that boost the communities they serve.

Muskegon will join the small but growing list of Essential Air Service communities that are now connected with nonstop flights to the state of Florida, but they will be the only EAS community in Michigan to have Florida flights.

#6233. Pentagon's top spies tasked with 'no-fail' mission as Hegseth puts foreign midterm meddling in crosshairs

President Donald Trump adds campaign stops in Iowa and Kansas after previously canceling them. Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt discusses the president’s 2026 midterm campaign blitz and the administration’s energy policy.

Ever since the 2016 presidential election that first got President Donald Trump elected and the ensuing Russiagate scandal, there has been increased scrutiny on foreign meddling in U.S. elections and threats to the American voting system.

Now, 10 years later, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is directing his entire intelligence and spy forces to ensure foreign adversaries do not interfere in Tuesday's midterms.

The Pentagon chief has ordered America's military intelligence and cyber agencies to mobilize against foreign threats to the 2026 elections by directing his department's sprawling intelligence apparatus to make election security a priority in what he calls a "no-fail mission."

The September directive reaches beyond U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency, instructing the entire Defense Intelligence Enterprise — including agencies responsible for military and geospatial intelligence — to "mobilize every authorized asset, capability, and partnership" against foreign election threats.

HOW TO WATCH CRITICAL 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RACES IN TX, OH, MI, WI, GA, IA, NV, ME AND FL

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth addressed reporters during a Pentagon news conference in Arlington, Virginia, on June 26, 2025. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The order puts some of the military's most sophisticated intelligence capabilities behind a mission that has grown considerably since Russia's interference in the 2016 presidential election. But with Americans preparing to vote, the extent to which Hegseth's directive has changed the Pentagon's existing election-security operations remains unclear.

The Department of War declined to provide Fox News Digital with additional details about how the order is being implemented. Cyber Command separately declined an interview request about its election-security efforts.

In practice, the directive can mean military intelligence agencies are tasked with identifying foreign hackers or influence operations overseas, warning civilian agencies about threats headed toward U.S. targets and, when authorized, Cyber Command taking action against the foreign actors or infrastructure behind them.

The military's role largely stops at the U.S. border: state and local officials run elections, while agencies such as the FBI and Department of Homeland Security handle the domestic side.

The Pentagon's election security mission is not new. Cyber Command and NSA have spent years tracking and disrupting foreign threats around American elections, including operations targeting Russian actors during previous election cycles.

The effort began taking its current shape ahead of the 2018 midterms, when the agencies formed a "Russia Small Group" focused on foreign interference. It later evolved into a joint Election Security Group, combining NSA's intelligence-gathering capabilities with Cyber Command's ability to conduct operations against foreign cyber threats.

An election official sorts ballots during early voting, Oct. 28, 2025, in Portland, Maine. (Robert F. Bukaty/AP)

By 2022, then-Cyber Command and NSA chief Gen. Paul Nakasone was describing election security as an "enduring, no-fail mission" — language echoed by Hegseth four years later.

"Rest assured, we were doing operations well before the midterms began, and we were doing operations likely on the day of the midterms," Nakasone said after the 2022 election, describing the military's role as "understanding your foreign adversaries and operating outside the United States."

The agencies again established an Election Security Group for the 2024 presidential election, but whether that structure was recreated for this year's midterms has been less clear.

Gen. Joshua Rudd, the current head of Cyber Command and NSA, told lawmakers in April that foreign interference was "reasonable to expect based on what we've seen in the past" and said his command was "postured and ready to support as required or tasked." He said at the time that he was unsure whether the Election Security Group had been reconvened.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

Five months later, Hegseth issued his department-wide directive, addressed not only to Cyber Command and NSA but also to the directors of the Defense Intelligence Agency and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

The order instructs military intelligence agencies to collect and analyze intelligence on foreign election threats while directing Cyber Command to use its existing authorities and capabilities to counter potential foreign cyber activity in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.

It does not publicly grant new authorities or establish a new election-security organization, instead reinforcing a mission the military has increasingly treated as an enduring responsibility.

U.S. intelligence officials, meanwhile, say they have seen no evidence that a foreign adversary has attempted to interfere with voting machines, physical election infrastructure or the counting of votes ahead of Tuesday's midterms.

Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, said last week that intelligence officials continue to see nothing contradicting that assessment, but urged Americans to remain "on high alert" for foreign disinformation, particularly as artificial intelligence makes such campaigns easier to spread.

But officials continue to track foreign influence efforts from Russia, China and Iran, with Russia remaining the most active foreign influence threat, CNN reported Sunday.

In this photo illustration, the names of the presidential candidates, including former President Donald Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris, appear on a vote-by-mail ballot on Oct. 2, 2024, in Miami, Florida (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

U.S. elections are attractive targets for foreign adversaries because the stakes extend far beyond who wins office: influencing American voters or undermining confidence in the process can shape U.S. policy, weaken public support for policies they oppose and deepen divisions without ever touching a voting machine.

Lawmakers briefed on classified intelligence last month said Russia was using disinformation to target candidates and undermine confidence in the election, while China's influence efforts were more narrowly focused on candidates viewed as hostile to Beijing.

The Pentagon's role focuses on threats originating overseas, while state and local officials administer elections and civilian federal agencies lead domestic election-security efforts.

Hegseth's directive makes that overseas mission a priority across the broader military intelligence enterprise, though the Pentagon has not disclosed whether it has resulted in additional personnel, resources or organizational changes ahead of Election Day.
